sections/machine-learning/concepts/embed.title: Embedding
sections/machine-learning/concepts/embed.content:
Embedding
A token’s vector — and the space it lives in, where directions carry meaning. Everything a transformer does is expressed as edits to positions in this space.
flowchart LR
  T[Token] --> WE[W_E lookup — one column per vocabulary item]
  WE --> V[A vector encoding that token and nothing else]
  P[Position, encoded in the same vector] --> V
  V --> A[Attention and MLP blocks edit the position]
  A --> C[A vector that has soaked up the surrounding context]
  C --> WU[W_U unembedding — one value per vocabulary token]
  WU --> L[Logits]
  L --> S[Softmax — a distribution over next tokens]
  CS[Context size — the attention pattern is its square] -->|a hard ceiling| A

The reason it exists at all is mundane: training only works on continuous values, so language has to be encoded as numbers. What makes it interesting is that the encoding is learned, and the geometry that emerges is legible.
The lookup table is only the starting point
The first matrix, W_E, has one column per vocabulary item — in GPT-3, 50,257 columns × 12,288 dimensions = 617,558,016 weights. At that moment a vector encodes one token and nothing else: “effectively a lookup table with no input from the surroundings.”
The network’s whole job is to stop that being true. transformers-tech-behind-llms-deep-learn frames it as the primary goal: let each vector “soak up meaning that is more rich and specific than what mere individual words can represent.” A vector that began as king can end up encoding a king who lived in Scotland, who took the throne by murdering his predecessor, described in Shakespearean language.
attention-transformers-step-by-step-deep gives the sharpest version of the requirement: feed in a mystery novel ending “Therefore the murderer was…” and the final vector, which started life embedding was, must have absorbed everything in the context relevant to the answer — because it is the only vector used for the prediction.


                  
                  What is a token's vector at the moment it leaves the embedding matrix? 
                  
                

A lookup with no input from its surroundings — it encodes that token and nothing else. Everything that follows exists to make that stop being true.




                  
                  Why must the last vector in a mystery novel carry the whole plot?
                  
                

Because it is the only vector used for the prediction. A vector that started life embedding “was” has to have absorbed everything in the context relevant to naming the murderer.


Directions have meaning, and the dot product tests them

Nearest neighbours of tower share a recognisable character.
woman − man ≈ king − queen. Sanderson immediately qualifies the classic example: in the model he used, queen sits farther off than the difference predicts, “presumably because the way queen is used in training data is not merely a feminine version of a king.” Family relations demonstrate it better.
Italy − Germany + Hitler lands near Mussolini — some directions apparently encode Italian-ness, others Axis leadership.



                  
                  Why does Sanderson qualify the king − man + woman ≈ queen example?
                  
                

In the model he used, queen sits farther off than the difference predicts — presumably because queen is not used in training data as merely a feminine king. Family relations demonstrate the property more cleanly.


The dot product turns a hunch about a direction into a measurement: positive when aligned, zero when perpendicular, negative when opposed. Take cats − cat as a candidate plurality direction and dot it against nouns — plurals score consistently higher, and one, two, three, four give increasing values, “as if it’s quantitatively measuring how plural the model finds a given word.”


                  
                  How do you test whether a direction in embedding space means what you think? 
                  
                

Dot it against words you have opinions about. Take cats − cat as a candidate plurality direction and plurals score higher; one through four give increasing values, which is the direction measuring degree rather than just membership.


This is the machinery every later block reuses: attention-transformers-step-by-step-deep scores key–query alignment by dot product, and might-llms-store-facts-deep-learning reads MLP rows as directions whose dot product with a vector asks a question about it.
Position is in there too
Embeddings also encode where a token sits, so a single vector’s entries tell you both what the word is and where it is in the context.
Context size is a hard ceiling
GPT-3’s context was 2048 tokens, so the data flowing through is a 2048-column array of ~12k-dimensional vectors. That limit is named as the direct cause of long early-ChatGPT conversations feeling as though the bot lost the thread — and because the attention pattern is the square of the context size, enlarging it is nontrivial.


                  
                  Why is enlarging the context window not simply a matter of allocating more memory? 
                  
                

The attention pattern is the square of the context size. Doubling the window quadruples that cost, which is why the limit that made early ChatGPT lose the thread was hard to lift.


Unembedding, and how many predictions get made
W_U maps the last vector to ~50,000 values, one per token — the same shape as W_E with rows and columns swapped, another ~617M parameters. Those raw unnormalised values are the logits; softmax turns them into a distribution.
Using only the final vector looks wasteful given thousands of context-rich vectors sitting in that layer. The reason is training efficiency: every vector in the final layer simultaneously predicts what follows it, so one passage acts as many training examples. attention-transformers-step-by-step-deep shows this is also why masking is required — later tokens must not leak backwards into earlier predictions.


                  
                  What are logits, and what turns them into a prediction? 
                  
                

The raw unnormalised values the unembedding matrix produces, one per vocabulary token. Softmax converts them into a probability distribution.




                  
                  Every final-layer vector predicts what follows it. What does that buy, and what does it require? 
                  
                

It buys training efficiency — one passage becomes many training examples. It requires masking, because a prediction made at an early position must not see the later tokens that would give away its answer.


How many meanings can a space hold?
More than its dimension count, and that turns out to matter enormously. See superposition.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/estim.title: Estimation and Uncertainty
sections/machine-learning/concepts/estim.content:
Estimation and Uncertainty
super-vip-cheatsheet-machine-learning places parameter estimation between probability definitions and machine-learning algorithms. A sample statistic estimates an unknown population quantity: the sample mean targets expectation, and sample variance targets dispersion.
flowchart LR
  P[Unknown population quantity] --> S[Sample statistic]
  S --> B[Sampling bias]
  S --> V[Sampling variance]
  S --> D[Approximate sampling distribution]
  D --> E[Standard error model]
  E --> C[Confidence interval]
  C --> M[Match precision claims to data generation]



                  
                  How do estimator bias and sampling variance differ? 
                  
                

Bias is the expected offset from the target; variance is how estimates change across possible datasets.




                  
                  What does a frequentist confidence interval describe? 
                  
                

Repeated-sampling coverage, not the probability that a fixed parameter lies in one realized interval.


Estimator bias is the difference between an estimator’s expected value and the parameter it targets. Sampling variance describes how much the estimate changes across possible datasets. These are properties of a sampling procedure, not of one observed number, and they underlie the bias-variance-tradeoff in predictive modelling.
The central limit theorem motivates an approximately normal sampling distribution for suitably normalized sums or means under its conditions. Confidence intervals combine an estimate with a standard-error model to express repeated-sampling coverage. They are not the probability that a fixed parameter lies in one realized interval under a frequentist interpretation.
The cheatsheet is a compact formula reference and does not enumerate all regularity assumptions. Dependence, heavy tails, selection, small samples, and model misspecification can invalidate routine approximations. Reported precision must therefore match the data-generating process rather than merely a memorized formula.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/evalu.title: Evaluation Metrics
sections/machine-learning/concepts/evalu.content:
Evaluation Metrics
Every claim a machine learning system makes about itself is a claim about a metric. Since each metric encodes a decision about which errors matter, choosing one is a modelling decision rather than a reporting formality.
flowchart TD
  Q[What decision must the metric support] --> C[Classification errors]
  Q --> R[Regression fit]
  Q --> G[Generated text quality]
  Q --> K[Ranking quality]
  Q --> P[Component behaviour]
  P --> E[End-to-end outcome]



                  
                  Why is choosing a metric a modelling decision rather than a reporting one? 
                  
                

Each metric encodes a judgement about which errors matter. Picking one has already decided what the system is allowed to get wrong.


The classical core
vip-cheatsheet-machine-learning-tips-tricks supplies the 2018 CS229 foundation the rest of this page extends. It names the error types (false negatives are Type II, false positives are Type I), tabulates accuracy/precision/recall/specificity/F₁ against their interpretations, and gives the ROC equivalences explicitly: TPR = recall = sensitivity, FPR = 1 − specificity. Its description of F₁ is exactly right and rarely stated so plainly — “a hybrid metric useful for unbalanced classes,” which is a claim about when to use it, not just what it is.
For regression it insists on the model-selection criteria that penalise parameter count — Mallow’s Cₚ, AIC, BIC, adjusted R². Fit alone is not evidence.
No ground truth is the hard case. vip-cheatsheet-unsupervised-learning states the problem it cannot solve: “it is often hard to assess the performance of a model since we don’t have the ground truth labels.” Its substitutes — the silhouette coefficient and the Calinski-Harabaz index — measure whether clusters are dense and well separated, which is a property of the partition, not of its correctness. The metric answers a question adjacent to the one being asked. That gap is the same one Reward-Model lives in.


                  
                  What do clustering metrics like the silhouette coefficient actually measure? 
                  
                

Whether the clusters are dense and well separated — a property of the partition, not of its correctness. With no ground truth available, the metric answers a question adjacent to the one being asked.


Classification: the confusion matrix and its readings
Accuracy, precision, recall, F₁, sensitivity, specificity, negative predictive value, ROC, AUROC, equal error rate, DET curves — all derived from the same four cells, differing in what they divide by.
amans-ai-journal-primers-evaluation-metrics devotes a section to precision/recall vs. sensitivity/specificity, which is right: they are the same matrix read by two communities with different denominators, and the confusion between them is where a large share of metric errors originate.


                  
                  Why is precision/recall confused with sensitivity/specificity so often? 
                  
                

They are the same confusion matrix read by two communities using different denominators. The cells are identical; only what each figure is divided by differs.


The primer also treats when F₁ becomes misleading under negative-class imbalance — the case where a healthy-looking score is measuring the wrong thing entirely. Its medical-diagnosis worked example makes the underlying point concrete: a false negative and a false positive are not comparable events, and no single number can pretend they are.


                  
                  What does the medical-diagnosis example establish about single-number scores? 
                  
                

That a false negative and a false positive are not comparable events. A missed diagnosis and a false alarm cost different things, and any single number has already assumed they cost the same.


Generative text: two instruments, two questions

Perplexity — how well the model predicts held-out data.
Burstiness — the diversity and variability of its output.

They answer different questions, which is the reason to carry both. A model can score well on perplexity while repeating itself endlessly; burstiness catches that and perplexity cannot.


                  
                  What failure does perplexity miss that burstiness catches? 
                  
                

Endless repetition. A model can predict held-out data well while producing no variety at all, so a good perplexity score says nothing about the diversity of what it generates.



BLEU — precision-oriented n-gram overlap, built for translation.
ROUGE / ROUGE-L — recall-oriented, built for summarisation. More reference sentences always improve the estimate.
BERTScore — embedding similarity instead of n-gram overlap, so paraphrase stops being penalised as error.



                  
                  Why is BLEU precision-oriented and ROUGE recall-oriented? 
                  
                

Because of the tasks they were built for. Translation asks whether what was produced is correct — precision. Summarisation asks whether what mattered was kept — recall.




                  
                  What error does BERTScore stop punishing? 
                  
                

Paraphrase. Scoring by embedding similarity rather than n-gram overlap means a correct answer in different words is no longer counted as wrong.


Each domain has its own family: regression, object detection, generative images, GANs, speech, clustering, code generation, compression, recommender systems. The breadth is itself the argument — there is no single number.
The primer’s major families now have focused graph pages:

classification-error-tradeoffs — denominators, thresholds, and asymmetric errors
regression-loss-geometry — absolute, squared, relative, and variance-based summaries
reference-based-text-evaluation — lexical overlap versus semantic similarity
rank-aware-evaluation — relevance, position, normalisation, and beyond-accuracy goals

Measure the components, not just the system
amans-ai-journal-primers-retrieval-augmented insists on evaluating retrieval and generation separately. A RAG system that answers badly may have retrieved perfectly and generated poorly, or retrieved garbage and generated from it faithfully. The aggregate score cannot distinguish them, and the two failures call for opposite fixes.
When the metric is itself a model
rlhf-reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedbackrlhf pushes this to its limit. The Reward-Model is a metric — a learned one, fit to comparisons rather than derived from a formula — and it inherits every property of a metric plus some new ones:

Its ceiling is the agreement of the people who produced its data: roughly 73% inter-labeler agreement.
It is only valid where it has seen data, and the policy being trained actively searches for the regions where it is wrong. Hence the KL penalty pinning the policy near its starting point.
Human preference is not a single function. Huyen prefers the losing response in a published example and says so — the metric is averaging a disagreement, not approximating a fact.



                  
                  What does a learned metric inherit that a formula-defined one does not? 
                  
                

A training distribution. It is only valid where it has seen data — and unlike a formula, an optimiser can be pointed at the regions where it is wrong.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/explo.title: Exploration vs. Exploitation
sections/machine-learning/concepts/explo.content:
Exploration vs. Exploitation
An agent that only exploits what already works never finds anything better. An agent that only explores never banks anything. amans-ai-journal-primers-reinforcement-learning calls the balance one of the most fundamental challenges in reinforcement learning and says plainly that optimal balancing remains an open problem.
flowchart LR
  U[Under-exploration — a sub-optimal policy locked in] --- K[One knob — epsilon, UCB, Thompson sampling, temperature]
  K --- O[Over-exploration — effort spent on actions that yield nothing]
  K --> C[Exploration costs samples, often millions of interactions]
  C --> D[Disqualifying where each interaction costs money, time or hardware]
  R[RLHF inverts it — the policy explores too eagerly] --> P[A KL penalty against the SFT policy constrains exploration]

The two failure directions

Over-exploration — effort spent on actions that yield nothing.
Under-exploration — a sub-optimal policy locked in because a better one was never tried.

The standard attacks are ε-greedy (act randomly with probability ε), upper-confidence-bound algorithms (prefer actions whose value is uncertain), and Thompson sampling (sample from a posterior over action values). All are heuristics for a problem with no general solution.


                  
                  What does an upper-confidence-bound method prefer, and why is that exploration? 
                  
                

Actions whose value is uncertain, not merely high. Uncertainty is where new information lives, so favouring it buys knowledge rather than immediate return.


Why it is expensive rather than merely hard
Exploration costs samples, and amans-ai-journal-primers-reinforcement-learning identifies sample inefficiency as the practical blocker on real deployment: state-of-the-art methods can require millions of environment interactions. Where each interaction costs money, time, or hardware — robotics, healthcare, autonomous driving — exploring is not merely slow but disqualifying. Experience replay helps and does not solve it.


                  
                  Why does sample inefficiency disqualify RL in robotics or healthcare rather than merely slow it? 
                  
                

Because each interaction has a real cost in money, time or hardware. Methods needing millions of environment interactions are unaffordable in those settings, not just protracted.


Sparse and delayed rewards make it worse. When success arrives only after a long sequence of actions, the agent may need very many trials just to stumble onto the sequence once, and then still has to work out which action mattered.


                  
                  What two separate difficulties does a sparse, delayed reward create? 
                  
                

Finding the rewarded sequence at all, which may take very many trials, and then working out which of its actions earned the reward. Discovery and credit assignment are distinct problems.


The formal setting, compressed
vip-cheatsheet-deep-learning gives the machinery in half a page: a Markov-Decision-Process as (S, A, {P_sa}, γ, R), the value function, the optimal Bellman equation, value iteration, and Q-learning as the model-free update

Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[R(s,a,s′) + γ·max_a′ Q(s′,a′) − Q(s,a)]

The max in that update is exploitation, stated in one symbol. What the formula does not contain — and what ε-greedy, UCB and Thompson sampling are all bolted on to supply — is any account of how the agent finds the actions worth maximising over. The exploration problem is precisely the part the equation leaves out.
The data consequences depend on on-vs-off-policy-learning. On-policy methods must explore with the policy being improved and rapidly age out old experience; off-policy methods can reuse trajectories from another behaviour policy, but inherit distribution-mismatch and stability problems.


                  
                  Where is exploration in the Q-learning update? 
                  
                

Nowhere. The max is exploitation stated in one symbol; nothing in the equation says how the agent finds actions worth maximising over. ε-greedy, UCB and Thompson sampling are all bolted on to supply exactly that gap.


The same knob, elsewhere in the field
Sampling temperature. unreasonable-effectiveness-recurrent-neural-networks gives the cleanest demonstration outside RL. Lowering the softmax temperature makes a language model more confident and more conservative; raising it yields more diversity at the cost of more errors. Karpathy shows both extremes — near-zero temperature collapses into a literal infinite loop about startups, while higher temperatures produce novelty and misspellings. Exploration and exploitation, exposed as a single scalar.


                  
                  What happens to generated text at near-zero sampling temperature, and why? 
                  
                

It collapses into a literal infinite loop. Always taking the most confident token is pure exploitation, so the model re-enters the same state and repeats — Karpathy’s example loops endlessly about startups.


Agent trial-and-error. llm-powered-autonomous-agents-lillog describes Reflexion resetting the environment when a heuristic judges the trajectory inefficient — an explicit decision to stop exploiting a bad path and explore another. Weng’s limitation carries the cost: LLMs struggle to revise a plan after an unexpected error, which is a failure to explore at the moment exploration is required.
RLHF’s KL penalty. rlhf-reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedbackrlhf shows the trade-off inverted. The policy is too eager to explore — it will find the regions where the Reward-Model is mistakenly generous. The KL term against the SFT policy is a deliberate constraint on exploration, keeping the model inside the space where its reward signal can be trusted. Here exploitation is not the failure mode; unconstrained exploration is.


                  
                  Where does the exploration/exploitation trade-off invert, and why? 
                  
                

In RLHF. Because the reward signal is only trustworthy near the training distribution, unconstrained exploration finds the reward model’s mistakes — so the KL penalty deliberately limits exploring rather than encouraging it.


Sample efficiency as a research frontier. ai-agents-depth-design-principles-engineering devotes a section of its post-training chapter to improving sample efficiency, and states the priority bluntly: data and environment matter more than algorithms. Exploration is expensive, so what you explore in is the lever.


                  
                  If exploration is expensive, what is the lever Li says matters most? 
                  
                

The environment and data, over the algorithm. Since every sample costs, the thing you explore in determines the return on exploring more than the rule choosing what to try.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/gradi.title: Gradient Descent
sections/machine-learning/concepts/gradi.content:
Gradient Descent
One update rule, applied to nearly everything in this section:

θ ← θ − α∇J(θ)

Move the parameters against the gradient of the cost, at a pace set by the learning rate α. vip-cheatsheet-supervised-learning introduces it once and then reuses it for linear regression, logistic regression and neural networks without restating it — which is the correct emphasis. The model is the loss and the hypothesis class; the optimiser is shared.
flowchart TD
  B[Take a batch] --> F[Forward propagate to obtain the loss]
  F --> G[Backpropagate — the chain rule, for the gradients]
  G --> U[Update — the parameters move against the gradient at rate alpha]
  U --> B
  S[Batch size — a full batch, or one example per update in SGD] --> B
  A[Alpha schedule — fixed, or adaptive per parameter as in Adam] --> U
  N[Newton's method — second order, far fewer steps] -->|the Hessian is unaffordable at scale| U
  U --> R[A point where the gradient vanishes in its basin — nothing global]



                  
                  What distinguishes one model from another, if they all share the same optimiser? 
                  
                

The loss and the hypothesis class. Linear regression, logistic regression and a neural network differ in what they are fitting and what they are penalised for — the update rule is the same for all three.


Batch size changes the gradient estimate

Batch gradient descent — update on a batch of examples.
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) — update per training example.

This is one important axis, not the only meaningful variant. Momentum changes the update state; adaptive optimisers such as RMSProp and Adam rescale coordinates using gradient history; schedules change α over time. vip-cheatsheet-deep-learning names Adam as the then-current standard, while unreasonable-effectiveness-recurrent-neural-networks reports RMSProp or Adam specifically “to stabilize the updates.”


                  
                  What is Adam or RMSProp chosen for in practice? 
                  
                

Stability, not speed. Per-parameter adaptive rates keep updates from blowing up, which is the reason Karpathy gives for using them.


Backpropagation is not a different algorithm
It is the chain rule, applied to get the gradients a layered model needs:

∂L(z,y)/∂w = (∂L/∂a)(∂a/∂z)(∂z/∂w)

and then the same update, w ← w − η·∂L/∂w. vip-cheatsheet-deep-learning gives the loop in four steps: take a batch, forward propagate to obtain the loss, backpropagate to get the gradients, use the gradients to update the weights.
The second-order alternative
Newton’s method finds θ with ℓ′(θ) = 0 via θ ← θ − ℓ′(θ)/ℓ″(θ), generalising to Newton-Raphson with the Hessian: θ ← θ − (∇²ℓ)⁻¹∇ℓ. It can converge in fewer local iterations, but explicitly forming and inverting a Hessian at modern parameter counts is generally unaffordable. This is why large-scale deep-learning optimisers are predominantly first-order, not a guarantee that Newton updates always converge faster or that second-order information is never approximated.


                  
                  Newton's method converges in far fewer steps. Why is deep learning first-order anyway? 
                  
                

The Hessian. Forming and inverting a second-derivative matrix over a modern network’s parameter count is unaffordable, and that single cost is why the whole field stays first-order.


Where the identities come from
matrix-calculus-for-learning collects the gradient, Hessian, trace, and matrix-derivative identities that the compiled sheet supplies for the normal equations θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, Newton-Raphson, and backpropagation. It also preserves the source’s limit: the sheet is a compact identity reference, not a derivation of every validity condition.
What it does not guarantee
Nothing about global optimality. It finds a point where the gradient vanishes in whatever basin it started in. That this works as well as it does on non-convex objectives is an empirical fact the field relies on and does not fully explain — and it is the mechanism by which scaling-beats-knowledge-engineering operates, since gradient descent over more data and more parameters is exactly the “learning” half of Sutton’s two scalable methods.


                  
                  What does gradient descent actually guarantee about the point it reaches? 
                  
                

Only that the gradient vanishes there, within whatever basin it started in. Nothing about global optimality — that it works on non-convex objectives is an empirical fact the field relies on without fully explaining.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/harne.title: Harness Engineering
sections/machine-learning/concepts/harne.content:
Harness Engineering
ai-agents-depth-design-principles-engineering names the thing that separates an agent demo from an agent product. Take the LLM as one component — the Model — and call everything built around it the Harness:
flowchart TD
  A[Agent system] --> M[Model]
  A --> H[Harness]
  H --> C[Context]
  H --> T[Tools]
  H --> N[Constrain]
  H --> V[Verify]
  H --> R[Correct]


Agent = LLM + [Context + Tools + Constrain + Verify + Correct] = Model + Harness

The first two bracketed terms are the original formula Agent = LLM + Context + Tools. The three added are safeguards: Constrain (what the agent may and may not do), Verify (whether it did the thing correctly), Correct (how to recover when it did not).


                  
                  What three terms does the harness add to Agent = LLM + Context + Tools?
                  
                

Constrain, Verify and Correct — what the agent may do, whether it did it correctly, and how to recover when it did not. The first two terms describe capability; these three describe reliability.


What it is a response to
Bojie Li’s framing is empirical rather than architectural. The basic ReAct loop demonstrably works — and is fragile in specific, enumerable ways: the model hallucinates tools or parameters that do not exist, picks the wrong tool, or cannot recover from an error. Those three failures are what the harness exists to absorb.


                  
                  Which three failures of the bare ReAct loop does a harness exist to absorb? 
                  
                

Hallucinating tools or parameters that do not exist, picking the wrong tool, and being unable to recover from an error.


The consequence follows: once competing systems have access to comparable models, the harness is where the difference lives. Li deliberately says “Model” rather than “LLM” here, because the principles apply to anything that can reason and call tools.


                  
                  Once competitors have comparable models, where does the difference between their agents live? 
                  
                

In the harness. The model becomes a commodity component; what is built around it — constraints, verification, recovery — is what still differs.


The same observation, three times
The section holds three independent statements of this:

llm-powered-autonomous-agents-lillog — “the reliability of model outputs is questionable, as LLMs may make formatting errors and occasionally exhibit rebellious behavior. Consequently, much of the agent demo code focuses on parsing model output.” Weng identifies the symptom in 2023 without naming the discipline.
amans-ai-journal-primers-agents — the workflow/agent distinction is a harness decision: how much of the control flow is code a human wrote versus decisions the model makes at run time.
ai-agents-depth-design-principles-engineering — names it, gives it an equation, and devotes the book to it.

The deepened primer turns those safeguards into three design surfaces. agent-control-boundary decides which transitions remain deterministic; tool-interface-design makes actions legible, bounded, validated, and recoverable; reflection-evaluator-loop adds critique and external checks instead of trusting a single pass. These are concrete harness choices, not extra model capabilities.
Evidence that it cannot be patched in later
Li cites the 2025 MAST study, which annotated ~150 execution traces across MetaGPT, ChatDev, AG2 and Magentic-One (inter-annotator κ = 0.88) and found 14 failure modes in three groups: system design flaws, inter-agent alignment failures, and missing task verification. Applying simple fixes gained ChatDev only 15.6%, and the authors concluded these are fundamental design flaws rather than bugs — patching one component is not enough, the system design must be rethought.
That third group is the harness’s Verify layer, absent. A system where an agent can report “completed” without any mechanism to confirm the result meets requirements has a hole no amount of prompt tuning closes.


                  
                  What does MAST's "missing task verification" group correspond to in harness terms? 
                  
                

The Verify layer, absent. An agent that can report “completed” with nothing checking the result against requirements has a hole prompt tuning cannot close.


Li adds two failure modes from engineering practice that the MAST taxonomy (focused on dialogue-based collaboration) does not cover: concurrency conflicts when multiple agents share a file system, and cascading amplification of errors across agents.
single-vs-multi-agent-economics explains why these costs appear at all: every new agent boundary serializes context and creates another coordination and verification surface. Multi-agent architecture earns that burden only when decomposition or independent checking produces measured gains.


                  
                  Which two multi-agent failures does MAST's dialogue-focused taxonomy miss? 
                  
                

Concurrency conflicts when several agents share a file system, and cascading amplification of an error across agents. Both come from engineering practice rather than from conversation traces.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/hybri.title: Hybrid Retrieval
sections/machine-learning/concepts/hybri.content:
Hybrid Retrieval
Hybrid retrieval combines signals that fail differently. amans-ai-journal-primers-retrieval-augmented contrasts lexical methods such as TF-IDF or BM25, dense embedding similarity, graph relationships, structured SQL, and metadata filtering.
flowchart LR
  L[Sparse lexical channel] --> P[Pooled candidates]
  D[Dense semantic channel] --> P
  G[Graph or relational channel] --> P
  M[Metadata and permission filters] --> P
  P --> F[Normalize scores or fuse ranks]
  F --> R[Rerank with richer matching]
  R --> E[Evidence set for generation]



                  
                  Why combine sparse and dense retrieval? 
                  
                

They fail differently: sparse retrieval preserves exact terms, while dense retrieval catches paraphrases.




                  
                  What happens after hybrid retrieval pools candidates from several channels? 
                  
                

Scores are normalized or rank-fused before the candidates are reranked.


Sparse lexical retrieval preserves exact names, rare terms, and identifiers but misses paraphrases. Dense retrieval finds semantic neighbours but can return plausible yet irrelevant passages. Graph or relational paths exploit explicit entities and constraints but depend on extracted structure and query formulation. Metadata filters enforce tenant, date, document type, or access boundaries before or after scoring.
A hybrid system retrieves from several channels, normalizes or rank-fuses their scores, and passes a pooled candidate set to reranking. The union can improve recall only if one channel recovers what another misses; naive concatenation can instead multiply duplicates and noise.
Boundary
The primer’s early suggestion that graph retrieval requires exact matching is an oversimplification, and vector-plus-graph systems do exist within the broader period covered by the evolving primer. The durable concept is complementary evidence signals, not a fixed database taxonomy.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/long-.title: Long-Term Dependency
sections/machine-learning/concepts/long-.content:
Long-Term Dependency
When the information needed to make a prediction sits far back in the sequence from the point where it is needed. It is the organising problem of sequence modelling, and most of the architectural history of the field is a series of answers to it.
flowchart LR
  D[Distant information must affect a later prediction] --> R[Plain recurrent path carries many steps]
  R --> L[LSTM gates preserve selected state]
  L --> A[Attention creates direct access across positions]
  A --> C[Distance cost becomes total context cost]
  D --> P[Delayed reward creates the same credit-assignment shape]

The two sentences
understanding-lstm-networks-colahs-blog states it with a minimal pair:

“The clouds are in the ___” — the answer is sky, and everything needed is right there.
“I grew up in France… I speak fluent ___” — recent words say the answer is a language. Which language is determined by a word that may be arbitrarily far back.

As that gap grows, vanilla recurrent networks stop being able to bridge it. The crucial detail is that this is a practical failure, not a theoretical one: RNNs are perfectly capable of representing such dependencies, and a human can hand-pick parameters that solve toy versions. They just do not learn them, for reasons established by Hochreiter (1991) and Bengio et al. (1994).


                  
                  Why is the RNN long-dependency failure practical rather than theoretical? 
                  
                

RNNs can represent such dependencies — a human can hand-pick parameters that solve toy versions. What fails is learning them by gradient descent, not representing them.


Three answers, in order
Gating. The LSTM adds a cell state that information traverses unchanged unless a gate deliberately alters it, inverting the default from decay to persistence. This bought roughly a decade of progress.
Attention. self-attention does not shorten the path; it deletes it. Every position reaches every other in one hop, so distance stops mattering entirely. What replaces it is a quadratic cost in total sequence length — the Transformer does not solve long-range dependency so much as convert it from a depth problem into a width problem, which is why the finite context window is now the binding constraint.


                  
                  In what sense does attention convert the long-dependency problem rather than solve it?
                  
                

It turns a depth problem into a width problem. Distance becomes free, and total sequence length becomes the cost — which is why the finite context window is now the binding constraint.


Retrieval. When the dependency exceeds any feasible context window, put it outside the model: Retrieval-Augmented-Generation, or the external vector store the agent literature calls long-term memory. Weng’s caveat carries the trade honestly — a vector store extends reach, but its representational power is weaker than full attention.
The same problem in reinforcement learning
amans-ai-journal-primers-reinforcement-learning describes credit assignment under sparse and delayed rewards: when success arrives only after many steps, identifying which early action earned it is genuinely hard. That is long-term dependency with a reward signal instead of a token — same structure, same difficulty. temporal-difference-bootstrap shortens the feedback path by updating from an observed reward plus a successor estimate, while reward shaping and eligibility traces supply other partial bridges. None is a general solution.


                  
                  How is RL credit assignment the same problem as long-term dependency? 
                  
                

Both ask which distant thing accounts for something here — an early action for a late reward, an early word for a late prediction. Same structure, and the mitigations rhyme: reward shaping and eligibility traces where sequence models use gating.


Evidence that models do learn it
unreasonable-effectiveness-recurrent-neural-networks shows LSTM cells tracking state across long spans: one that switches on inside a URL and off outside, one giving a position-in-scope coordinate across a [[ ]] environment, one counting through “www”. Karpathy’s samples also show where it breaks — the generated C code has correct local syntax and functions that return values despite a void signature, which he identifies as a long-range interaction failure. Fluent in form, wrong across distance.


                  
                  What does a void function that returns a value diagnose in generated code?
                  
                

A long-range interaction failure. The local syntax is correct because it depends on nearby tokens; the signature is far enough back that the model no longer holds it. Fluent in form, wrong across distance.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/matri.title: Matrix Calculus for Learning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/matri.content:
Matrix Calculus for Learning
Matrix calculus expresses how scalar objectives change with vector or matrix parameters. super-vip-cheatsheet-machine-learning collects the gradient, Hessian, trace, determinant, transpose, and inverse identities repeatedly used across linear models, PCA, Newton-style optimization, and neural-network backpropagation.
flowchart TD
  O[Scalar objective] --> G[Gradient — first-order sensitivity]
  O --> H[Hessian — local curvature]
  G --> D[Choose a descent direction]
  H --> S[Rescale a step by curvature]
  T[Trace and matrix identities] --> C[Compact differentiable forms]
  C --> G



                  
                  How do a gradient and a Hessian differ? 
                  
                

The gradient gives first-order sensitivity; the Hessian describes local curvature through second derivatives.




                  
                  Why can a matrix-calculus identity sheet not prove an optimizer is well behaved? 
                  
                

Shape, invertibility and regularity conditions still have to hold.


For a scalar-valued function, the gradient has the shape of the parameter and records first-order sensitivity. The Hessian collects second derivatives and describes local curvature; positive semidefiniteness links curvature to convexity under appropriate conditions. Trace identities often turn sums and quadratic forms into expressions that differentiate compactly.
These operations connect to gradient-descent: the gradient selects a local descent direction, while Hessian information can rescale a step according to curvature. Eigendecomposition and singular-value decomposition connect linear algebra to principal components, rank, and stable factorization.
Boundary
A sheet of identities cannot replace shape checks or regularity conditions. Gradients require a scalar output in the convention used by the source; inverses require nonsingularity; Hessian-based conclusions are local; and equivalent-looking numerator- versus denominator-layout conventions can transpose results. The refresher is a navigation aid for derivations, not a proof that an optimization problem is well behaved.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/multi.title: Multi-Hop Retrieval Planning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/multi.content:
Multi-Hop Retrieval Planning
A multi-hop question contains evidence dependencies: the first result identifies an entity, relation, or constraint needed to formulate the next query. amans-ai-journal-primers-retrieval-augmented explains why one-shot RAG fails here—the original query may not directly resemble every supporting passage.
flowchart LR
  Q[Original multi-hop question] --> D[Decompose the first information need]
  D --> R[Retrieve evidence]
  R --> U[Update entities relations and unresolved variables]
  U --> N[Construct the next query]
  N --> R
  U --> S[Synthesize only when the evidence chain closes]



                  
                  Why can one-shot retrieval fail on a multi-hop question? 
                  
                

The original query may not resemble passages whose identity is only revealed by an earlier result.




                  
                  Why must a multi-hop system retain provenance at every hop? 
                  
                

An early wrong entity can redirect every later search while leaving a fluent final answer.


The system decomposes the question into intermediate information needs, retrieves for the first need, updates state with the evidence, and constructs the next query. A final answer is synthesized only after the chain connects the original question to supporting passages. Hierarchical retrieval is a constrained form in which hops move from document to section to chunk.
Each hop introduces branching and error propagation. A wrong entity in step one can redirect all later retrieval; a fluent final answer may hide a broken chain. Systems need per-hop provenance, explicit unresolved variables, evidence deduplication, and a stopping condition based on support rather than a fixed number of searches.
agentic-retrieval-routing can choose sources and hops dynamically, while a deterministic planner can encode known dependency patterns. The control choice does not eliminate the need to evaluate intermediate retrieval.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/offli.title: Offline Policy Evaluation
sections/machine-learning/concepts/offli.content:
Offline Policy Evaluation
Offline policy evaluation (OPE) estimates how a target policy would perform without deploying it. amans-ai-journal-primers-reinforcement-learning frames the problem around logs generated by a behaviour policy: the desired policy may choose actions the dataset rarely or never contains, so its outcomes are counterfactual.
flowchart TD
  L[Logged behaviour-policy data] --> O[Estimate target-policy value]
  O --> D[Direct outcome model]
  O --> I[Importance reweighting]
  O --> R[Doubly robust combination]
  O --> Q[Fitted action-value evaluation]
  O --> M[Learned transition and reward model]
  O --> C[Check coverage bias variance and horizon error]



                  
                  What makes offline policy evaluation fundamentally counterfactual? 
                  
                

The target policy may choose actions that the behaviour-policy log rarely or never contains.




                  
                  What tradeoff separates direct methods from importance sampling in OPE? 
                  
                

Direct models introduce model bias; importance weights can introduce very high variance.


The primer groups the estimators by what they trust:

Direct methods fit rewards or outcomes and simulate the target policy; model error creates bias.
Importance sampling reweights logged outcomes by target-to-behaviour action probabilities; large ratios create high variance.
Doubly robust methods join a direct model with importance correction, reducing dependence on either one while retaining both failure surfaces.
Fitted Q evaluation learns the target policy’s action values through Bellman updates on the log.
Model-based evaluation learns transitions and rewards, then simulates; compounded model error can dominate long horizons.

No estimator creates support where none exists. If the target policy systematically selects unseen actions, neither weighting nor a learned model can provide strong evidence without assumptions. Results should therefore be sliced by coverage, accompanied by uncertainty, and checked against limited online tests where safe.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/on-vs.title: On- vs Off-Policy Learning
sections/machine-learning/concepts/on-vs.content:
On- vs Off-Policy Learning
The distinction asks whether experience comes from the policy being learned about. amans-ai-journal-primers-reinforcement-learning calls the data-generating policy the behaviour policy and the policy being evaluated or improved the target policy.
flowchart TD
  P[Policy being learned about] --> O[On-policy]
  P --> F[Off-policy]
  O --> S[Current target policy generates data]
  S --> C[Matched distribution but continual collection]
  F --> D[Another policy or replay log generates data]
  D --> R[Reuse data with coverage and correction risk]



                  
                  What determines whether learning is on-policy or off-policy? 
                  
                

Whether the data-generating behaviour policy is the same policy being learned about.




                  
                  What does off-policy learning gain and risk? 
                  
                

It gains data reuse and sample efficiency but risks distribution mismatch and unstable correction.


On-policy methods collect trajectories from the current target policy. Their data match the current action distribution, which simplifies estimation, but policy updates make old experience stale and require continual interaction. SARSA and common policy-gradient loops are examples.
Off-policy methods learn a target policy from experience produced by another policy: an exploratory behaviour policy, an older checkpoint, human demonstrations, or a replay buffer. Q-learning is the standard tabular example. Data reuse can improve sample efficiency and supports offline learning, but target actions may be poorly represented in the log.
Importance sampling corrects some mismatch by weighting actions according to target-to-behaviour probability ratios. Large ratios create high variance, especially over long trajectories. Value-function approximation and bootstrapping can add instability when coverage is weak.
Operational consequence
Freshness, replay, clipping, and drift monitoring are not merely implementation choices; they control the distance between behaviour and target distributions. offline-policy-evaluation is difficult for the same reason: it asks what a different policy would have done using only actions another policy selected.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/rag-v.title: RAG vs Long Context
sections/machine-learning/concepts/rag-v.content:
RAG vs Long Context
Long context and retrieval allocate evidence differently. amans-ai-journal-primers-retrieval-augmented presents long context as sending more of the corpus into the model, while RAG searches first and sends a selected subset.
flowchart TD
  E[Evidence allocation choice] --> L[Long context sends more of the corpus]
  E --> R[RAG searches then selects a subset]
  L --> C[More cross-document context with higher cost and attention competition]
  R --> S[Lower input cost with retrieval-coverage risk]
  L --> H[Hybrid retrieval plus a moderately long context]
  R --> H
  H --> V[Validate quality recall latency cost and failure severity]



                  
                  How do long context and RAG allocate evidence differently? 
                  
                

Long context sends more of the corpus; RAG searches first and sends a selected subset.




                  
                  What is the characteristic evidence failure of each approach? 
                  
                

Long context may ignore available evidence; RAG may exclude the needed evidence before generation.


Long context preserves cross-document details a retriever might omit and simplifies pipelines for bounded corpora. Its costs grow with input length: memory, latency, throughput, and attention competition. Capacity also does not guarantee utilization; the primer cites position sensitivity in which evidence in the middle of a long prompt is less reliably used.
RAG reduces input cost and can update or permission evidence independently, but it can silently exclude the needed passage through ingestion, query, chunking, or ranking error. Its answer is bounded by retrieval coverage. A hybrid can retrieve documents or sections, then use a relatively long context within the selected scope.
Decision rule
Use validation data rather than context-window size alone. Measure answer quality, evidence recall, latency, cost, and failure severity across corpus sizes and query types. A larger window changes the useful retrieval granularity; it does not automatically make retrieval obsolete.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/rank-.title: Rank-Aware Evaluation
sections/machine-learning/concepts/rank-.content:
Rank-Aware Evaluation
Rank-aware evaluation treats relevance and position as separate inputs. Returning
the right items is insufficient if the most useful ones appear after the user has
stopped looking.
flowchart LR
  R[Relevance labels] --> C[Cumulative gain]
  P[Rank position] --> D[Position discount]
  C --> G[Discounted cumulative gain]
  D --> G
  I[Ideal ordering] --> N[NDCG = DCG / ideal DCG]
  G --> N

Cumulative gain sums relevance without order, so two permutations can tie. DCG
discounts gains at later ranks. NDCG divides by the gain of the ideal ordering,
placing the result on a comparable 0–1 scale across recommendation lists.


                  
                  What does normalisation add after DCG has already included rank position? 
                  
                

It compares the observed ordering with the best ordering available for that list, allowing scores from lists with different attainable gains to be averaged.


The primer notes an NDCG caveat: irrelevant results may escape penalty depending on
the relevance scheme and list length. It therefore lists objectives beyond ranking
accuracy—novelty, diversity, personalisation, satisfaction, hit rate, and future
impact. A recommender can rank known relevance well while remaining repetitive or
unsatisfying.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/refer.title: Reference-Based Text Evaluation
sections/machine-learning/concepts/refer.content:
Reference-Based Text Evaluation
Reference-based text evaluation compares generated text with one or more accepted
answers. The metric chooses what counts as a match: exact surface units, contextual
token similarity, or distance between embedded distributions.
flowchart LR
  C[Candidate text] --> L[Lexical overlap]
  R[Reference set] --> L
  C --> E[Embedding similarity]
  R --> E
  L --> B[BLEU: precision-oriented n-grams]
  L --> G[ROUGE: recall-oriented overlap]
  E --> S[BERTScore: contextual token matches]
  E --> M[MoverScore: transport distance]

BLEU asks how much produced n-gram content is supported by references and was
developed for translation. ROUGE asks how much reference content was recovered and
was developed for summarisation; ROUGE-L uses longest common subsequences.
BERTScore replaces exact tokens with contextual embedding matches and reports
precision, recall, and F₁. MoverScore measures the work required to move embedded
content between candidate and reference.


                  
                  What limitation do BERTScore and MoverScore address that BLEU and ROUGE retain? 
                  
                

They allow semantically similar paraphrases to match even when surface n-grams differ. They change the definition of similarity rather than eliminating dependence on a reference.


More varied references can represent more valid phrasings, but reference quality
remains the ceiling. None of these scores alone establishes factuality, usefulness,
style, or safety. Perplexity answers predictive fit, and burstiness answers output
variation; neither is a substitute for reference agreement.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/refle.title: Reflection-Evaluator Loop
sections/machine-learning/concepts/refle.content:
Reflection-Evaluator Loop
A reflection-evaluator loop replaces one-pass generation with four stages: produce a draft, evaluate it against a goal, convert the evaluation into actionable feedback, and revise. amans-ai-journal-primers-agents presents reflection as a simple agentic pattern and evaluator-optimizer as a workflow in which generation and judgment have distinct roles.
flowchart LR
  D[Produce a draft] --> E[Evaluate against explicit criteria]
  E --> F[Convert findings into actionable feedback]
  F --> R[Revise]
  R --> E
  E --> P[Stop when a candidate passes or attempts are exhausted]



                  
                  What are the four stages of a reflection-evaluator loop? 
                  
                

Draft, evaluate, turn findings into feedback, then revise.




                  
                  Why are external checks valuable in a reflection loop? 
                  
                

A model critiquing itself can repeat the same blind spots as its draft.


The evaluator may be the same model under a critique prompt, a separate critic agent, or an external tool. Unit tests can check generated code; search or a database can challenge factual claims. External signals matter because fluent self-critique can repeat the same blind spots as the draft. The loop improves only when evaluation is informative and revision actually addresses its findings.
The pattern does not require full autonomy. Code can fix the order and stopping rule while models supply the draft and critique, placing it on the workflow side of the agent-control-boundary. A multi-agent implementation separates generator and critic, but that separation also adds communication and cost.
Failure modes
An evaluator can reward style over correctness, invent defects, or accept correlated errors. Unlimited iteration can oscillate or spend tokens without measurable gain. Reliable loops therefore need explicit criteria, external validation where possible, bounded attempts, and a rule for escalation when no candidate passes.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/regre.title: Regression Loss Geometry
sections/machine-learning/concepts/regre.content:
Regression Loss Geometry
Regression loss geometry is the choice of how residuals are transformed before
aggregation. The transformation decides whether one large miss should dominate,
whether the score remains in the target unit, and whether absolute or relative
error matters.








































MetricTransformationWhat the summary emphasisesMAEabsolute residuallinear cost; target unitsMSEsquared residualdisproportionately large missesRMSEsquare root of MSElarge-miss emphasis in target unitsRMSLEsquared log-space residualrelative rather than absolute scaleR²explained variationfit relative to a baselineadjusted R²R² adjusted for predictorsdiscourages gratuitous parameters


                  
                  Why can MAE and RMSE rank the same models differently? 
                  
                

MAE weights residual magnitude linearly, while RMSE inherits squared-error emphasis on large misses. The disagreement reports a choice about whether tail errors should dominate.


The metric must match the consequence surface. If a ten-unit miss costs exactly
twice a five-unit miss, absolute error reflects that premise. If large misses are
disproportionately harmful, squared error reflects a different premise. A unitless
fit statistic such as R² answers neither cost question by itself.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/retri.title: Retrieval Chunking Boundary
sections/machine-learning/concepts/retri.content:
Retrieval Chunking Boundary
The chunking boundary determines what unit a retriever can return. amans-ai-journal-primers-retrieval-augmented describes the core tradeoff: smaller chunks match narrow queries precisely but can detach a statement from its definition or qualification; larger chunks preserve surrounding context but introduce unrelated material and spend more of the generation budget.
flowchart TD
  B[Choose a chunk boundary] --> S[Smaller chunks]
  B --> L[Larger chunks]
  S --> P[Precise narrow matching]
  S --> C[Context can be detached]
  L --> K[More surrounding context]
  L --> N[More noise and budget use]
  B --> T[Test against corpus and query granularity]



                  
                  What is the central chunk-size tradeoff in retrieval? 
                  
                

Small chunks match precisely but lose context; large chunks preserve context but add noise and cost.




                  
                  Why is there no corpus-independent optimal chunk size? 
                  
                

Document structure, query granularity, task, model limits and synthesis budget all change the useful boundary.


Fixed-size chunking is cheap and predictable, with overlap reducing boundary loss at the cost of duplicate evidence. Sentence, paragraph, recursive, and format-aware methods follow visible structure. Semantic chunking groups neighbouring units until similarity changes. Late chunking or late interaction tries to preserve broader context during representation while retaining fine-grained retrieval.
There is no corpus-independent optimal size. Document structure, embedding input limits, query granularity, retrieval metric, synthesis budget, and task type all change the boundary. The primer’s practical test is whether a chunk makes sense without hidden surrounding text, followed by empirical evaluation across candidate sizes.
Failure signature
Fragmented retrieval returns an answer-bearing phrase without its scope; oversized retrieval returns the right phrase buried in noise. Overlap can make several near-duplicates look like independent support. Chunking must therefore be evaluated together with reranking and context recall and precision.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/retri.title: Retrieval-Reranking Funnel
sections/machine-learning/concepts/retri.content:
Retrieval-Reranking Funnel
A retrieval-reranking funnel separates broad candidate discovery from precise evidence selection. amans-ai-journal-primers-retrieval-augmented treats first-stage retrieval as a high-recall operation: sparse, dense, or hybrid indexes cheaply return more candidates than the generator can consume.
flowchart LR
  C[Large corpus] --> R[High-recall first-stage retrieval]
  R --> P[Pooled candidate set]
  P --> K[Costlier reranking]
  K --> E[Small evidence set]
  E --> G[Generator context]
  M[Metadata permissions and budget rules] --> K



                  
                  Why does a retrieval-reranking funnel use a broad first stage? 
                  
                

The first stage cheaply maximizes recall over a large corpus.




                  
                  What is the reranker buying with its extra computation? 
                  
                

More precise selection of the small evidence set that deserves prompt space.


The second stage spends more computation per candidate. Cross-encoders can jointly read query and passage; late-interaction models retain token-level matching; instruction-following rerankers apply task criteria; metadata and business rules remove ineligible results. Personalization and context-budget constraints may alter the final order even when semantic relevance is unchanged.
The funnel exists because one score rarely serves both scale and precision. Approximate nearest-neighbour search makes a large corpus searchable; reranking decides which small set deserves scarce prompt space. When multiple retrievers contribute, score calibration or rank fusion is needed before comparison.
Evaluation boundary
Reranking cannot recover a relevant item absent from the candidate pool. Candidate recall and post-rerank precision must therefore be measured separately through component-wise-rag-evaluation. Filtering can also encode policy or personalization errors that look like retrieval failure unless stages are logged.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/rewar.title: Reward Proxy Failure
sections/machine-learning/concepts/rewar.content:
Reward Proxy Failure
A reinforcement-learning agent optimizes the reward it receives, not the intention the designer had. amans-ai-journal-primers-reinforcement-learning describes reward hacking as exploiting a proxy or loophole to raise measured reward without completing the intended task.
flowchart LR
  I[Intended objective] --> P[Measurable reward proxy]
  P --> O[Agent optimizes the measured signal]
  O --> L[Find loophole or omitted dimension]
  L --> H[Reward rises while intended task fails]
  H --> M[Monitoring and adversarial evaluation]
  M --> R[Redesign reward constraints or oversight]



                  
                  Why can a reinforcement-learning agent satisfy its reward while failing the task? 
                  
                

It optimizes the measurable proxy it receives, not the designer’s unobserved intention.




                  
                  Why can reward shaping create new failure modes? 
                  
                

Every added intermediate signal becomes another target the agent can optimize independently of the real objective.


Production systems often need proxies because the final objective is delayed or hard to observe. A coding assistant might be rewarded for suggestion acceptance, test passage, or task completion signals. Each measures something useful and incomplete: acceptance can favour superficial convenience, a narrow test can be gamed, and a completion report can be false. Combining signals does not automatically recover the latent objective.
Reward shaping adds intermediate feedback to sparse tasks, accelerating credit assignment while also adding targets that can be optimized independently. Guardrails, regression tests, quality metrics, failure slices, human review, and online monitoring therefore belong in reward design. They test whether reward improvement transfers to the actual outcome.
Boundary
Poor performance and reward hacking are different. Hacking means the policy found a high-reward behaviour that violates intent; ordinary learning failure may simply receive low reward. A Reward-Model can make the proxy adaptive, but its learned preferences remain a proxy and can be exploited or drift.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/scali.title: Scaling Beats Knowledge Engineering
sections/machine-learning/concepts/scali.content:
Scaling Beats Knowledge Engineering
The claim that general methods which convert computation into performance eventually beat methods encoding human understanding of the domain — named and argued in bitter-lesson, and visible as an empirical pattern well before Sutton named it.
flowchart TD
  A[Assume available compute is fixed] --> K[Encode domain knowledge]
  K --> S1[Short-term gain, and it is personally satisfying]
  S1 --> P[Plateau]
  P --> O[Then it obstructs later use of general computation]
  C[Compute arrives regardless] --> G[General methods — search and learning]
  G --> W[Keeps improving with no human in the loop]
  W --> B[The breakthrough arrives by the rejected route — hence bitter]
  T[An architecture encoding how to spend compute] --> G
  D[An architecture encoding what is true about the domain] --> K

The argument
Researchers optimise as though available compute were fixed. Under that assumption, encoding domain knowledge is the only available lever. But over a horizon longer than a single research project, dramatically more compute arrives regardless — and only methods that can absorb it keep improving.


                  
                  What false assumption makes knowledge engineering look like the right move? 
                  
                

That available compute is fixed. Under that assumption domain knowledge is the only lever; over a horizon longer than one research project, far more compute arrives anyway, and only methods that can absorb it keep improving.


The two need not conflict, but in practice they do: time spent on one is time not spent on the other, people become psychologically committed to their approach, and knowledge-based methods tend to complicate the system in ways that make it worse at exploiting general computation later.


                  
                  Beyond opportunity cost, how does built-in knowledge actively harm later progress? 
                  
                

It complicates the system in ways that make it worse at exploiting general computation. The structure added to help does not merely stop paying — it obstructs the method that would have scaled.


Only two things scale arbitrarily: search and learning. Both turn compute into performance without a human in the loop.


                  
                  Which two methods does Sutton say scale arbitrarily, and what do they share? 
                  
                

Search and learning. Both convert compute into performance with no human in the loop, which is why more hardware improves them without more research.


Four repeats






























DomainThe knowledge approachWhat wonChessHuman understanding of chess structureMassive deep search — Kasparov, 1997GoEncoding human knowledge to avoid searchSearch plus self-play learning, 20 years laterSpeechPhonemes, vocal tract models, word knowledgeStatistical HMMs, then deep learningVisionEdges, generalised cylinders, SIFT featuresConvolution and invariance, everything else discarded
Why it is “bitter”
Building in human knowledge always helps in the short term and is personally satisfying. Then it plateaus, and then it actively inhibits progress. The eventual breakthrough arrives by the opposing route, so the success is a defeat for a favoured, human-centric approach — which is why Sutton says it is resented and incompletely digested rather than learned once and remembered.


                  
                  Why is the lesson "bitter" rather than merely surprising? 
                  
                

Because the breakthrough arrives by the route the researchers rejected. Every win for scale is a defeat for a favoured human-centric approach, so it is resented and incompletely digested instead of learned once.


The second, less-quoted half
Sutton’s deeper point is about what not to build in. The contents of minds are “tremendously, irredeemably complex.” Space, objects, multiple agents, symmetries — these belong to the arbitrary outside world, and their complexity is endless. Build the meta-methods that find complexity, not the complexity itself. “We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what we have discovered.”


                  
                  What should be built in, if not knowledge about the domain? 
                  
                

The meta-methods that find complexity. The contents of minds are irredeemably complex and the world they describe is endless, so the buildable thing is the capacity to discover, not the discoveries.


An instance four years early
unreasonable-effectiveness-recurrent-neural-networks is the same claim as a demonstration. A character-level model given raw text learns spelling, syntax, quote matching, brace nesting, and markdown structure — none of it specified. Karpathy’s summary of the interpretability finding is the argument in miniature: “We didn’t have to hardcode at any point that if you’re trying to predict the next character it might be useful to keep track of whether or not you are currently inside or outside of quote.”
The case that complicates it
Architecture is human design, and the Transformer is unmistakably designed. If Sutton is right that built-in structure plateaus, why did the biggest recent gain come from an architectural change?
The reconciliation is what the architecture encodes. The Transformer contains almost no knowledge about language — no phonemes, no grammar, no parse structure. What it supplies is a way to spend more compute usefully: parallelism across positions, and a mechanism indifferent to modality. It is a general method that scales, which is exactly the category Sutton says survives. amans-ai-journal-primers-transformers makes this legible by showing how little changes between text and vision — the Vision Transformer’s architecture is nearly identical to the 2017 original, with images cut into patches so patches can play the role tokens play.
Read that way, the lesson is not “architecture does not matter.” It is that the architectures that last encode how to use compute, not what is true about the domain.


                  
                  What distinguishes an architecture that lasts from one that plateaus? 
                  
                

What it encodes. A lasting architecture encodes how to spend compute — parallelism, modality-indifference. A plateauing one encodes what is true about the domain, like phonemes or parse structure.


Sources

bitter-lesson (primary — the argument and the four historical cases)
unreasonable-effectiveness-recurrent-neural-networks (an empirical instance, 2015)

sections/machine-learning/concepts/self-.title: Self-Attention
sections/machine-learning/concepts/self-.content:
Self-Attention
Letting every position in a sequence look at every other position and decide, by learned similarity, how much of each to absorb. It is the only operation in a Transformer that connects positions to one another.
flowchart LR
  E[Input embedding] --> P[Project to a query, a key and a value]
  P --> S[Score — this query against every key]
  S --> D[Divide by the square root of d_k, for gradient stability]
  D --> M[Softmax — positive weights summing to 1]
  M --> V[Multiply each value by its weight]
  V --> O[Sum — the output for this position]
  P --> H[Eight heads, eight representation subspaces]
  H --> C[Concatenate and project through W_O]
  O --> C

The computation, in six steps
From illustrated-transformer-jay-alammar-visualizing-machine:

Project each input embedding into a query, a key, and a value (dimension 64 against an embedding dimension of 512 — an architecture choice that keeps multi-head computation roughly constant).
Score each position against every position: dot product of this query with that key.
Divide by 8 — √dk — for gradient stability.
Softmax, so the scores are positive and sum to 1.
Multiply each value vector by its score, drowning out the irrelevant ones.
Sum. That is the output for this position.

In practice all of it is one matrix expression, which is exactly why it parallelises.


                  
                  What are the three roles a query, a key and a value play? 
                  
                

The query is what this position is looking for, the key is what a position offers for matching, and the value is what actually gets carried across once the match is scored. Query·key decides how much of the value to absorb.




                  
                  Why divide the attention scores by √d k before the softmax?
                  
                

For gradient stability. Dot products grow with dimension, and large scores push the softmax into its flat region where gradients vanish.




                  
                  What does the softmax step do to the attention scores? 
                  
                

Makes them positive and sum to 1, so they act as weights over the value vectors — the irrelevant positions are scaled toward zero and drowned out of the sum.


What it is for
The canonical example: “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.” What does “it” refer to? Trivial for a reader, not for an algorithm. Self-attention is the mechanism that binds “it” to “animal”, and visualising the top encoder shows the binding happening.
Chadha’s variant in amans-ai-journal-primers-transformers is harder — “The owl spied a squirrel. It tried to grab it with its talons but only got the end of its tail” — and makes the same point: a model attending only to nearby words cannot resolve which “it” is which, while a model connecting every word to every other can work out that the owl grabbed and the squirrel lost part of its tail.


                  
                  Why does pronoun resolution defeat a model that only attends locally? 
                  
                

The antecedent can be arbitrarily far away, and several candidates may sit nearby. Resolving which “it” is which requires connecting every word to every other, not just to its neighbours.


Multi-head: several opinions at once
Eight independently initialised sets of Q/K/V matrices produce eight outputs, concatenated and projected by a further matrix WO. The gain is representation subspaces: in the same example, one head attends to “the animal” while another attends to “tired,” so the encoding of “it” absorbs both. With a single head, the position’s own value tends to dominate.


                  
                  What failure mode does a single attention head have? 
                  
                

Its own position’s value tends to dominate the weighted sum, so little context actually gets absorbed. Several heads give several subspaces, letting one bind “it” to “the animal” while another binds it to “tired.”


What it costs
Attention compares every pair of positions, so it is O(n²) in sequence length where recurrence is O(n). Distance within the sequence becomes free — position 1 and position 500 are one hop apart — but total length becomes expensive. Every long-context technique in the field is an attempt to pay less for that n².


                  
                  What does attention make free, and what does it make expensive? 
                  
                

Distance becomes free — position 1 and position 500 are one hop apart. Total length becomes expensive, because every pair of positions is compared: O(n²) where recurrence was O(n).


Removing recurrence also removes all notion of order, which is why positional encoding has to be added back explicitly.
Cross-attention: the same idea across modalities
Take queries from one source and keys and values from another and the mechanism fuses two different kinds of data. amans-ai-journal-primers-transformers argues this is the deeper significance — not that attention is good at language, but that it is indifferent to what the sequence contains, which is what made one architecture serve text, images and audio.


                  
                  What single change turns self-attention into cross-attention? 
                  
                

Taking the queries from one source and the keys and values from another. That one substitution lets the mechanism fuse two different kinds of data, which is what made one architecture serve text, images and audio.


Predicted before it arrived
unreasonable-effectiveness-recurrent-neural-networks (May 2015) calls attention “the most interesting recent architectural innovation in neural networks,” discussing soft attention from Neural Turing Machines and the efficiency cost that motivates hard attention. understanding-lstm-networks-colahs-blog (August 2015) closes by naming attention as the next step after LSTMs. Both precede Attention is All You Need by two years.
