sections/machine-learning/concepts/singl.title: Single- vs Multi-Agent Economics
sections/machine-learning/concepts/singl.content:
Single- vs Multi-Agent Economics
Architecture choice trades unified reasoning against structured coordination. amans-ai-journal-primers-agents recommends a single-agent baseline because one trajectory retains the full context and token budget, avoids handoffs, and preserves global state. This suits sequential, tightly coupled work where omissions at a boundary can cascade.
flowchart TD
  T[Architecture choice] --> S[Start with one agent]
  S --> C[Preserve context coherence and token depth]
  T --> D[Task has intrinsic decomposition or independent checking]
  D --> M[Add specialist or verifier roles]
  M --> L[Pay communication and coordination costs]
  L --> E[Keep multi-agent only if measured gains exceed costs]



                  
                  Why is one agent the recommended baseline? 
                  
                

It preserves global context, avoids handoffs and keeps the token budget in one reasoning trajectory.




                  
                  When does a multi-agent design earn its coordination cost? 
                  
                

When intrinsic decomposition, parallel work or an independent verifier produces measured gains.


Multi-agent systems earn their cost when the task already contains semi-independent parts: parallel search, specialist roles, diverse hypotheses, or an explicit reviewer. They can also partition a long or noisy context into smaller views. Their benefit comes from task-aligned decomposition or verification, not from agent count itself.
Every additional agent introduces an economic ledger:

tokens and latency for duplicate context and communication;
information lost when state is serialized or summarized;
conflicts between concurrent actions;
error propagation through trusted handoffs;
orchestration, permission, and governance complexity.

Under a fixed compute budget, distributing tokens can leave each agent with less reasoning depth. Stronger base models can also absorb workflows that once required explicit teams. The primer therefore treats multi-agent coordination as a deliberate escalation: strengthen planning, routing, tools, and reflection within one agent first, then measure whether added roles improve the target task.
Decision rule
Prefer one agent when coherence dominates. Escalate when decomposition is intrinsic, independent work can run in parallel, or a distinct verifier produces measurable reliability gains. Central coordination can reduce error amplification, but it becomes a bottleneck and must itself be evaluated.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/super.title: Superposition
sections/machine-learning/concepts/super.content:
Superposition
The reason a neuron almost never means one thing — and a candidate explanation for why scaling works as well as it does. One idea answering two questions is what makes it worth a page.
flowchart LR
  N[n dimensions hold exactly n perpendicular directions] --> R[Relax to nearly perpendicular, tolerating a little interference]
  R --> J[Johnson-Lindenstrauss — capacity grows exponentially with dimension]
  J --> T[The angular tolerance dominates the number]
  J --> M[A layer probes far more features than it has neurons]
  M --> S[A feature is a combination of neurons, not one neuron]
  S --> U[Weights look uninterpretable by property, not by accident]
  U --> SA[Sparse autoencoders as the tool for recovering features anyway]
  J --> SC[A candidate mechanism for scaling — offered as a might]

The counting argument
In n dimensions you can fit exactly n mutually perpendicular directions. That is the definition of dimension, and it looks like a hard ceiling on how many independent features a space can hold.
Relax “perpendicular” to “nearly perpendicular” — say 85° to 95°, tolerating a little interference — and the ceiling moves. A consequence of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma is that the number of nearly-perpendicular vectors you can cram in grows exponentially with dimension. In low dimensions this buys almost nothing, which is what makes the high-dimensional behaviour counterintuitive.
So a space with ten times the dimensions stores far more than ten times the independent ideas.


                  
                  What does relaxing "perpendicular" to "nearly perpendicular" buy? 
                  
                

The capacity stops being n and starts growing exponentially with dimension. Tolerating a little interference between features is what lifts the hard ceiling the definition of dimension seemed to impose.




                  
                  Why is superposition counterintuitive to reason about? 
                  
                

Because in low dimensions the near-perpendicular relaxation buys almost nothing. The exponential behaviour only shows up at high dimension, so small-space intuition points the wrong way.


The numbers, after the correction
might-llms-store-facts-deep-learning is unusually good evidence here because it publishes its own error. The video’s demo pushed 10,000 vectors in 100 dimensions to pairwise angles of 89°–91°, but a bad cost function let a few pairs escape to dot products near ±1, and Sanderson states plainly that 100 dimensions is not enough for a range that tight. Corrected figures, credited to viewer Nick Yoder:






























ToleranceDimensionsCapacity89°–91°—uninteresting below ~250,000 dimensions85° (dot product 0.087)—scales very quickly85°12,288 (GPT-3 embedding)well over 40 billion, likely > 10¹⁷85°116,000 (plausible for later models)over a googol, likely > 10¹⁶⁰
The tolerance you accept dominates the answer. That is the substantive content of the correction, and it is why the original demo’s tightness mattered.


                  
                  Which parameter dominates how many features a space can hold? 
                  
                

The angular tolerance. At 89°–91° the capacity is uninteresting below ~250,000 dimensions; at 85° the same 12,288-dimensional space holds well over 40 billion directions.


What follows for interpretability
If a layer exploits this capacity, it is probing far more features than it has neurons — GPT-3’s ~50,000-neuron MLP layer could be asking orders of magnitude more questions. But then a feature cannot appear as one neuron lighting up. It has to appear as a specific combination of neurons: a superposition.


                  
                  Why can't a feature be one neuron, if a layer exploits superposition? 
                  
                

There are more features than neurons. Once a layer probes orders of magnitude more directions than it has units, each feature must be carried by a specific combination of them.


This is why might-llms-store-facts-deep-learning retracts its own worked example. “Michael Jordan → basketball” as one neuron implementing an AND gate is a clean, correct account of the mechanics, and almost certainly not what any real neuron does. What survives is structural: rows of the up-projection are directions, columns of the down-projection are edits. What does not survive is the assumption that either corresponds to a single human-legible concept.


                  
                  Which part of the "one neuron stores one fact" account survives superposition, and which does not? 
                  
                

The mechanics survive — rows are directions that ask, columns are edits that answer. What does not survive is the assumption that either corresponds to a single human-legible concept.


The tool for recovering features anyway is the sparse autoencoder; Sanderson points to Anthropic’s Toy Models of Superposition and Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning.
The older version of the same disappointment
analyzing-our-neural-network-3blue1brown found this seven years earlier at a scale of 13,002 parameters: the digit classifier’s first-layer weights, visualised, look almost random rather than like the edge detectors the architecture was motivated by. The 2017 explanation was a happy local minimum; the 2024 explanation is that clean single-feature neurons may not be what a well-trained network wants in the first place.


                  
                  How did the explanation for uninterpretable weights change between 2017 and 2024? 
                  
                

From “the network settled into a happy local minimum” to “clean single-feature neurons may not be what a well-trained network wants at all.” The observation is the same; the second reading makes it a property rather than an accident.


And why it may explain scaling
Because capacity in nearly-perpendicular directions grows exponentially rather than linearly with dimension, a bigger model does not merely get proportionally more room for ideas. Sanderson offers this as a possible reason “why model performance seems to scale so well with size” — a mechanism-level candidate for the pattern scaling-beats-knowledge-engineering asserts empirically. He offers it as a might, and it should be read that way.


                  
                  How would superposition explain why scaling works so well? 
                  
                

Because capacity grows exponentially with dimension rather than linearly, a bigger model gets disproportionately more room for ideas — not merely proportionally more. Sanderson offers this as a candidate mechanism, not a result.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/tempo.title: Temporal-Difference Bootstrapping
sections/machine-learning/concepts/tempo.content:
Temporal-Difference Bootstrapping
Temporal-difference (TD) learning updates a value estimate before a trajectory ends. amans-ai-journal-primers-reinforcement-learning gives the one-step error as (\delta_t=r_t+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)): observed reward plus the current successor estimate, minus the current-state estimate.
flowchart LR
  S[Current state estimate] --> T[Add observed reward and discounted successor estimate]
  T --> E[Temporal-difference target]
  E --> D[Compute prediction error]
  D --> U[Update current value estimate]
  U --> S
  B[Bootstrapping learns before the trajectory ends] --> T



                  
                  Why is temporal-difference learning called bootstrapping? 
                  
                

One learned successor-value estimate is used to train the current value estimate.




                  
                  What does TD gain and risk by updating before a trajectory ends? 
                  
                

It gains earlier, lower-variance updates but inherits bias from an inaccurate successor estimate.


This is bootstrapping because one learned estimate trains another. Dynamic programming also bootstraps but assumes known transition dynamics and takes expectations over successors. Monte Carlo methods avoid bootstrapping by waiting for a complete sampled return. TD occupies the middle: it learns from experience online while using its present model of the future.
The benefit is earlier, lower-variance updating and no requirement to wait for episode termination. The cost is bias from an inaccurate successor estimate; coupled with function approximation and off-policy data, that bias can destabilize learning. Multi-step methods and eligibility traces trade between short bootstrap targets and longer sampled returns.
TD also exposes temporal credit assignment. A delayed outcome must influence earlier states through successive updates, which can be slow when rewards are sparse or horizons are long. Bootstrapping helps propagate information but does not solve the general problem.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/tool-.title: Tool Interface Design
sections/machine-learning/concepts/tool-.content:
Tool Interface Design
Giving an LLM-Agent a function does not make the function usable. amans-ai-journal-primers-agents treats the interface as part of the agent system: names and descriptions guide tool selection, schemas constrain arguments, middleware formats results, and validation and error handling determine whether a failed call can be repaired.
flowchart TD
  T[Usable tool contract] --> S[Selection]
  T --> I[Invocation]
  T --> O[Outcome]
  T --> F[Recoverable failure]
  T --> B[Security boundary]



                  
                  What four things must a usable tool contract make legible? 
                  
                

Selection, invocation, outcome and recoverable failure.




                  
                  Why is a schema insufficient to make a tool call correct? 
                  
                

It constrains argument syntax, not whether the action is intended, authorized or appropriate.


A useful contract makes four things legible:

Selection — what the tool does, when it applies, and how it differs from neighbouring tools.
Invocation — required arguments, allowed values, types, and examples.
Outcome — structured results that preserve the information needed for the next decision.
Failure — specific, recoverable errors rather than an opaque exception or misleading success.

Security belongs to the same contract. Authentication, least-privilege permissions, sandboxing, confirmation for consequential actions, and limits on returned data bound what a correct-looking call may do. This is why tool design sits inside harness-engineering, not outside the model as ordinary API plumbing.
Boundary
More tools can reduce reliability by making selection harder and expanding the action surface. Schemas constrain syntax, not intent; a valid call can still be the wrong action. Tool-interface evaluation must therefore test selection, argument construction, authorization, execution, result interpretation, and recovery separately.

sections/machine-learning/concepts/value.title: Value, Return, and Advantage
sections/machine-learning/concepts/value.content:
Value, Return, and Advantage
amans-ai-journal-primers-reinforcement-learning separates an observed outcome from two expectations built around it.
flowchart TD
  T[One sampled trajectory] --> G[Realized discounted return]
  G --> V[State value averages return from a state]
  G --> Q[Action value averages return after an action]
  Q --> A[Advantage compares action value with state value]
  V --> A
  V --> B[Bellman relation links present and successor value]



                  
                  How does return differ from value in reinforcement learning? 
                  
                

Return is realized on one trajectory; value is an expectation over possible returns under a policy.




                  
                  What does advantage measure? 
                  
                

How much better or worse an action is than the policy’s average action in that state.



Return (G_t) is the discounted reward realized from time (t) onward along one sampled trajectory.
State value (V^\pi(s)) is the expected return from state (s) when policy (\pi) is followed.
Action value (Q^\pi(s,a)) is the expected return after taking action (a) in (s), then following (\pi).
Advantage (A^\pi(s,a)=Q^\pi(s,a)-V^\pi(s)) measures how much better or worse that action is than the policy’s average action in the state.

Return varies between trajectories even from the same state. Value averages over that stochasticity and is tied to a particular policy. Advantage subtracts a baseline, letting policy-gradient updates emphasize relative performance rather than the absolute scale of outcomes; this can reduce gradient variance.
The Bellman relation makes value recursive: present value equals expected immediate reward plus discounted successor value. temporal-difference-bootstrap turns that relation into an incremental learning target.
Boundary
These quantities are definitions; practical algorithms estimate them. Function approximation, limited coverage, changing policies, and long horizons introduce error. An accurate value for the specified reward can also be misaligned with the intended task when reward-proxy-failure is present.

sections/machine-learning/entities/diffu.title: Diffusion Models
sections/machine-learning/entities/diffu.content:
Diffusion Models
A family of generative models that destroys data with noise in a fixed forward process and learns only the reverse. Inspired by non-equilibrium thermodynamics, formalised across Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015), noise-conditioned score networks (Song & Ermon, 2019), and DDPM (Ho et al., 2020).
flowchart LR
  X[Data] --> F[Forward — small Gaussian noise over T steps, on a fixed schedule]
  F --> G[Isotropic Gaussian noise]
  X -->|closed form, straight to any timestep| J[Jump to a random step and denoise there]
  J --> R[Reverse — the only learned part, predicting the noise]
  R --> S[Sampling, over many reverse steps]
  S --> C[The price paid — slow sampling]
  C --> A[Fewer steps, distillation, consistency models, latent diffusion]
  CF[Classifier-free guidance — interpolate conditional and unconditional] --> R

The bargain each generative family strikes
are-diffusion-models-lillog frames diffusion by what it declines to pay:

























FamilyPrice of tractabilityGANUnstable adversarial training, reduced sample diversityVAEOptimises a surrogate loss, not the thing you wantFlowArchitecture constrained to be invertibleDiffusionSlow sampling — many reverse steps per sample
Diffusion pays in inference time rather than in training stability or architectural freedom. That turned out to be the affordable price, since inference cost can be attacked by distillation and by moving to a latent space, while adversarial instability cannot be engineered away as cleanly.


                  
                  What price does diffusion pay for tractability, and why was it the affordable one? 
                  
                

Slow sampling — many reverse steps per sample. It was affordable because inference cost yields to distillation and latent-space training, whereas a GAN’s adversarial instability cannot be engineered away as cleanly.


Forward: fixed and closed-form
A Markov chain adds small Gaussian noise over T steps under a variance schedule βt. As T → ∞ the result is isotropic Gaussian noise.
The property that makes training feasible: xt can be sampled directly from x0 in closed form via the reparameterisation trick. Training never simulates the chain step by step — it jumps to a random timestep and learns to denoise there.


                  
                  What makes diffusion training feasible despite the chain having many steps? 
                  
                

xt can be sampled directly from x0 in closed form. Training jumps to a random timestep and denoises there, so it never has to simulate the chain step by step.


Reverse: the only learned part
The true reverse conditional needs the whole dataset and is intractable. But conditioned additionally on x0, the reverse posterior is Gaussian and tractable — which is what makes the objective computable at all.


                  
                  The true reverse conditional is intractable. What makes the training objective computable anyway? 
                  
                

Conditioning additionally on x0. The reverse posterior is then Gaussian, so the variational bound reduces to KL divergences between Gaussians, which have closed forms.


The variational lower bound then decomposes into a constant term (no learnable parameters, ignorable), a sum of KL divergences between Gaussians (closed form), and a final discrete decoder term. diffusion-noise-prediction carries the practical DDPM simplification: sample one timestep and predict its added noise ε rather than parameterising the reverse mean directly.
Unlike a VAE, the latent has the same dimensionality as the data and the inference procedure is fixed rather than learned. The model’s entire job is denoising.


                  
                  How does a diffusion latent differ from a VAE latent? 
                  
                

It has the same dimensionality as the data, and the procedure that produces it is fixed rather than learned. Nothing about the encoder is trained — the model’s entire job is denoising.


Conditioning is what made it useful

Classifier guidance — steer the reverse process with the gradient of a separately trained classifier.
Classifier-free guidance — train conditional and unconditional predictions jointly and combine them at sampling time. diffusion-guidance makes the resulting trade explicit: stronger conditioning can improve prompt adherence while reducing diversity or introducing artifacts.



                  
                  What does classifier-free guidance remove from the classifier-guidance recipe? 
                  
                

The separately trained classifier. Conditional and unconditional models are trained jointly and interpolated at sampling time, so steering needs no second network — which is what text-to-image systems actually run on.


Speed, attacked four ways
Fewer sampling steps; progressive distillation; consistency models; and latent diffusion — running the whole process in a compressed latent space instead of pixel space.
A note on the date
Published July 2021 and revised repeatedly since: classifier-free guidance, GLIDE, unCLIP and Imagen in 2022; latent diffusion in 2022; distillation, consistency models and a model-architecture section in 2024. The publication date understates what the page now contains.

sections/machine-learning/entities/llm-a.title: LLM Agent
sections/machine-learning/entities/llm-a.content:
LLM Agent
A system in which a language model acts as controller rather than as text generator — deciding what to do next, calling out to tools, and carrying state across steps.
flowchart TD
  S[Agentic system] --> W[Workflow — a human wrote the code paths]
  S --> A[Agent — the model directs its own process]
  A --> P[LLM as policy]
  A --> C[Context as observation space]
  A --> T[Tools as action space]
  P --> PL[Planning — decomposition, reflection, refinement]
  C --> M1[Short-term — in-context, bounded by the window]
  C --> M2[Long-term — an external vector store, retrieval renamed]
  T --> TU[Tool use — the hard part is knowing when and how]
  PL --> R[ReAct — thought, action, observation interleaved]
  R --> RF[Reflexion — detect an inefficient trajectory and reset]

Two definitions, and the argument between them
amans-ai-journal-primers-agents draws the distinction that dissolves most disputes about what agents can do, following Anthropic’s framing:

Workflow — LLMs and tools orchestrated through code paths a human wrote.
Agent — the LLM directs its own process, deciding how to use tools and sequence work.

Both are agentic systems. They fail in different ways and should be evaluated differently, and a great deal of disagreement about “agent reliability” turns out to be two people describing different architectures.
agent-control-boundary makes this a continuum rather than a label: a system can leave retrieval or tool choice to the model while keeping permissions, termination, and other transitions deterministic.


                  
                  What separates a workflow from an agent? 
                  
                

Who chose the control flow. In a workflow a human wrote the code paths the model and tools move through; in an agent the model directs its own process and sequences the work.


One formula, two decompositions
ai-agents-depth-design-principles-engineering compresses the whole object to Agent = LLM + Context + Tools, and gives the mapping that makes it rigorous rather than a slogan: LLM ↔ policy, Context ↔ observation space, Tools ↔ action space. An agent is a reinforcement learning agent whose policy happens to be a language model.


                  
                  What is the reinforcement-learning reading of Agent = LLM + Context + Tools?
                  
                

LLM ↔ policy, Context ↔ observation space, Tools ↔ action space. It makes an LLM agent an RL agent whose policy happens to be a language model, rather than a slogan.


That formula and Weng’s three components below are the same decomposition at different grains — Li’s Context absorbs Weng’s memory, and planning becomes something the policy does rather than a separate component. The production form adds three safeguards: Agent = Model + Harness, covered under harness-engineering.
Three components
llm-powered-autonomous-agents-lillog supplies the decomposition the field settled on:
Planning — subgoal decomposition, plus reflection and refinement. Chain of Thought spends test-time compute breaking a task into steps. Tree of Thoughts generates several thoughts per step and searches the resulting tree (BFS or DFS, states scored by a classifier or majority vote). LLM+P outsources planning entirely to a classical PDDL planner, translating in and out of natural language.
Memory — short-term is in-context learning, bounded by the context window; long-term is an external vector store queried at retrieval time, which is Retrieval-Augmented-Generation under another name. Weng maps these onto human memory (sensory / short-term / long-term) and is explicit that the mapping is a rough analogy.
Tool use — calling external APIs for what is not in the weights. MRKL routes queries to expert modules, neural or symbolic. TALM and Toolformer finetune the model to call APIs. HuggingGPT uses the LLM as a task planner selecting HuggingFace models across four stages. tool-interface-design separates access from reliability: schemas, validation, bounded permissions, useful errors, and result formatting determine whether a failed call can be understood and recovered.


                  
                  What distinguishes an agent's short-term memory from its long-term memory? 
                  
                

Short-term is in-context learning, bounded by the context window. Long-term is an external vector store queried at retrieval time — which is retrieval-augmented generation under another name.


MRKL’s finding is the sharp one: knowing when and how to use a tool is the hard part, not the tool. Their 7B model could not reliably extract arguments for basic arithmetic from a verbal problem, though a calculator was available and perfectly reliable.


                  
                  What did MRKL's arithmetic failure show about tool use? 
                  
                

That the hard part is knowing when and how to call a tool, not the tool itself. Their 7B model could not reliably extract the arguments from a verbal problem even though the calculator it needed was available and perfectly reliable.


Self-reflection is what makes trial and error possible
ReAct interleaves Thought / Action / Observation and beats an act-only baseline on both knowledge-intensive and decision-making tasks — the reasoning trace earns its tokens. Reflexion adds a heuristic that detects inefficient trajectories and hallucination, defined operationally as a run of identical actions producing identical observations, and can reset the environment to start a fresh attempt. reflection-evaluator-loop generalises the pattern to generate, critique, externally test, and revise; an executable check or separate evaluator can catch what self-critique misses.


                  
                  How does Reflexion detect hallucination operationally? 
                  
                

As a run of identical actions producing identical observations. The agent is repeating itself and learning nothing, which is a signal available without knowing what the right answer was. Chain of Hindsight conditions on a sequence of past outputs annotated with feedback and ranked by reward.


Four design patterns
amans-ai-journal-primers-agents classifies the workflows: Reflection (the agent evaluates and revises its own output — the simplest, and reliably effective), Tool Use, Planning, and Multi-agent Collaboration (distinct roles contributing specialised work). single-vs-multi-agent-economics supplies the missing selection rule: add agent boundaries only when parallelism, specialization, or independent verification repays their latency, serialization, information loss, and governance cost.
The protocol layer
agent-protocol-layer distinguishes two connection boundaries: MCP standardises how a model application reaches tools and data, while A2A describes discovery, tasks, messages, and artifacts between agents. Neither protocol supplies correctness, permissions, or competent tool choice by itself.
Three limits Weng names

Finite context length — vector stores extend reach, but their representational power is weaker than full attention.
Brittle long-horizon planning — LLMs struggle to revise a plan after an unexpected error, where humans learn from trial and error.
Natural language is an unreliable interface — the model may produce malformed output or decline to follow an instruction, which is why so much agent code is output parsing.



                  
                  Why doesn't a vector store simply solve the finite-context limit? 
                  
                

Its representational power is weaker than full attention. Retrieval extends reach but does not give the model the same access to the retrieved material that having it in context would.




                  
                  What does long-horizon planning break on? 
                  
                

Revising a plan after an unexpected error. Trial and error is where humans learn most, and it is the case LLM planners handle worst.


Multi-agent failure is structural
ai-agents-depth-design-principles-engineering cites the 2025 MAST study — ~150 execution traces across MetaGPT, ChatDev, AG2 and Magentic-One, human-annotated at κ = 0.88 — which found 14 failure modes in three groups: system design flaws, inter-agent alignment failures, and missing task verification. Simple fixes gained ChatDev only 15.6%, and the authors concluded these are design flaws rather than bugs.
This is the empirical answer to amans-ai-journal-primers-agents’s multi-agent collaboration pattern: the pattern is real, and current implementations of it fail for reasons that do not yield to patching.


                  
                  What made MAST conclude multi-agent failures are design flaws rather than bugs? 
                  
                

Simple fixes bought ChatDev only 15.6%. The 14 failure modes cluster into system design, inter-agent alignment and missing verification — categories patching does not reach.

sections/machine-learning/entities/lstm.title: LSTM
sections/machine-learning/entities/lstm.content:
LSTM
Long Short-Term Memory—a recurrent architecture introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997), whose repeating module uses a cell state and learned gates. It was designed to reduce the long-term-dependency difficulty of plain recurrent networks and became a widely used sequence model before attention-based architectures.
flowchart LR
  C1[Cell state arriving from the previous step] --> FG[Forget gate — what to drop]
  FG --> AD[Input gate, with a tanh proposing candidates — what to add]
  AD --> C2[Cell state — a belt of minor linear interactions only]
  C2 --> OG[Output gate — how much of the state to expose]
  OG --> H[Hidden output for this step]
  C2 --> C3[Carried forward, persisting unless actively forgotten]
  S[Step t must finish before step t+1] --> P[Training time scales with sequence length]
  P --> T[Displaced by the Transformer — on parallelism, not accuracy]

The cell state is the idea
understanding-lstm-networks-colahs-blog reduces the architecture to one image: the cell state is a conveyor belt running the length of the chain, subject only to minor linear interactions. Information flows along it unchanged unless something deliberately changes it. Everything else in the LSTM is machinery for deciding what changes.
Olah frames this as an inversion of the vanilla RNN’s practical tendency: the cell state supplies a path along which information can persist unless a gate changes it. That does not guarantee perfect memory—gate values, training, finite precision, and recurrent depth still matter—but it makes long retention easier to learn.


                  
                  What default does the cell state invert, relative to a vanilla RNN? 
                  
                

In a plain RNN information decays unless actively preserved; along the cell state it persists unless actively forgotten. Remembering becomes the default rather than the thing the network has to learn.




                  
                  Why does the cell state only take linear interactions?
                  
                

Because repeated non-linear transformation is what destroys information across many steps. Keeping the belt to minor linear operations is what lets a signal travel the length of the chain intact.


Three gates
A gate is a sigmoid layer followed by a pointwise multiply. The sigmoid emits a value in [0, 1] per component — 0 lets nothing through, 1 lets everything through.

Forget gate — what to drop from the cell state.
Input gate (with a tanh layer proposing candidate values) — what to add.
Output gate — what portion of the cell state to expose as this step’s output.

Olah’s running example carries all three: a language model holding the grammatical gender of the current subject so it can pick the right pronoun, dropping it when a new subject appears, and outputting singular/plural in case a verb comes next.


                  
                  Why is a gate a sigmoid followed by a pointwise multiply? 
                  
                

The sigmoid emits a value in [0, 1] per component, and multiplying by it scales that component between “let nothing through” and “let everything through” — so the gate is a learned, per-component, continuous filter rather than a switch.




                  
                  What distinguishes the output gate's job from the forget and input gates'? 
                  
                

Forget and input edit the cell state itself; the output gate decides only how much of that state is exposed as this step’s output. The network can hold something it is not currently using.


The one-line version
vip-cheatsheet-deep-learning compresses all of the above into a sentence — “a long short-term memory (LSTM) network is a type of RNN model that avoids the vanishing gradient problem by adding ‘forget’ gates” — plus a table naming each gate by the question it answers: input (“write to cell or not?”), forget (“erase a cell or not?”), output (“reveal a cell or not?”), and the gate proper (“how much writing?”). Set beside Olah’s essay it shows how much of understanding is pacing: the same content, at two very different speeds, for two different purposes.
The variants are a footnote
Peephole connections let the gates see the cell state. Coupled forget/input gates decide together. The GRU merges forget and input into one update gate and merges cell state with hidden state, ending up simpler. Greff et al. (2015) compared the popular variants and found them about the same; Jozefowicz et al. (2015) searched over ten thousand architectures. The lesson is that the cell-state-plus-gating idea is doing the work, not any particular arrangement of it.


                  
                  What do the LSTM variant comparisons establish? 
                  
                

That no particular gate arrangement matters much — the popular variants perform about the same across large comparisons and searches. The work is being done by the cell-state-plus-gating idea itself.


What it could do
unreasonable-effectiveness-recurrent-neural-networks supplies the empirical half — every experiment in that post is an LSTM. Trained on raw characters it produces plausible Shakespeare, valid markdown, syntactically coherent C, and LaTeX. Visualising individual cells finds one that switches on inside a URL, one that tracks position within a [[ ]] scope, one that counts through “www”. Roughly 5% of cells learn something legible, and nobody specified any of it.


                  
                  What is the significance of a single cell that switches on inside a URL? 
                  
                

The structure was never specified — the model was trained on raw characters. It shows that interpretable, discrete features emerge from character prediction alone, in roughly 5% of cells.


Why it stopped being the default for many large models
Parallelism was a central reason. An LSTM must process step t before step t+1, which limits parallel execution across sequence positions; the Transformer removed that recurrent dependency during training. The shift was not literally independent of accuracy or scaling behaviour, and LSTMs remain useful where their recurrence and state fit the task. Olah’s 2015 conclusion already identified attention as the next architectural step.


                  
                  What ended the LSTM's dominance, and what did not?
                  
                

A central factor was parallelism: recurrent step t precedes t+1, while transformer training can process positions in parallel. Accuracy, scaling, and task fit also contributed, and LSTMs were not eliminated.

sections/machine-learning/entities/marko.title: Markov Decision Process
sections/machine-learning/entities/marko.content:
Markov Decision Process
A Markov decision process (MDP) formalizes sequential choice under partly stochastic outcomes. amans-ai-journal-primers-reinforcement-learning defines it through states (S), actions (A), transition probabilities (P(s’\mid s,a)), rewards (R(s,a,s’)), and a discount factor (\gamma). A policy (\pi(a\mid s)) selects actions, and its objective is to maximize expected discounted return.
flowchart LR
  S[Current state] --> P[Policy selects an action]
  P --> A[Action]
  A --> R[Reward]
  A --> N[Stochastic next state]
  N --> S
  R --> O[Expected discounted return guides the objective]



                  
                  What does a policy specify in a Markov decision process? 
                  
                

An action distribution for each state.




                  
                  What objective does an MDP policy optimize? 
                  
                

Expected discounted return.


The transition distribution separates what the agent controls from what the environment determines. Choosing an action changes the distribution over possible next states; it does not guarantee one outcome. The discount factor controls how future reward contributes to the present objective, with smaller values emphasizing near outcomes and values closer to one extending the horizon.
The Markov assumption says the represented state contains the information needed to model the next transition. If relevant history is omitted, the representation is not Markov even if the algorithm treats it as one. Real applications may therefore require memory or belief state rather than a raw observation.
Why it matters
The MDP makes policy, value, and learning targets refer to the same object. value-return-advantage evaluates outcomes under a policy; temporal-difference-bootstrap uses successor estimates implied by the process; exploration-exploitation concerns which transitions to sample. Deep networks expand representation capacity but do not remove these structural assumptions.
Related

offline-policy-evaluation — estimating a target policy from logged transitions

sections/machine-learning/entities/multi.title: Multilayer Perceptron
sections/machine-learning/entities/multi.content:
Multilayer Perceptron
The plainest neural network there is: alternate a matrix multiplication (plus a bias) with a term-wise non-linear function, and stack. Nothing connects one position’s computation to another’s.
Why the second layer matters
10-neural-networks-nature-code reaches the architecture from its smallest case. A single perceptron multiplies inputs by weights, adds a bias, and thresholds the sum; geometrically, it can learn only one straight decision boundary. That is enough for AND or OR but not XOR, whose true and false cases are not linearly separable. Combining neurons makes the missing composition possible: one can represent OR, another NOT-AND, and their outputs together represent XOR. Hidden layers generalize this move from one boundary to learned combinations of boundaries.
The same construction also explains the bias. Without it, the decision boundary is forced through the origin because zero inputs always yield zero weighted input. A constant input of one with its own learned weight lets the boundary shift. In this geometric reading, weights determine the boundary’s orientation and the bias determines its offset.
flowchart LR
  A[Attention moves information between positions] --> X[Input vector]
  X --> U[Up-projection — rows are directions that ask a question]
  W[Weights say which pattern] --> U
  B[Bias says how much is enough] --> U
  U --> R[ReLU — a neuron is the value leaving it]
  N[Without the non-linearity the stack collapses to one linear function] --> R
  R --> D[Down-projection — columns are edits in embedding space]
  D --> O[Added back to what flowed in]
  O --> S[Neurons rarely carry one clean feature — see superposition]


a⁽¹⁾ = σ(W a⁽⁰⁾ + b)

but-neural-network-3blue1brown builds one to classify handwritten digits — 784 input neurons, two hidden layers of 16, 10 outputs, 13,002 weights and biases — and might-llms-store-facts-deep-learning then finds the identical structure inside GPT-3, where it holds about two-thirds of the 175 billion parameters. It is the same object at two very different scales, which is why it is worth one page.
What the parts are for
Sanderson derives every component from a requirement rather than asserting it:

Weights say which pattern a neuron responds to. Drawn as a 28×28 grid, a band of positive weights sums brightness in a region — but that also fires on blobs, so negative weights above and below make it fire on a narrow edge specifically.
The bias says how much is enough. A bias of −10 means the neuron only becomes meaningfully active once the weighted sum exceeds 10.
The non-linearity is structurally required, not decorative. Without it every layer is matrix-multiply-plus-offset, the whole network collapses into one linear function, and expressiveness drops dramatically.



                  
                  Why do the weights of an edge-detecting neuron carry negatives above and below the band? 
                  
                

A band of positive weights alone sums brightness in a region, which also fires on a solid blob. The negative weights either side make the neuron fire only when the bright region is narrow — an edge.




                  
                  What does the bias contribute that the weights cannot? 
                  
                

A threshold. Weights say which pattern the neuron responds to; the bias says how strong that match has to be before the neuron becomes meaningfully active.




                  
                  What happens to a deep network with the non-linearities removed? 
                  
                

Every layer becomes matrix-multiply-plus-offset, so the whole stack collapses into a single linear function. Depth buys nothing without it.


Why ReLU helped deep optimisation
Sigmoid saturates at both extremes, so its derivative can become very small and weaken a gradient propagated through many layers. ReLU retains a constant positive-side derivative, which often makes deep optimisation easier. It is still flat for negative inputs and can produce inactive or “dead” units, so the source’s claim that it “never flattens” is useful shorthand only on the positive side. might-llms-store-facts-deep-learning notes that transformer MLPs often use smoother alternatives such as GELU.


                  
                  Why did ReLU displace sigmoid, and why did depth make that decisive? 
                  
                

Sigmoid’s derivative becomes small at both extremes. ReLU keeps a nonzero derivative on its positive side, which often preserves stronger gradients through deep stacks—but it is flat on the negative side and can create dead units.


Two readings of the two matrices
The most useful thing might-llms-store-facts-deep-learning adds is that the two matrix multiplications should be read in different orientations:




















MatrixRead asMeaningW↑ (up-projection)rowseach row is a direction; the dot product asks a question about the input vectorW↓ (down-projection)columnseach column is a direction in embedding space; it is the edit added when its neuron is active
Rows ask, columns answer. In GPT-3, W↑ has just under 50,000 rows — exactly four times the 12,288 embedding dimensions, for no principled reason beyond hardware friendliness.


                  
                  Why are the two MLP matrices read in different orientations? 
                  
                

The up-projection’s rows are directions the input is dot-producted against — each row asks a question. The down-projection’s columns are directions in embedding space — each column is the edit added when its neuron fires. Rows ask, columns answer.


”Neurons” means the post-ReLU values
Worth pinning down, because the word is overloaded. In a transformer, a neuron is a value leaving the ReLU — active when positive, inactive at zero. The familiar dots-and-lines diagram depicts exactly this: a matrix multiplication followed by a term-wise non-linearity.
Inside a transformer it is the block that does not communicate
transformers-tech-behind-llms-deep-learn places it alternating with attention: attention lets vectors pass information between positions, then the MLP processes every vector independently and in parallel, and its output is added back to what flowed in. Attention moves information among positions; the MLP applies learned feature transformations at each position. Describing it as “storage” is the source’s interpretive model, not a literal separation between memory and computation.


                  
                  What is the division of labour between attention and the MLP block? 
                  
                

Attention moves information between positions; the MLP processes each position independently and adds its result back. One supplies context, the other supplies the stored capacity.


What it does not do, in either era

analyzing-our-neural-network-3blue1brown shows the digit network’s learned first-layer weights look almost random rather than edge-like, and it declares random noise to be a 5 with full confidence. Nothing in the architecture uses the fact that pixels are adjacent, or transfers a pattern learned in one region to another — the gap that motivates convolution.



                  
                  What does an MLP fail to exploit about image data? 
                  
                

That pixels are adjacent. Nothing in the architecture knows about spatial locality, and a pattern learned in one region cannot transfer to another — which is the gap convolution was invented to fill.



might-llms-store-facts-deep-learning finds the same disappointment at scale: an MLP neuron rarely represents one clean feature. See superposition.

Sources

sections/machine-learning/entities/rlhf.title: RLHF
sections/machine-learning/entities/rlhf.content:
RLHF
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: the third phase of the pipeline that turns a pretrained language model into a chat assistant. Teaching machines from human preferences is over a decade old, and OpenAI began exploring it as a safety technique — the original argument being that writing an explicit goal function for a complex objective is dangerous. That it also made better products is what brought the audience.
flowchart LR
  P[Pretraining — capability, about 98 percent of the compute] --> S[Supervised finetuning — format, answering not continuing]
  S --> C[Comparison data — which of two responses is better]
  C --> R[Reward model trained on the pairwise loss]
  R --> O[PPO optimises the SFT policy against the reward model]
  K[KL penalty against the SFT policy] --> O
  O --> A[Preference — the better of several valid answers]
  S -->|cloning answers past the model's knowledge| H[Hallucination, which RLHF made worse]

Three phases, three different problems

























PhaseSolvesScalePretrainingCapability — statistical knowledge of language~98% of total compute; trillions of tokensSupervised finetuningFormat — answering rather than continuing~14.5K (prompt, response) pairs for InstructGPTRLHFPreference — which of several valid answers is better50K prompts → 300K–1.8M comparisons
rlhf-reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedbackrlhf is blunt about the ratio: SFT and RLHF are best understood as unlocking capability the pretrained model already has but which prompting cannot reach.


                  
                  Why are SFT and RLHF described as unlocking capability rather than adding it?
                  
                

Pretraining takes ~98% of the compute and all the trillions of tokens. The later phases run on thousands of examples — far too little to install knowledge, but enough to reach knowledge prompting cannot.


Why SFT alone is insufficient: demonstration data shows the model which responses are plausible. It never says how good one is. A pretrained model asked “How to make pizza” may validly add context, ask follow-ups, or answer — SFT picks the third. It cannot rank two answers that are both in the right shape.


                  
                  What can demonstration data never tell a model? 
                  
                

How good a response is. Demonstrations show which responses are plausible, so SFT can fix the shape of an answer but cannot rank two answers that are both in the right shape.


The comparison trick
Labelers cannot give consistent absolute scores. They can reliably say which of two responses is better. So the Reward-Model trains on (prompt, winning_response, losing_response) with loss −log σ(sw − sl), which does nothing but push the winner above the loser. Absolute scores emerge from relative judgements.


                  
                  Why does the reward model train on comparisons rather than scores? 
                  
                

Labelers cannot give consistent absolute scores but can reliably say which of two responses is better. The loss only pushes the winner above the loser, and absolute scores emerge from those relative judgements.


The ceiling on this is measurable: inter-labeler agreement is about 73%. Ask ten people to rank two responses and seven agree.


                  
                  What does ~73% inter-labeler agreement bound? 
                  
                

The reward model’s achievable accuracy. Its training signal is only as consistent as the humans producing it, so roughly a quarter of the comparisons it learns from disagree with each other.


The KL term is load-bearing
PPO optimises the SFT model against the reward model, but the objective includes a KL-divergence penalty against the SFT policy. Without it, the policy drifts toward regions the reward model never saw, where it assigns extremely high scores by mistake, and optimisation chases those errors. A second term keeps performance on plain text completion from degrading.


                  
                  What breaks if the KL penalty is removed from PPO? 
                  
                

The policy drifts into regions the reward model never saw, where it scores things extremely highly by mistake, and optimisation chases those errors instead of the preference they were meant to stand in for.


This is the concrete form of reward-proxy-failure: you are not optimising human preference, but a learned proxy for it, and policy optimisation actively searches for gaps between the two.
It made hallucination worse
The finding rlhf-reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedbackrlhf refuses to soften. Schulman’s hypothesis is that behavior cloning causes hallucination — SFT trains the model to imitate answers a human wrote using knowledge the human had and the model does not, which teaches it to produce confident text beyond its knowledge. RLHF was expected to help. The InstructGPT paper shows it made hallucination worse, while improving enough else that labelers still preferred the result.


                  
                  By what mechanism would behaviour cloning cause hallucination?
                  
                

The model imitates answers a human wrote using knowledge the human had and it does not. What it learns from those examples is the habit of producing confident text past the edge of what it knows.


Why it works: three hypotheses, no proof
Via Yoav Goldberg — the diversity hypothesis (SFT penalises valid-but-different answers), the negative feedback hypothesis (demonstrations only ever show good responses; RL can show bad ones), and the hallucination hypothesis. Huyen states plainly that she has not seen a foolproof argument for why RLHF beats SFT.
The agent-era update
ai-agents-depth-design-principles-engineering places RLHF inside a wider post-training landscape (Ch. 7) and adds two things Huyen’s 2023 account predates. First, an explicit account of when to choose SFT and when to choose RL, rather than treating the three phases as a fixed pipeline everyone runs. Second, multi-turn credit assignment: RLHF as described scores a single response, but an agent’s reward arrives after a long trajectory of tool calls, which is the credit-assignment problem from classical RL returning at the application layer.
The classical vocabulary sharpens the mapping. A sampled generation has a realised return; a critic estimates expected return; advantage measures whether a chosen token or action did better than the policy’s baseline. PPO is an on-policy method in the sense captured by on-vs-off-policy-learning, so new policy updates depend on trajectories close to the current policy rather than unrestricted reuse of old generations.


                  
                  Why does the agent setting reopen credit assignment for RLHF? 
                  
                

RLHF as described scores one response. An agent’s reward arrives only after a long trajectory of tool calls, so something must decide which of those steps earned it.


Li’s stated priority — data and environment matter more than algorithms — is a direct echo of the reward-model problem: the algorithm is not usually what limits you.

sections/machine-learning/entities/retri.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
sections/machine-learning/entities/retri.content:
Retrieval Augmented Generation
Giving a language model access to an external knowledge source at query time, so that what it knows is not limited to what is in its weights. The claim underneath: weights are an expensive and uncorrectable place to store facts, and a database is a cheap and correctable one.
flowchart LR
  I[Ingest — chunk, embed, store the corpus] --> Q[Embed the query in the same space]
  Q --> R[Retrieve semantically similar segments]
  V[Vector store — flexible, returns confident irrelevance] --> R
  GR[Graph store — precise, needs near-exact matching] --> R
  SQ[Relational SQL — reliable, semantically rigid] --> R
  R --> K[Re-rank — the stage most implementations skip]
  K --> G[Generate — retrieved context plus the query]



                  
                  What is the argument for keeping facts out of the weights? 
                  
                

Weights are an expensive and uncorrectable place to store a fact; a database is cheap and correctable. Knowledge held outside the model can be audited, updated and cited.


The pipeline

Ingest — choose a retrieval-chunking-boundary, represent the units, and store them.
Embed the query — the same embedding space.
Retrieve — find semantically similar segments.
Re-rank — run the retrieval-reranking-funnel for precision, business rules, personalisation, context, and response budget.
Generate — concatenate retrieved context with the query and hand the whole thing to the model.

amans-ai-journal-primers-retrieval-augmented treats step 4 as the one people skip and shouldn’t. Stated plainly, the LLM is the last and least interesting stage; nearly all the engineering difficulty lives in retrieval.


                  
                  Which stage of a RAG pipeline carries most of the engineering difficulty? 
                  
                

Retrieval — and re-ranking in particular, the stage most implementations skip. The LLM is the last and least interesting step.


Three retriever families

Vector database — dense embeddings (BERT-style) or sparse (TF-IDF). Semantically flexible, and will happily return confidently irrelevant neighbours.
Graph or structured retrieval — traverses explicit entities and relations. It can answer relational queries directly, but depends on schema quality, extraction, and translating the question into the right path.
Relational SQL — structured and reliable, semantically rigid.



                  
                  What is the trade between a vector store and a graph store as retrievers? 
                  
                

Dense retrieval is flexible enough to recover paraphrases but can return irrelevant neighbours. Graph retrieval exploits explicit relations, but only relations the system represented and queried correctly. The trade is learned semantic similarity against structured relational coverage.


hybrid-retrieval combines lexical exact-term matching, dense semantic retrieval, metadata filters, and structured paths to improve candidate recall; its practical problem is score normalization or fusion before unlike candidates can be compared.
Retrieval or memory, depending who is asking
llm-powered-autonomous-agents-lillog describes the same machinery under a different name. What RAG calls a vector store, the agent literature calls long-term memory: an external store the agent attends to at query time, contrasted with the short-term memory of the context window. The engineering is identical — approximate nearest neighbour search via LSH, ANNOY, HNSW, FAISS or ScaNN — and Weng’s caveat applies to both framings: a vector store extends reach, but its representational power is weaker than full attention.
Where it goes
Multi-hop RAG chains retrievals when one lookup cannot answer the question, preserving each intermediate dependency and its provenance. Hierarchical and multimodal RAG extend the index. Agentic RAG makes retrieval a decision the model takes — which store, how many hops, whether to retrieve at all — rather than a fixed pipeline stage, which is where this entity meets LLM-Agent.


                  
                  What changes when RAG becomes agentic? 
                  
                

Retrieval stops being a fixed pipeline stage and becomes a decision the model takes — which store to hit, how many hops, whether to retrieve at all.


RAG vs. long context is treated as a design trade rather than a winner-take-all contest. Retrieval reduces tokens and isolates evidence; long context preserves material a retriever might omit. Longer windows change what needs retrieving and move the cost around.
RAG 2.0 means optimising retriever and generator end to end instead of bolting a frozen retriever onto a frozen model.


                  
                  Why doesn't a longer context window simply retire retrieval? 
                  
                

It changes what needs retrieving and moves the cost around rather than removing it. The question is treated as open, not settled by window size.


The alternative it competes with
When a model does not know something there are two broad responses: look it up, or change the weights. Domain pretraining or supervised finetuning can internalise patterns, while RLHF primarily tunes preferences and behaviour rather than installing general knowledge. Retrieval keeps evidence outside the weights, where it can be audited, updated, access-controlled, and cited.
Evaluate the halves separately
component-wise-rag-evaluation separates retrieval precision, recall, and relevance from groundedness and answer quality. A system that answers badly may have retrieved perfectly, or retrieved garbage and generated from it faithfully. One aggregate score cannot distinguish those, and they call for opposite fixes.


                  
                  Why can't one aggregate score diagnose a RAG system? 
                  
                

A bad answer can come from perfect retrieval badly used, or from garbage retrieval faithfully used. The two look identical end-to-end and need opposite fixes.

sections/machine-learning/entities/rewar.title: Reward Model
sections/machine-learning/entities/rewar.content:
Reward Model
A learned scoring function that takes a (prompt, response) pair and returns a scalar. It exists because the reward in RLHF cannot be written down: nobody can specify “a good answer” as a function, but people can recognise one.
flowchart LR
  R[A good answer cannot be written as a function] --> C[But people can recognise one]
  C --> P[Pairwise comparisons — the winner pushed above the loser]
  P --> M[A learned scorer, initialised from the SFT model]
  M --> S[Absolute scores emerge from ordering consistently]
  M --> L1[Preferences are not one function — it averages a disagreement]
  M --> L2[About 73 percent labeler agreement caps its accuracy]
  M --> L3[Off its training distribution the scores go wildly wrong]
  L3 --> H[A policy hunting maxima is hunting those errors specifically]
  H --> K[The KL penalty pins the policy where the scorer is valid]



                  
                  Why does a reward model have to be learned rather than written? 
                  
                

Nobody can specify “a good answer” as a function, but people can recognise one. Fitting a scorer to recognition is the only route from the judgement that exists to the scalar the optimiser needs.


Trained on comparisons, not scores
Asking labelers for absolute quality scores produces data too inconsistent to learn from. Asking which of two responses is better does not. So the training data is (prompt, winning_response, losing_response) and the loss is

−log σ(sw − sl)

which is large when the winner scores below the loser and small otherwise. The model is never told what a 7/10 looks like; absolute scores are an emergent side effect of consistently ordering pairs.


                  
                  Where do a reward model's absolute scores come from, if it is never shown one? 
                  
                

They are a side effect of consistently ordering pairs. The loss only ever pushes a winner above a loser; a usable scale falls out of doing that consistently across the data.


Practical detail from rlhf-reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedbackrlhf: ranking four responses A > B > C > D yields six pairs, so annotator time multiplies. And initialising the reward model from the SFT model works better than training from scratch — the intuition being that a scorer must be at least as capable as the thing it scores.


                  
                  Why initialise the reward model from the SFT model rather than from scratch? 
                  
                

A scorer has to be at least as capable as the thing it scores. Starting from the policy’s own weights gives it the understanding of the responses it is being asked to rank.


Three limits, all structural
1. Preferences are not one function. Huyen prefers the losing response in an example from Anthropic’s HH-RLHF dataset and says so in the post. Human preferences are diverse and cannot be captured in a single mathematical formulation — so the reward model is not approximating a fact, it is averaging a disagreement.


                  
                  What is a reward model actually approximating, if not a fact? 
                  
                

A disagreement. Human preferences are diverse and do not reduce to one function, so fitting a single scorer to them averages people who genuinely want different answers.


2. Agreement caps accuracy. Inter-labeler agreement runs around 73%. The reward model cannot be more reliable than the signal it was fit to.
3. It is only valid where it has seen data. Off its training distribution the reward model can assign badly wrong scores. Since the policy is actively searching for high scores, it will find those errors. This is reward-proxy-failure under optimisation pressure, and it is why the RLHF objective carries a KL penalty pinning the policy near the SFT model — the constraint exists specifically to keep the policy inside the region where the reward model is more trustworthy.


                  
                  Why is a policy searching for high reward guaranteed to find a reward model's errors? 
                  
                

Because the errors are high scores. Off-distribution mistakes look exactly like the objective, so an optimiser hunting maxima is hunting them specifically — the KL penalty exists to keep it where the scorer is valid.


The same problem, older name
amans-ai-journal-primers-reinforcement-learning treats reward design as a first-class challenge in classical RL: sparse and delayed rewards break credit assignment, and reward shaping — adding intermediate rewards to guide the agent — is the standard mitigation, with no general solution. The reward model is what reward design becomes when the reward cannot be hand-specified at all: instead of shaping a reward function, you fit one. Its scalar then supplies the trajectory signal from which return, value, and advantage are estimated.


                  
                  How does a reward model relate to classical reward design? 
                  
                

It is the same problem past the point where hand-specification is possible. Classical RL shapes a reward function you can write; when you cannot write one at all, you fit one from data instead.


Schulman’s proposed fix for hallucination is a reward-model change — punish the model more for making things up — which is reward shaping under a different name.

sections/machine-learning/entities/trans.title: Transformer
sections/machine-learning/entities/trans.content:
Transformer
The architecture introduced in Attention is All You Need (2017): a stack of encoders and decoders in which the only operation connecting positions to each other is self-attention. Everything else — the feed-forward network, the residual connections, the layer normalisation — acts on each position independently.
That single structural fact is the whole advantage. Because positions interact only in the attention layer, the rest of the network runs in parallel across the sequence, which is what removed the sequential training bottleneck that limited LSTM models.
flowchart TD
  S[Positions interact only inside the attention layer] --> P[Everything else runs in parallel across the sequence]
  P --> T[The sequential training bottleneck is removed]
  S --> Q[Cost becomes quadratic in sequence length]
  Q --> LC[Long-context research exists because of this cell]
  S --> O[Order is no longer implicit in a recurrence]
  O --> PE[Positional encoding added back into the embeddings]
  S --> M[Masking — future positions to minus infinity, so generation stays causal]
  S --> MO[Indifferent to modality — patches can play the role tokens play]
  MO --> B[Encodes how to spend compute, not what is true about language]



                  
                  Why can a Transformer train in parallel across a sequence when an RNN cannot? 
                  
                

Positions interact only inside the attention layer. Everything else — feed-forward, residuals, layer norm — acts on each position independently, so there is no step-by-step dependency to serialise on.


What replaced what

























Recurrent modelsTransformerState carried step by stepEvery position attends to every other from layer oneO(n·d²) — linear in sequence length, quadratic in hidden dimensionO(n²·d) — quadratic in sequence length, linear in model dimensionOrder is implicit in the recurrenceOrder must be added back as positional encodingLong-range dependency degrades with distanceDistance costs nothing; sequence length costs quadratically
The complexity row is the honest trade, and amans-ai-journal-primers-transformers spells it out: Transformers win on parallelism and lose quadratically on sequence length. Long-context research exists because of that cell in the table.


                  
                  What does the Transformer pay for removing the recurrence? 
                  
                

Cost quadratic in sequence length (O(n²·d)) instead of linear. Distance between two positions becomes free, but total length becomes expensive — which is why long-context research exists.




                  
                  Why does a Transformer need positional encoding at all? 
                  
                

Order was implicit in the recurrence it removed. With every position attending to every other from layer one, nothing in the architecture distinguishes sequence order, so it has to be added back into the embeddings.


The pieces

Query / key / value — three learned projections per position. Score by dot product of query against every key, scale by √dk, softmax, weight the values, sum.
Multi-head attention — eight independently initialised Q/K/V sets, giving eight “representation subspaces,” concatenated and projected by WO. In Alammar’s example one head binds “it” to “the animal” while another binds it to “tired.”
Positional encoding — sinusoidal vectors added to the input embeddings, because removing recurrence removed all notion of order.
Masking — decoder self-attention sets future positions to −inf before the softmax, so generation stays causal.
Cross-attention — queries from one source, keys and values from another. This is the mechanism that makes the architecture multimodal rather than merely linguistic.



                  
                  What does multi-head attention buy over a single attention head? 
                  
                

Several independently initialised Q/K/V sets give several representation subspaces, so different heads can bind the same word to different antecedents — one head tying “it” to “the animal” while another ties it to “tired.”




                  
                  What does decoder masking do, and why is it necessary? 
                  
                

It sets future positions to −inf before the softmax. Without it, attention over the whole sequence would let a position see the tokens it is supposed to be predicting, so generation would not be causal.


Why it generalised beyond language
amans-ai-journal-primers-transformers argues the durable claim is not that Transformers are good at text but that they are indifferent to modality. The Vision Transformer’s architecture is nearly identical to the 2017 original; the only real adaptation is cutting the image into 16×16 patches so that patches can play the role tokens play. Earlier architectures were, in Chadha’s phrase, “one trick ponies” with a separate specialised model per data type.


                  
                  What is the single adaptation that turns a Transformer into a Vision Transformer? 
                  
                

Cutting the image into 16×16 patches so patches can play the role tokens play. The architecture is otherwise nearly identical to the 2017 original — which is the evidence that it is indifferent to modality.


The prediction that landed
understanding-lstm-networks-colahs-blog closes, in August 2015, by naming attention as the next big step after LSTMs. unreasonable-effectiveness-recurrent-neural-networks, three months earlier, calls attention “the most interesting recent architectural innovation in neural networks.” Both were written two years before the Transformer paper.
Read against bitter-lesson, the Transformer is an awkward case: it is unmistakably a piece of human architectural design, and Sutton’s argument is that such design plateaus. The reconciliation is that it encodes almost no knowledge about language — it is a general method for converting compute into performance, which is exactly the kind of thing Sutton says survives.


                  
                  How does the Transformer escape the Bitter Lesson's verdict on human architectural design? 
                  
                

It encodes almost no knowledge about language. What Sutton says plateaus is built-in domain knowledge; a general method for turning compute into performance is the category he says survives.

sections/machine-learning/index.content:
Machine Learning

A section of Symposium · Subject: How machines learn from data — architectures, training, evaluation, and the systems built on them


Authors: Grant Sanderson 26% (9) · Afshine Amidi 14% (5) · Aman Chadha 14% (5) · Shervine Amidi 14% (5) · Lilian Weng 6% (2) · Vinija Jain 5% (2) · Andrej Karpathy 3% (1) · Bojie Li 3% (1) · Chip Huyen 3% (1) · Christopher Olah 3% (1) · Daniel Shiffman 3% (1) · Jay Alammar 3% (1) · Richard S. Sutton 3% (1) — 35 sources in total


This is the central node of the section. Every concept, entity, topic, and source below
connects back here.
Browse: all sources in this section

The Core Thesis
Drawn from the twelve works this section is built on:


Methods that convert computation into performance outlast methods that encode human understanding of a domain. bitter-lesson argues this from four historical repeats — chess, Go, speech, vision — and names search and learning as the only two things that scale arbitrarily. unreasonable-effectiveness-recurrent-neural-networks demonstrates it four years earlier, without naming it.


The history of architecture is a sequence of answers to one question: how does information reach across distance? Gating (LSTM), then one-hop attention (self-attention, Transformer), then external memory (Retrieval-Augmented-Generation). Each answer trades the previous problem for a new one — the current binding constraint is the context window, which is the attention answer’s bill coming due.


What a system optimises for is never quite what you wanted, and the gap is where the interesting failures live. evaluation-metrics treats metric choice as a modelling decision; Reward-Model is what happens when the metric must itself be learned, complete with a 73% agreement ceiling and a KL penalty to stop the policy exploiting its errors.



Domain Map













































DomainFocusFoundationsThe classical core every later result assumes — gradient-descent, bias-variance-tradeoffArchitecturesHow the network is wired — Transformer, LSTM, self-attention, long-term-dependencyGenerative modellingLearning to produce rather than classify — Diffusion-ModelsTraining and alignmentTurning a pretrained model into a usable one — RLHF, Reward-ModelReinforcement learningLearning from consequences rather than labels — exploration-exploitationGrounding and retrievalKnowledge kept outside the weights — Retrieval-Augmented-GenerationAgentsThe model as controller rather than generator — LLM-Agent, context-engineering, harness-engineeringMeasurementWhat a claim about performance actually claims — evaluation-metricsResearch strategyWhat the field should spend its effort on — scaling-beats-knowledge-engineering

Open Questions

Does long context obviate retrieval, or relocate it? amans-ai-journal-primers-retrieval-augmented treats this as live rather than settled — longer windows change what needs retrieving and move the cost rather than removing it.
Why does RLHF beat SFT? Three hypotheses (diversity, negative feedback, hallucination) and, in rlhf-reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedbackrlhf’s own words, no foolproof argument for any of them.
Does architectural design contradict the bitter lesson? The Transformer is human design, and it delivered the largest recent gain. The reconciliation offered in scaling-beats-knowledge-engineering — that it encodes how to use compute, not what is true about language — is a claim worth testing against the next architecture rather than a settled answer.
Can an agent revise a plan after an unexpected error? llm-powered-autonomous-agents-lillog names this as an open limitation; amans-ai-journal-primers-agents adds protocols and frameworks around it without resolving it.
