sections/machine-learning/sources/10-neu.title: Chapter 10: Neural Networks
sections/machine-learning/sources/10-neu.content:
Chapter 10: Neural Networks

Neural networks become understandable when learning is reduced to repeated, visible operations: weight inputs, measure error, adjust the weights, and test whether the resulting decision rule generalizes to data it has not seen.

Key Concepts

Connectionist learning — Shiffman distinguishes a neural network from a linear sequence of programmed instructions. Many simple nodes process signals in parallel, while weighted connections adapt in response to error. This makes the network a complex adaptive system: the programmer supplies examples and a learning process rather than directly encoding every decision rule.
Three learning settings — supervised learning compares predictions with labelled answers; unsupervised learning searches unlabelled data for patterns such as clusters; reinforcement learning adjusts behaviour from environmental rewards and penalties. The chapter develops supervised learning and defers reinforcement learning to the book’s neuroevolution chapter.
The perceptron as the smallest useful model — a single neuron multiplies each input by a weight, sums the results, and sends the sum through a sign activation function. A constant bias input lets its decision boundary move away from the origin. The model can learn a binary boundary by updating each weight in proportion to error × input × learning constant.
Learning rate controls correction size — larger updates can reach a solution quickly but overshoot useful weights; smaller updates refine the boundary more cautiously and require more training. Shiffman’s animated classifier makes the evolving boundary visible rather than treating its parameters as unexplained numbers.
Weights have geometric meaning — for two-dimensional data, the learned weights define a line separating the two classes; in higher dimensions they define a separating hyperplane. Input normalization prevents one feature’s numeric scale from dominating this geometry.
Why a network needs layers — one perceptron can solve only linearly separable problems. XOR cannot be divided by one line, but combining neurons can compose the OR and NOT-AND boundaries that solve it. A Multilayer-Perceptron adds hidden layers for these nonlinear relationships, and backpropagation assigns responsibility for the final error across their many connections.
Problem definition comes before tooling — Shiffman adds a “step 0” to the standard machine-learning life cycle: decide what must be predicted. A discrete label makes the task classification; a continuous quantity makes it regression. That choice determines the training data, the output representation, and the model architecture.
The full life cycle — collect and prepare data, choose a model, train it, evaluate it, tune hyperparameters, and deploy it. Preparation includes consistent data shape, normalization, and separate training, validation, and test sets. Overfitting appears when performance improves on training examples while deteriorating on held-out validation data.
Libraries hide machinery, not decisions — ml5.js builds on TensorFlow.js to make browser-based neural networks accessible to p5.js creative coders. Its gesture-classifier example still requires the practitioner to define inputs and labels, gather representative examples, normalize them, choose epochs, inspect loss, preserve held-out data, and send deployment inputs with the same shape used in training.

The worked gesture classifier deliberately uses only eight hand-written examples for a task that ordinary conditionals could solve. Its value is diagnostic: because the expected directions are obvious, a learner can see every stage from labelled vectors through loss and confidence scores. Shiffman warns that this toy setup is too small for a proper train–validation–test split and is especially vulnerable to overfitting; production use requires broader examples that represent how gestures actually vary.
Connects to

sections/machine-learning/sources/ai-age.title: AI Agents in Depth: Design Principles and Engineering Practice
sections/machine-learning/sources/ai-age.content:
AI Agents in Depth: Design Principles and Engineering Practice

An agent is exhaustively described by LLM + Context + Tools, and the gap between a demo that runs and a product that works is not model quality but the harness — the constraining, verifying and correcting code wrapped around the model.

Key Concepts

The core formula, and its three readings. Agent = LLM + Context + Tools, all three indispensable. Intuitively: brain + eyes + hands and feet. Formally, for readers coming from RL: LLM ↔ policy, Context ↔ observation space, Tools ↔ action space. Li is careful that “eyes” is a rough analogy — Context includes tool definitions, so what the agent sees also includes what it can do.
Harness engineering — the book’s distinctive contribution. Expanded, the production-grade composition is Agent = LLM + [Context + Tools + Constrain + Verify + Correct] = Model + Harness. The three added layers are what handle a model that hallucinates tools, picks the wrong one, or cannot recover from an error. Li’s framing: the first half of Chapter 1 answers what an agent is, the second answers how one runs reliably in production, and the harness is where competitiveness lives once everyone has access to similar models.
Context as the binding constraint (Ch. 2) — context determines the upper limit of agent capability. Concrete engineering follows: KV-cache-friendly context design (ordering the prompt so the cache survives across turns), dynamic prompts and agent skills, an “agent status bar” carrying meta-information about the trajectory, and explicit context-compression strategies.
Memory and knowledge (Ch. 3) — user memory systems, RAG as the knowledge-acquisition pipeline, and “beyond flat text”: knowledge graphs and structured retrieval where chunked embeddings fail.
Tools as a design discipline (Ch. 4) — classification, universal design principles, MCP and the tool-selection problem that arrives once there are too many tools to fit in context, and event-driven asynchronous agents.
Evaluation gets a full chapter (Ch. 6, twelve sections) — automated evaluation environments, task-dataset design, statistical significance of results, observability, and the progression from external benchmarks to internal evaluation infrastructure to simulation environments that feed post-training.
Post-training (Ch. 7) — pretraining/SFT/RL as one panorama, when to choose SFT over RL, RLHF, algorithm comparison, and multi-turn credit assignment. Li’s blunt claim: data and environment matter more than algorithms.
Multi-agent failure is structural, not incidental (Ch. 10) — cites the 2025 MAST taxonomy, built from ~150 human-annotated traces across MetaGPT, ChatDev, AG2 and Magentic-One (annotator agreement κ = 0.88). Fourteen failure modes in three groups: system design flaws, inter-agent alignment failures, and missing task verification. Simple fixes bought ChatDev only 15.6% — the researchers concluded these are design flaws, not bugs. Li adds two engineering modes of his own: concurrency conflicts on shared file systems, and cascading error amplification.


“Agents are something entirely new in the history of cosmic evolution: by generating code they can bootstrap and evolve themselves, like a programmer who writes another programmer, who in turn writes the next.”

sections/machine-learning/sources/amans-.title: Primers • Agents
sections/machine-learning/sources/amans-.content:
Primers • Agents

Agentic systems trade fixed human-written control paths for model-directed decisions in degrees; reliable designs choose that boundary deliberately, build evaluation and tool contracts around it, and add multi-agent coordination only when task structure earns the cost.

System boundary
Following Anthropic’s vocabulary, the primer places workflows and agents under the broader category of agentic systems. In a workflow, code fixes the route through models and tools; in an agent, the model dynamically chooses its route. agent-control-boundary treats this as a design variable rather than a binary badge: autonomy can be granted for retrieval, planning, tool choice, or termination while other transitions remain deterministic.
The basic LLM-Agent contains a model core, memory, tools, and planning. Short-term state supports the current task; vector retrieval supplies longer-lived context; tools connect the model to APIs and executable environments; planning decomposes and reprioritizes work. Production reliability depends on the surrounding harness-engineering layer—context discovery, sandboxing, durable execution, review, evaluation, and recovery—not on autonomy alone.
Reusable workflow patterns
The primer separates four agentic design patterns: reflection, tool use, planning, and multi-agent collaboration. Its reflection-evaluator-loop turns a one-pass answer into generate, critique, externally test, and revise. A separate evaluator or executable test can expose errors that self-critique misses. Prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-worker, and evaluator-optimizer are presented as workflow compositions; none requires handing the whole process to one autonomous agent.
Tool use expands the action space, but availability is not reliability. tool-interface-design captures the operational contract: descriptions and schemas must make selection and argument construction legible; validation, bounded permissions, useful errors, and result formatting must make failure recoverable. The model’s decision to call a function is only one step in that contract.
Architecture economics
single-vs-multi-agent-economics frames the architecture choice as coherence versus coordination. One agent retains a unified context and full token budget, which suits tightly coupled or sequential reasoning. Multiple agents can parallelize independent searches, specialize roles, filter noisy contexts, or add explicit verification, but every boundary serializes state and introduces latency, information loss, conflict, and governance work. The primer recommends starting with a single-agent baseline and escalating when decomposition is intrinsic and measured gains justify the overhead.
Cursor is the production case study: its agent harness joins dynamic context discovery, semantic retrieval, specialized coding models, sandboxed execution, offline and online evals, trace learning, review, durable cloud runs, and planner-worker coordination. The case supports the primer’s broader claim that deployed agent quality lives in the system around the model.
Protocols and retrieval
agent-protocol-layer distinguishes MCP, which standardizes a model application’s access to tools and data, from A2A, which describes discovery, tasks, messages, and artifacts between agents. The protocols solve different connection boundaries and do not by themselves make an agent safe or competent.
agentic-retrieval-routing moves retrieval from a fixed pre-generation stage into the control loop. An agent can decide whether retrieval is needed, which source or specialist to query, and whether another hop is warranted. This flexibility can improve multi-source work, but it adds routing errors, latency, cost, and harder evaluation relative to vanilla Retrieval-Augmented-Generation.
The later sections survey reinforcement learning for agent policies, benchmarks, use cases, frameworks, and responsible-agent governance. They broaden the map but do not establish that higher autonomy is generally better; the repeated design principle is measured control over what a model may decide and how its actions are checked.

sections/machine-learning/sources/amans-.title: Primers • Evaluation Metrics
sections/machine-learning/sources/amans-.content:
Primers • Evaluation Metrics

Aman Chadha surveys evaluation as a family of question-specific instruments.
Every scalar discards structure, so metric selection decides which errors,
scales, positions, and notions of similarity the report will preserve.

Classification: start with the error table
For binary classification, the confusion matrix separates true positives, true
negatives, false positives, and false negatives. Accuracy recombines all four but
can conceal a classifier that predicts only the majority class. classification-error-tradeoffs
keeps the denominators visible:

Precision asks how many predicted positives are actually positive.
Recall or sensitivity asks how many actual positives were found.
Specificity asks how many actual negatives were rejected.
Negative predictive value asks how many predicted negatives are actually negative.

A threshold moves the false-positive/false-negative balance. Precision and recall
should therefore be reported together rather than selecting the favorable side of
the trade-off. F₁ uses their harmonic mean, but its equal weighting and omission of
true negatives can be misleading when error costs or class structure differ. ROC,
precision–recall, DET, AUROC, and equal-error-rate views each preserve a different
part of the threshold sweep.
Regression: choose an error geometry
regression-loss-geometry separates absolute, squared, rooted, logarithmic, and
variance-relative summaries. MAE keeps errors in the target unit and weights them
linearly. MSE makes large residuals dominate; RMSE restores the target unit without
removing that emphasis. RMSLE shifts attention toward relative error, while R² and
adjusted R² compare explained variation and penalise added parameters differently.
No member is “the regression metric” independent of the application.
Structured outputs need structured questions
Object detection composes overlap and ranking: intersection-over-union defines a
match; average precision summarises a precision–recall curve; mAP averages across
classes or conditions. Code evaluation separates syntax, semantics, test success,
utility, human judgment, and runtime. Clustering scores such as silhouette and DBCV
describe partition geometry when ground-truth labels are absent; they do not prove
that the clusters are substantively correct.
Generated text: overlap, prediction, and semantics
Perplexity measures predictive fit to held-out text, while burstiness concerns
variation in generated output. reference-based-text-evaluation separates
surface overlap from embedding similarity: BLEU is precision-oriented n-gram
overlap, ROUGE is recall-oriented, BERTScore matches contextual token embeddings,
and MoverScore uses transport distance between embedded text. More references can
cover more valid phrasings, but every reference metric still inherits the quality
and scope of its reference set.
Ranking: relevance has position
rank-aware-evaluation follows cumulative gain into DCG and NDCG. DCG discounts
relevant items appearing later; NDCG divides by the ideal ordering so scores can be
compared across lists. The primer also lists MRR, MAP, hit rate, novelty, diversity,
and satisfaction measures, showing that ranking accuracy is only one objective of
a recommender.
Graph extraction

evaluation-metrics — cross-domain synthesis and component-wise evaluation
classification-error-tradeoffs — confusion-matrix denominators and thresholds
regression-loss-geometry — what each residual aggregation emphasises
reference-based-text-evaluation — lexical and semantic reference metrics
rank-aware-evaluation — relevance, order, normalisation, and beyond-accuracy goals

Written by Aman Chadha · original

sections/machine-learning/sources/amans-.title: Primers • Reinforcement Learning
sections/machine-learning/sources/amans-.content:
Primers • Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement learning replaces labelled correct answers with consequences from sequential action; this makes policy, value, exploration, credit assignment, reward design, and evaluation parts of one coupled problem.

The decision problem
The primer organizes RL as interaction among an agent, environment, state, action, reward, and policy. A Markov-Decision-Process adds transition dynamics and a discount factor, expressing the objective as expected cumulative—not merely immediate—reward. A policy may be deterministic or stochastic and represented by a table or network; deep RL changes the function approximator and scale, not the underlying sequential-decision problem.
value-return-advantage separates three quantities often blurred together. Return is the discounted reward actually realized along one trajectory. A state or action value is the expected return under a policy. Advantage compares one action’s value with the policy’s average action value in that state. The Bellman equation recursively joins immediate reward to discounted successor value.
How learning differs
Dynamic programming assumes a model and sweeps expectations; Monte Carlo learning waits for completed trajectories; temporal-difference-bootstrap updates from an observed reward plus the current estimate of the next state. Value-based methods learn which situations or actions are valuable, policy-gradient methods directly optimize action probabilities, and actor-critic methods pair a policy-producing actor with a value-estimating critic.
on-vs-off-policy-learning asks whether the data-producing behaviour policy is the same as the policy being evaluated or improved. On-policy methods learn from fresh trajectories under the current policy but discard data quickly. Off-policy methods can reuse experience from other policies, at the cost of correcting distribution mismatch and controlling instability. This distinction cuts across tabular, deep, and language-model RL.
Data, reward, and evaluation
Offline RL learns from a fixed log and cannot explore beyond its support; online RL can collect new trajectories and adapt, but exploration may be expensive or unsafe. offline-policy-evaluation addresses the deployment question—how to estimate a target policy from behaviour-policy data—through direct models, importance weighting, doubly robust combinations, fitted Q evaluation, or learned environment models. Each estimator trades modelling bias, variance, and sensitivity to policy mismatch.
The primer’s production coding-agent case study treats online RL as a system of fresh trajectories, reward instrumentation, regression gates, deployment slices, and drift monitoring. It emphasizes that the environment must expose outcomes close to the deployed objective. reward-proxy-failure captures the danger: suggestion acceptance, test passage, or another measurable proxy can be optimized without producing the intended result. Guardrails and multi-metric evaluation are part of reward design, not afterthoughts.
Persistent constraints
exploration-exploitation remains unresolved: too little exploration freezes a suboptimal policy; too much wastes or endangers interactions. Sample inefficiency makes millions of trials unacceptable in robotics, healthcare, or other costly environments. Sparse and delayed rewards make temporal credit assignment difficult, while high-dimensional state/action spaces, non-stationary data, function-approximation error, and sensitive hyperparameters make convergence fragile.
Policy optimisation for language models maps tokens to actions, generations to trajectories, and a learned Reward-Model to environmental feedback. Reference, reward, value, and policy models serve distinct roles; using RL vocabulary does not remove the need to validate what the learned reward actually represents.

sections/machine-learning/sources/amans-.title: Primers • Retrieval Augmented Generation
sections/machine-learning/sources/amans-.content:
Primers • Retrieval Augmented Generation

RAG makes external evidence a query-time dependency rather than a fixed part of model weights, so corpus design, chunk boundaries, candidate retrieval, reranking, evidence coverage, and component-level evaluation determine whether generation can be grounded.

The pipeline is an evidence funnel
The base Retrieval-Augmented-Generation pipeline ingests a corpus, represents retrievable units, transforms a query, retrieves candidates, selects evidence within a context budget, and synthesizes an answer. External knowledge can be refreshed, removed, access-controlled, and cited without retraining the language model. That advantage is conditional: missing, stale, or irrelevant retrieval places an upper bound on the generator.
retrieval-chunking-boundary makes ingestion a modelling decision. Small chunks improve local match but may sever definitions from qualifications; large chunks preserve context but add noise and consume prompt budget. Fixed-size, overlapping, sentence-aware, structure-aware, semantic, late-chunking, and late-interaction approaches choose different points in that tradeoff. The correct boundary depends on corpus structure, retriever limits, query type, and validation results.
Candidate discovery and selection
The primer separates lexical retrieval, dense semantic retrieval, graph or structured retrieval, and hybrid-retrieval. Sparse methods preserve exact terms; dense embeddings recover paraphrases; metadata filters enforce scope; graph or SQL paths exploit explicit structure. Combining methods broadens recall, but scores must be normalized or fused before candidates can be compared.
retrieval-reranking-funnel distinguishes cheap high-recall candidate generation from expensive high-precision selection. Cross-encoders, late-interaction models, instruction-following rerankers, metadata rules, personalization, and business constraints can reorder or discard candidates before synthesis. Retrieval is therefore not a single nearest-neighbour call.
multi-hop-retrieval-planning covers questions whose evidence dependencies cannot be satisfied by one query. An initial result supplies an entity or relation needed for the next retrieval; the system must plan intermediate questions, preserve provenance, and stop only when the chain supports the final answer. Hierarchical RAG uses a related coarse-to-fine route through document, section, and chunk levels.
Generation and evaluation
Long prompts do not guarantee that evidence is used. The primer discusses position sensitivity and “lost in the middle,” query rewriting for multi-turn dialogue, structured conversation state, and answer synthesis constrained to retrieved context. rag-vs-long-context treats retrieval and context capacity as complementary design choices: retrieval reduces tokens and isolates evidence, while long context preserves material a retriever might omit.
component-wise-rag-evaluation separates context precision, context recall, and relevance from groundedness, answer relevance, semantic similarity, and exact-match-style measures. An end-to-end score cannot reveal whether a failure came from ingestion, retrieval, reranking, or synthesis. Evaluation needs both component diagnostics and product-level outcomes.
Agentic and adaptive variants move retrieval decisions into the model’s control loop. agentic-retrieval-routing covers tool and source selection; its flexibility adds routing, latency, and stopping failures. “RAG 2.0” proposes optimizing retriever and generator jointly, which can improve the whole pipeline while making component attribution and update isolation harder.

sections/machine-learning/sources/amans-.title: Primers • Transformers
sections/machine-learning/sources/amans-.content:
Primers • Transformers

The Transformer earned its position not by being better at language but by being architecture-agnostic about modality: the same mechanism that lets every token attend to every other token also makes it the first plausible single architecture for text, vision, and audio at once.

Key Concepts

Built from the bottom — Chadha starts below the architecture, at one-hot encoding and dot products, then representation learning for NLP, then attention. The primer is a reference manual, not an essay: derivations, PyTorch implementations of scaled dot-product attention (batched and unbatched, with shape assertions), tokenizer training, and an end-to-end trace from input embeddings to next-token prediction.
The contrast with recurrence is about locality — a vanilla language model groups nearby words first. A Transformer connects every element to every other from the first layer, so it sees traces of the entire input as soon as training starts. Chadha’s worked example: “The owl spied a squirrel. It tried to grab it with its talons but only got the end of its tail” — a model attending only locally cannot resolve the pronouns.
The contrast with convolution is about where global context appears — a CNN starts local (edges, corners) and builds toward global over many layers. In a Transformer even the first attention layer models global context. Chadha’s image: a CNN zooms out from a pixel; a Transformer brings the whole fuzzy image into focus.
Vision Transformers change almost nothing — ViT’s architecture is nearly identical to the 2017 original. Self-attention over every pixel would be prohibitive, so the image is cut into patches (16×16 by default) that act as tokens. The adaptation is discretisation, not redesign.
Multimodality is the real argument — earlier architectures were “one trick ponies” with a separate specialised model per data type. Cross-attention — queries from one source, keys and values from another — gives one architecture that fuses modalities, which Chadha frames as a convergence of neural net architectures rather than merely another NLP result.
The complexity trade is explicit — RNNs are O(n·d²): n sequential steps, each dominated by a d×d matrix multiply. Transformers are O(n²·d): every pair of tokens compared, at model dimension d. Transformers win on parallelism and on d, and lose quadratically on sequence length — which is the whole reason long-context research exists.
An unusual connection — a section relating Transformers to graph neural networks, treating self-attention as message passing over a fully connected graph of tokens.

Connects to

Written by Aman Chadha · original

sections/machine-learning/sources/analyz.title: Analyzing our neural network
sections/machine-learning/sources/analyz.content:
Analyzing our neural network

Sanderson returns to the edge-detection story he motivated the architecture with and reports that it is false: the trained network’s first-layer weights look almost random, it classifies 96% of unseen digits correctly anyway, and it will confidently declare random noise to be a 5 — so accuracy is not evidence that a network learned the structure you imagined.

Key Concepts

The accuracy numbers, stated plainly — the two-hidden-layers-of-16 network gets about 96% of new images right. Tweaking the hidden-layer structure gets it to about 98%. Modern networks with more sophisticated ideas reach 99.75%, at which point Sanderson doubts most humans do better on MNIST.
The hypothesis from chapter 1 does not hold — visualising the first-to-second-layer weights as pixel grids shows not isolated little edges but patterns that “look, well, almost random.” Some loose structure, “hardly the ones we might expect.” In the 13,002-dimensional space of parameters the network “found itself a happy little local minimum” that classifies well without picking up generalisable patterns.
The random-noise test is the sharp diagnostic — feed in random pixels and the network confidently reports a 5. An intelligent system might activate no output neuron strongly, or all of them evenly. Instead it is as sure about noise as about a real digit. Sanderson’s conclusion: “even if this network can recognize digits, it has no idea how to draw them.”
The cost function is the culprit, and it was never asked to do otherwise — from the network’s point of view “the entire universe consists of nothing but clearly defined unmoving digits centered on a tiny grid,” and the cost function “never gave it an incentive to be anything but utterly confident in its decisions.” Overconfidence is a property of the objective, not a bug in the weights.
The pedagogical defence — Sanderson answers the obvious objection to motivating a structure by a story that turns out wrong: the edge story “is not meant to be an end goal, but instead a starting point.” This is 1980s–90s technology, and you need it before the modern variants.
What is missing points directly at convolution — nothing in the learning algorithm lets a pattern learned in one region transfer to another, or supports inference about scale; in fact “nothing about our training algorithm even uses the fact that some pixels are adjacent to others.” Thinking about how to fix that is how you arrive at convolutional networks.
The interactive version carries an experiment the video could not — with live-updating neurons, draw a 3 and slowly extend it into an 8, watch the moment the prediction flips, and identify which second-layer neurons changed and why.


“It seems that in the unfathomably large 13,002-dimensional space of possible weights and biases, the network found itself a happy little local minimum that, despite successfully classifying most images, doesn’t exactly pick up on more generalizable patterns.”

sections/machine-learning/sources/are-di.title: What are Diffusion Models?
sections/machine-learning/sources/are-di.content:
What are Diffusion Models?

Each earlier family of generative model pays a price for tractability — GANs unstable adversarial training, VAEs a surrogate loss, flows a reversibility constraint on the architecture — and diffusion models avoid all three by fixing the forward process entirely and learning only how to reverse it.

Key Concepts

Forward process — a Markov chain that adds small Gaussian noise over T steps under a variance schedule βt. As T → ∞ the sample becomes isotropic Gaussian noise. Crucially it has a closed form: xt can be sampled directly from x0 via the reparameterisation trick, so training never has to simulate the chain step by step.
Reverse process — q(xt−1 | xt) is intractable because it would need the whole dataset, so a model pθ approximates it. When additionally conditioned on x0 the reverse posterior is tractable and Gaussian, which is what makes the training objective computable.
The objective decomposes — the variational lower bound splits into LT (constant, no learnable parameters, ignorable), a sum of KL terms between two Gaussians (closed form), and L0 (a separate discrete decoder in Ho et al. 2020). diffusion-noise-prediction carries the practical DDPM simplification: predict the sampled noise ε rather than parameterizing the reverse mean directly.
What is fixed and what is learned — unlike a VAE, the latent has the same dimensionality as the data and the inference procedure is fixed rather than learned. The model’s only job is denoising.
Connection to score-based methods — the same object arrives from stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, which samples from p(x) using only ∇x log p(x); injecting Gaussian noise into the updates is what avoids collapse into local minima. Noise-conditioned score networks and DDPM are the same idea from two directions.
Conditioning and control — diffusion-guidance separates classifier guidance, which steers with a separate classifier’s gradient, from classifier-free guidance, which learns conditional and unconditional predictions in one model and combines them during sampling.
The cost is sampling speed — a diffusion model needs many reverse steps. The fixes surveyed are fewer sampling steps, progressive distillation, consistency models, and moving the whole process into a compressed latent space (latent diffusion) rather than pixel space.
A living document — first published July 2021, then extended with classifier-free guidance, GLIDE, unCLIP, Imagen (2022), latent diffusion (2022), and distillation, consistency models and the architecture section (2024). The post’s date understates what it now contains.

What the graph separates
The fixed forward process, learned reverse transition, and variational objective define the model family. diffusion-noise-prediction explains why one randomly sampled timestep is enough for a training example and why an epsilon-prediction loss stands in for the relevant bound terms. diffusion-guidance explains how conditioning changes the reverse score and why increasing prompt adherence can reduce diversity or introduce artifacts. Sampling acceleration is a third, orthogonal problem: distillation, alternative solvers, consistency models, and latent-space diffusion reduce the cost of traversing the learned path without changing what guidance means.
The score-based connection supplies another view of the same learned vector field. Langevin-style dynamics use gradients of log density plus injected noise; noise-conditioned score networks learn those gradients across corruption levels. The post presents DDPM and score models as converging formulations, not identical implementations in every detail.

sections/machine-learning/sources/attent.title: Attention in transformers, step-by-step | Deep Learning Chapter 6
sections/machine-learning/sources/attent.content:
Attention in transformers, step-by-step | Deep Learning Chapter 6

Attention is derived as a question-and-answer market — each token’s query asks something, each token’s key advertises an answer, and the value vector is the actual edit made to the asker’s embedding — and Sanderson ends by arguing the mechanism’s success owes less to any behaviour it enables than to the fact that it parallelises.

Key Concepts

The problem in three phrases — “American shrew mole,” “One mole of carbon dioxide,” “Take a biopsy of the mole.” After embedding, all three vectors for mole are identical, because the embedding is “effectively a lookup table with no reference to the context.” An attention block’s job is to compute what to add to that generic vector to move it toward one of several distinct meaning-directions.
Updates compose over distance — tower is a generic tall-noun direction; preceded by Eiffel it should move toward Paris, France and iron; preceded also by miniature it should stop correlating with large tall things at all. The extreme case: feed in a mystery novel ending “Therefore the murderer was…” and the final vector, which began life embedding was, must have absorbed everything in the context window relevant to the answer.
Query and key, with the made-up example flagged as made up — for “A fluffy blue creature roamed the verdant forest,” imagine each noun asking “are there any adjectives sitting in front of me?” W_Q maps each embedding to a lower-dimensional query; W_K maps each to a key in the same small space, thought of as potential answers. Sanderson repeatedly warns the adjective-noun story is one behaviour the matrices could implement, not what they do; asked what W_Q does to non-nouns, he answers “Who knows.”
The attention pattern is a softmax over dot products — key·query measures alignment; large positive means fluffy attends to creature, while the against creature gives something small or negative. Raw scores run −∞ to ∞, so softmax is applied column by column to make each column a distribution.
The paper’s formula, reconciled with the diagrams — softmax(KᵀQ/√d_k)·V. Sanderson notes the Attention is All You Need convention differs: their K and Q hold vectors in rows, and they write QKᵗ, so their diagram is flipped diagonally from his. The √d_k denominator is for numerical stability.
Masking follows from an efficiency trick in training — the model predicts the next token after every subsequence simultaneously, so one training example acts as many. That makes it essential that later tokens never influence earlier ones, which would give away the answer. Entries where they would are set to negative infinity before softmax, so they become zero while the columns stay normalised. Not all attention variants mask; GPT always does.
The attention pattern is the square of the context size — one row and one column per token. “This is why context size could act as a significant limitation for large language models and why scaling it up is nontrivial.”
The value matrix answers a different question — “if this word is relevant to adjusting the meaning of another word, what specific adjustments should be made?” Value vectors live in the full embedding space; weight them by the attention-pattern column, sum, and you get ΔE⃗, added to the original embedding to yield the refined E⃗′.
The value map is deliberately low-rank — a square 12,288×12,288 value matrix would cost 150,994,944 parameters, far more than the key and query matrices at 12,288×128 = 1,572,864 each. In practice it is factored into Value↓ (down to 128) and Value↑ (back up), constraining the overall map to a low-rank transformation and making all four matrices the same size: about 6.3 million parameters per head.
Multi-head, counted — GPT-3 runs 96 attention heads per block, each with its own key, query and value maps, producing 96 distinct attention patterns and 96 proposed ΔE⃗ per position, all summed and added to that position’s embedding. About 600 million parameters per multi-headed attention block; across 96 layers, just under 58 billion parameters — roughly a third of GPT-3’s 175 billion. “Even though attention gets all of the attention, the majority of parameters come from the blocks sitting in between these steps.”
The naming detail that trips people reading papers — in practice all the Value↑ matrices across heads are stapled into one giant output matrix belonging to the whole multi-headed block, and “the value matrix for a given attention head” usually means only the Value↓ projection.
Self- vs. cross-attention — everything above is self-attention. Cross-attention is nearly identical but the key and query maps act on different datasets (e.g. two languages in translation), and there is typically no masking, since there is no notion of later tokens affecting earlier ones.
Sanderson’s closing claim about why attention won — “A big part of the story for the success of the attention mechanism is not so much any specific kind of behavior that it enables, but the fact that it’s extremely parallelizable.” Given that scale alone has produced qualitative gains, parallelisable architectures have a structural advantage.


“It is the job of an attention block to calculate what it needs to add to the generic embedding, as a function of its context, to move it to one of those specific directions.”

sections/machine-learning/sources/backpr.title: Backpropagation calculus
sections/machine-learning/sources/backpr.content:
Backpropagation calculus

The entire calculus of backpropagation is derived on a network with one neuron per layer, where it is three chain-rule factors; going to real layer widths “isn’t much more than a few more indices to keep track of,” with exactly one substantive change — a neuron feeding many successors requires summing over its paths of influence.

Key Concepts

What the gradient vector actually contains — the partial derivatives of the cost with respect to every weight and bias, ∂C/∂w⁽¹⁾, ∂C/∂b⁽¹⁾, …, ∂C/∂w⁽ᴸ⁾, ∂C/∂b⁽ᴸ⁾. Backpropagation is the method for finding those derivatives, nothing more.
Superscripts index layers, not exponents — stated explicitly, because subscripts are being saved for neuron indices later. The intermediate weighted sum gets its own name: z⁽ᴸ⁾ = w⁽ᴸ⁾a⁽ᴸ⁻¹⁾ + b⁽ᴸ⁾, then a⁽ᴸ⁾ = σ(z⁽ᴸ⁾).
The dependency tree is the whole idea — weight, previous activation and bias produce z⁽ᴸ⁾, which produces a⁽ᴸ⁾, which with the target y produces the cost. A nudge to w⁽ᴸ⁾ nudges z⁽ᴸ⁾, which nudges a⁽ᴸ⁾, which nudges C₀; the chain rule multiplies the three ratios. Read ∂w⁽ᴸ⁾ as “some tiny nudge, like a change by 0.01” and ∂C₀ as “whatever the resulting nudge to the cost is.”
The three constituent derivatives, and what each one means — ∂z⁽ᴸ⁾/∂w⁽ᴸ⁾ = a⁽ᴸ⁻¹⁾; ∂a⁽ᴸ⁾/∂z⁽ᴸ⁾ = σ′(z⁽ᴸ⁾); ∂C₀/∂a⁽ᴸ⁾ = 2(a⁽ᴸ⁾ − y). Multiplied: ∂C₀/∂w⁽ᴸ⁾ = a⁽ᴸ⁻¹⁾ · σ′(z⁽ᴸ⁾) · 2(a⁽ᴸ⁾ − y). Sanderson reads two of them out loud — the first says a weight matters more when the previous neuron is more active, which is where “neurons that fire together, wire together” appears in the math; the third is proportional to how wrong the output is, so a badly wrong output makes even small activation nudges expensive.
The bias derivative is the same expression with one factor replaced by 1 — since z⁽ᴸ⁾ = w⁽ᴸ⁾a⁽ᴸ⁻¹⁾ + b⁽ᴸ⁾, ∂z⁽ᴸ⁾/∂b⁽ᴸ⁾ = 1. Two gradient entries done.
Averaging is a separate, outer step — C = (1/n)Σ Cₖ, so ∂C/∂w⁽ᴸ⁾ = (1/n)Σ ∂Cₖ/∂w⁽ᴸ⁾. The per-example derivative and the gradient entry are not the same object.
Going backwards means recursing on the activation you cannot control — ∂z⁽ᴸ⁾/∂a⁽ᴸ⁻¹⁾ = w⁽ᴸ⁾, so a previous activation’s influence is proportional to the weight. You cannot set activations directly, but a⁽ᴸ⁻¹⁾ has its own weights and biases, so you iterate the same chain rule backwards; the derivative with respect to an early weight is simply a longer product.
Real layer widths change exactly one thing — index layer (L−1) by k and layer (L) by j; the weight becomes w⁽ᴸ⁾ⱼₖ (an ordering Sanderson notes “might feel backwards” but matches the weight matrix from chapter 1), and ∂C₀/∂w⁽ᴸ⁾ⱼₖ is the identical three-factor product. What genuinely changes is ∂C₀/∂a⁽ᴸ⁻¹⁾ₖ: that neuron influences the cost through every neuron in layer L, so the derivative is a sum over j of chain-rule expressions, one per path of influence.
The transferable skill is named, and it is not the formulas — implementation is a library’s job; “the most important and generalizable understanding here is how you can reason about the sensitivity of one variable to another by breaking down the chain of dependencies.”
Where Sanderson sends you next — Michael Nielsen’s free Neural Networks and Deep Learning (with runnable code for this exact example), Chris Olah’s blog and Distill, Welch Labs’ Learning to See and Neural Networks Demystified, and Goodfellow–Bengio–Courville’s Deep Learning for anyone who has exhausted those.


“Even relatively simple pieces of math, like matrix multiplication and derivatives, can enable you to build genuinely incredible technology when put into the right context.”

sections/machine-learning/sources/backpr.title: What is backpropagation really doing?
sections/machine-learning/sources/backpr.content:
What is backpropagation really doing?

Backpropagation is derived here with “a complete disregard for notation”: it is bookkeeping over what each layer wishes the previous layer would do, propagated recursively backwards — and the nudges it produces mirror Hebbian theory, “neurons that fire together wire together.”

Key Concepts

The definition, kept narrow — backpropagation is an algorithm for computing the negative gradient of the cost function. It is not a learning rule and not a different flavour of descent.
Gradient components read as sensitivity — if one weight’s component is 3.2 and another’s is 0.1, the cost function is 32 times more sensitive to the first: the same wiggle produces 32× the change in cost. This reframing is what makes 13,002 dimensions tractable to think about.
Notation is deferred deliberately — Sanderson names index-chasing as the most confusing part of learning this and postpones it entirely, so that when the notation arrives (in the next chapter) it “acts to articulate something you already know, rather than acting as a code to be decrypted.”
Three avenues to raise one activation — for the digit-2 output neuron sitting at 0.2, the only levers are: increase the bias, increase the weights, or change the activations of the previous layer. The bias is simplest because its effect on the weighted sum is constant and predictable.
“Bang for your buck” is the recurring criterion, and it appears twice, symmetrically — adjust each weight in proportion to its incoming activation (connections from the brightest neurons move the cost most, since the weight is multiplied by a larger number), and adjust each desired activation in proportion to its weight.
Hebbian theory falls out of the math — the largest weight increases occur between the neurons that are most active and the ones you want to become more active. Sanderson flags the limit of the analogy himself: the untrained network is not “thinking” about a 2; the training label is hardcoding what it should be thinking about.
Backward propagation is the resolution of competing requests — activations cannot be changed directly, so you record what is wished for. All ten output neurons issue their own desired nudges to the second-to-last layer, weighted by how far off each is; these cannot all be satisfied, so you add them up to get one overall desired change, then recurse on the weights and biases that produced those activations.
One example alone is a trap — “if we only listened to what that image of a 2 wanted, the network would ultimately be incentivized to just classify all images as a 2.” Run the routine for every training example and average the desired changes; that average is the negative gradient, or something proportional to it.
Stochastic gradient descent as the practical concession — shuffle the data into mini-batches of, say, 100, and take one step per mini-batch. Each step is a worse approximation of the true gradient but takes 1/100th the time, and after 100 steps every example has had its say. The picture is “a drunk man stumbling aimlessly down a hill but taking quick steps rather than a carefully calculating man who takes slow, deliberate steps.”


“The magnitude of each component of the gradient tells you how sensitive the cost function is to each corresponding weight and bias.”

sections/machine-learning/sources/bitter.title: The Bitter Lesson
sections/machine-learning/sources/bitter.content:
The Bitter Lesson

Seventy years of AI research show that general methods which leverage computation beat methods that encode human knowledge about the domain — and by a large margin — because compute per dollar keeps falling exponentially while human insight does not.

Key Concepts

The core claim — researchers optimise as if available compute were fixed, in which case encoding domain knowledge is the only lever; but over a horizon longer than one research project, vastly more compute arrives regardless, and only methods that can absorb it keep improving.
Four historical repeats — chess (deep search beat Kasparov in 1997 over the objections of knowledge-based researchers), Go (the same story delayed twenty years, with self-play learning added), speech recognition (1970s DARPA competition: statistical HMMs beat hand-coded knowledge of phonemes and the vocal tract), and vision (edges, generalised cylinders and SIFT features discarded in favour of convolution).
Only two things scale arbitrarily — search and learning. Both are ways of turning more computation into more performance without a human in the loop.
Why the lesson is “bitter” — building in human knowledge always helps in the short term and is personally satisfying, but plateaus and then actively inhibits progress. The eventual win is over a favoured, human-centric approach, so it is resented and incompletely digested.
The second, deeper point — the contents of minds are “tremendously, irredeemably complex.” Space, objects, agents and symmetries are features of the arbitrary outside world, not things to be built in. Build the meta-methods that find complexity, not the complexity itself.
Note the tension with unreasonable-effectiveness-recurrent-neural-networks: Karpathy’s char-RNN is an empirical instance of exactly this claim, and with amans-ai-journal-primers-transformers, where an architecture is the thing that made the compute usable.


“We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what we have discovered. Building in our discoveries only makes it harder to see how the discovering process can be done.”

sections/machine-learning/sources/but-ne.title: But what is a Neural Network?
sections/machine-learning/sources/but-ne.content:
But what is a Neural Network?

A neural network is not a black box but a very large ordinary function — 13,002 tunable numbers in the digit-recognition case — and the entire architecture follows from one question: what knobs does a layer need so that a weighted sum can express “there is an edge here”?

Key Concepts

The problem is defined by what humans cannot articulate — you identify handwritten threes instantly, yet writing a program that maps a 28×28 pixel grid to a digit 0–9 “goes from comically trivial to dauntingly difficult.” If-statements and for-loops are the wrong tool. That gap, not biological fidelity, is the motivation for brain-inspired software.
A neuron is a thing that holds a number — its activation, between 0.0 and 1.0. Input layer: 784 neurons (28×28), one per pixel, set to that pixel’s brightness. Output layer: 10 neurons, one per digit, whose activation is how much the system thinks the image is that digit.
The two hidden layers of 16 neurons are admittedly arbitrary — Sanderson says so outright: two layers because of how he wants to motivate the structure, and 16 “was simply a nice number to fit on the screen.” Naming the arbitrary choices is part of the pedagogy.
Why layers are the hope, not the guarantee — the aspiration is that layer 2 detects small edges, layer 3 assembles edges into loops and long lines, and the last layer learns which combinations of subcomponents make which digit. Sanderson is explicit that “whether or not this is how our final network actually works is another question” — deferred to analyzing-our-neural-network-3blue1brown. The general payoff is that layered abstraction fits many tasks: raw audio → sounds → syllables → words → phrases.
Weights are derived from the edge-detection requirement — set most of the 784 weights to 0 and a band of them positive, and the weighted sum just adds up brightness in that region. But that also fires on big blobs, so you add negative weights above and below; now the sum is largest when a narrow band is bright and its surroundings are dark. The weight grid is drawn as a 28×28 image, blue for positive, red for negative.
Weights say which pattern, bias says how much is enough — the sigmoid σ squishes the unbounded weighted sum into [0, 1]; adding a bias of, say, −10 first means the neuron only becomes meaningfully active once the sum exceeds 10. Weights choose the pattern; the bias sets the threshold.
13,002 knobs and dials — 784×16 weights plus 16 biases for the first transition alone; the whole network comes to 13,002 weights and biases. Learning, covered in the next chapter, means getting a computer to find a good setting for all of them.
Compact notation is not cosmetic — stack activations into a column vector, weights into a matrix whose rows are one target neuron’s connections, biases into a vector, and one layer becomes σ(W a⁽⁰⁾ + b). This makes code cleaner and faster, “since many libraries optimize the heck out of matrix multiplication.”
The sigmoid asterisk, and why ReLU won — Lisha Li (Amplify Partners) appears in the original video to name sigmoid’s drawback: it goes very flat at the extremes, so wiggling weights does almost nothing and training crawls. ReLU (zero for negative input, unchanged for positive) never flattens, so wiggles always give useful feedback — which matters most as layers stack, “which is where the ‘deep’ in ‘deep learning’ comes from.”
Why any non-linearity at all — without a squishing function each layer is matrix multiply plus offset, so the whole network collapses to a single linear function and becomes dramatically less expressive. Sanderson hands this off to Chris Olah’s post on neural networks, manifolds and topology.


“Somehow identifying digits is incredibly easy for your brain to do, but almost impossible to describe how to do.”

sections/machine-learning/sources/gradie.title: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn
sections/machine-learning/sources/gradie.content:
Gradient descent, how neural networks learn

“Learning” is a provocative word for what is actually a calculus exercise: define a cost function over the network’s 13,002 parameters and repeatedly step against its gradient — and the gradient’s real payload is not the direction but the relative importance it assigns to each weight.

Key Concepts

What makes it machine learning — you never write an algorithm for recognising digits. You write an algorithm that takes labelled examples and adjusts the 13,002 weights and biases to do better on them. MNIST supplies tens of thousands of labelled images for free; a held-out set the network has never seen tests whether the learning generalised.
The cost function, stated concretely — initialise all weights and biases randomly and the output layer is “utter trash.” Cost for one example = the sum of the squares of the differences between the actual output activations and the desired ones (0 everywhere, 1 at the right digit). Small when the network is confidently right, large when it has no idea.
Averaging over the training set inverts the roles — the cost function’s inputs are the 13,002 weights and biases; its output is one number; the tens of thousands of training images are a massive set of parameters baked into its definition. The network is a complicated function, the cost is a layer of complexity on top of it, and the gradient is one more layer on top of that.
Why not just solve for slope = 0 — calculus students can sometimes find a minimum explicitly, but not for a 13,002-input function defined over that much data. So: start at a random input, find the slope, step downhill, repeat. Sanderson deliberately teaches it in one dimension, then two, before claiming the 13,002-dimensional case.
Two properties fall out of the one-dimensional picture — there are many valleys, so which local minimum you land in depends on where you randomly started, with no guarantee it is the global one. And if step size is proportional to the slope, steps shrink automatically as the slope flattens, which keeps you from overshooting.
The gradient generalises slope to a direction — in higher dimensions “slope” is not a single number; ∇C is the direction of steepest ascent, so −∇C is steepest descent, and the vector’s length says how steep. Each practical step is −η∇C, where the learning rate η trades approach speed against overshooting and oscillating around the minimum.
The non-spatial reading is the useful one — stack the weights and biases into a column vector of 13,002 entries; the negative gradient is another 13,002-entry vector, read as a list of nudges. Each component’s sign says up or down, but the relative magnitudes say which changes matter more: “which changes will carry the most bang for your buck.” Some connections simply matter more for this training data than others.
Backpropagation is named here as the efficient way to compute that vector, not as a separate learning algorithm — the derivation is deferred to the next two chapters.


“Although it can be provocative to describe a machine as ‘learning’, once you see how it works, it feels a lot less like some crazy sci-fi premise and a lot more like a calculus exercise.”

sections/machine-learning/sources/illust.title: The Illustrated Transformer
sections/machine-learning/sources/illust.content:
The Illustrated Transformer

The Transformer’s advantage over recurrent sequence models is not that attention is cleverer but that it removes the sequential dependency: every position can be computed in parallel, and the entire architecture can be understood by following one sentence’s worth of vectors through it.

Key Concepts

The shape of the thing — six stacked encoders and six stacked decoders (the number is arbitrary; nothing magical about six). Each encoder is self-attention followed by a feed-forward network; each decoder inserts an encoder-decoder attention layer between the two.
Where the parallelism comes from — each position flows through its own path. Positions interact only in the self-attention layer; the feed-forward layer has no cross-position dependency, so those paths execute in parallel. This is the actual source of the training-speed advantage.
Query, key, value — three learned projections of each input embedding (dimension 64 against an embedding dimension of 512, an architecture choice that keeps multi-head computation roughly constant). Score = dot product of one position’s query with every position’s key; divide by 8 (√64, for gradient stability); softmax; use the result to weight the value vectors; sum.
The worked disambiguation — “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.” Self-attention is what lets the model bind “it” to “animal”. Visualising encoder #5 shows the binding directly.
Multi-head attention buys representation subspaces — eight independently initialised sets of Q/K/V matrices produce eight output matrices, concatenated and projected by a further matrix WO. In the example, one head attends to “the animal” while another attends to “tired,” so “it” absorbs both.
Order has to be added back — with no recurrence there is no notion of position, so a positional encoding vector (sine and cosine signals) is added to each input embedding. Alammar’s July 2020 update notes the paper interweaves the two signals rather than concatenating them as Tensor2Tensor does.
The parts easy to skip — a residual connection plus layer normalisation around every sub-layer; decoder self-attention masks future positions to −inf before the softmax; encoder-decoder attention takes queries from below and keys/values from the encoder stack; a final linear layer projects to a vocabulary-wide logits vector, then softmax.
Decoding is a choice, not a given — greedy decoding takes the argmax at each step; beam search keeps the top k partial hypotheses and picks by total error. Both are hyperparameters, not part of the model.

sections/machine-learning/sources/large-.title: Large Language Models explained briefly
sections/machine-learning/sources/large-.content:
Large Language Models explained briefly

An LLM is “a sophisticated mathematical function that predicts what word comes next for any piece of text” — a chatbot is that function applied repeatedly to a script it is completing, and the reason nobody can explain a particular output is that the behaviour is emergent from hundreds of billions of parameters nobody set by hand.

Key Concepts

The torn-off movie script framing — imagine a script of a person talking to an AI assistant with the assistant’s reply torn off, plus a machine that predicts the next word. Feed in what you have, take the prediction, append, repeat. “When you interact with a chatbot, this is exactly what’s happening.”
A chatbot is a prompt plus a loop — lay out text describing a user/assistant interaction, append what the user typed, then have the model repeatedly predict what the hypothetical assistant would say.
Determinism plus sampling explains the variability — the model assigns a probability to all possible next words, and the chatbot deliberately does not always pick the most likely one, because “the output tends to look a lot more natural if you allow it to select less likely words along the way at random.” So the model itself is deterministic while the same prompt gives different answers each run.
The scale figures Sanderson chooses to make concrete — reading the text GPT-3 trained on would take a human “non-stop, 24-7, for over 2,600 years,” and GPT-4 trained on much more. If you could do a billion additions and multiplications every second, the operations in training the largest models would take you “well over 100,000,000 years.”
Parameters begin random and nobody ever sets them — training is tuning dials on a very big machine; “what puts the large in large language model is how they can have hundreds of billions of these parameters.” Pass in all but the last word of an example, compare the prediction to the true last word, and backpropagation nudges every parameter to make the true word a little more likely and the rest a little less.
Pre-training is only part of it — auto-completing internet text is a different goal from being a good assistant, so chatbots also get RLHF: workers flag unhelpful or problematic predictions and their corrections shift the parameters toward what users prefer.
Parallelism is the reason the transformer exists — the computation is only feasible on GPUs, chips optimised for many operations in parallel, but “prior to 2017, most language models would process text one word at a time.” Transformers “don’t read text from the start to the finish, they soak it all in at once, in parallel.”
Two operations, iterated — first each word is associated with a long list of numbers, since training only works on continuous values. Attention lets those lists communicate and refine their meanings from surrounding context: the vector for bank shifts given river and jumped into to encode something closer to riverbank. Feed-forward layers add capacity to store patterns learned in training. Data flows through many iterations of the two, then one final function on the last vector produces the next-word distribution.
Emergence is named as the reason for opacity — researchers design the framework for each step, but “the specific behavior is an emergent phenomenon based on how those hundreds of billions of parameters are tuned during training. This makes it incredibly challenging to understand why the model makes the exact predictions that it does.”

sections/machine-learning/sources/llm-po.title: LLM Powered Autonomous Agents
sections/machine-learning/sources/llm-po.content:
LLM Powered Autonomous Agents

An LLM agent is not a monolith but an LLM acting as controller over three separable components — planning, memory, and tool use — and decomposing it that way makes both the working systems and the failure modes legible.

Key Concepts

The three components — planning (subgoal decomposition, plus reflection and refinement over past actions), memory (short-term = in-context learning, bounded by the context window; long-term = an external vector store queried at retrieval time), and tool use (calling external APIs for what is not in the weights).
Planning has a spectrum — Chain of Thought spends test-time compute decomposing a task into steps; Tree of Thoughts generates multiple thoughts per step and searches the resulting tree by BFS or DFS with a classifier or majority vote at each state; LLM+P outsources planning entirely to a classical PDDL planner, translating in and out of natural language.
Self-reflection is what makes trial-and-error possible — ReAct interleaves Thought / Action / Observation and beats an act-only baseline on both knowledge-intensive and decision-making tasks. Reflexion adds a heuristic that detects inefficient trajectories and hallucination (defined operationally as a run of identical actions producing identical observations) and can reset the environment. Chain of Hindsight conditions on a sequence of past outputs annotated with feedback, ranked by reward.
Memory mapped onto human memory — sensory memory as learned embeddings of raw input; short-term memory as in-context learning; long-term memory as an external vector store. The mapping is explicitly a rough analogy, and Weng credits ChatGPT for helping draft the section.
Retrieval is an engineering constraint — long-term memory means fast maximum inner-product search, which in practice means approximate nearest neighbours: LSH, ANNOY (random projection trees), HNSW (hierarchical small-world graphs), FAISS (vector quantisation within clusters), ScaNN (anisotropic quantisation that preserves inner product rather than distance).
Tool use, concretely — MRKL routes to expert modules, neural or symbolic; TALM and Toolformer finetune the model to call APIs; HuggingGPT uses the LLM as a task planner selecting HuggingFace models across four stages (task planning, model selection, task execution, response generation). MRKL’s finding is the sharp one: knowing when and how to use a tool is the hard part, not the tool.
Three limitations Weng names — finite context length (vector stores extend reach but their representational power is weaker than full attention); brittle long-horizon planning (LLMs struggle to revise a plan after an unexpected error); and the unreliability of natural language as the interface between the LLM and its components, which is why so much agent code is output parsing.

sections/machine-learning/sources/might-.title: How might LLMs store facts | Deep Learning Chapter 7
sections/machine-learning/sources/might-.content:
How might LLMs store facts | Deep Learning Chapter 7

An MLP is only “two matrix products, each with a bias added, and a simple clipping function in between,” and it can be read as an AND gate that detects “Michael Jordan” and adds a “basketball” direction — but the chapter’s real payload is the retraction of that reading: superposition means individual neurons almost never carry one clean feature.

Key Concepts

The question has an empirical starting point — in December 2023 Google DeepMind researchers studied exactly this athlete-to-sport example and reported that facts seem to live in the multi-layer perceptrons. A full mechanistic account remained unsolved; these were partial results.
The MLP is where most of the parameters are, and it is the simpler block — “compared to attention, the computations in the MLPs are relatively simple… However, interpreting what these computations are doing is exceedingly challenging.” Vectors do not exchange information here, so understanding one vector’s path explains all of them; every position is processed in parallel, and the block’s output is added to what flowed in.
The assumptions are stated as assumptions — suppose nearly perpendicular directions exist for first-name Michael, last-name Jordan, and basketball, and read a dot product of 1 as “encodes this,” 0 or negative as “does not.” Because “Michael Jordan” spans two tokens, this also assumes an earlier attention block already moved the first-name information into the Jordan vector.
Step 1: rows of W↑ are questions — read matrix multiplication as dot products between each row and E⃗. If the first row were M⃗ + J⃗, the dot product distributes to M⃗·E⃗ + J⃗·E⃗, giving 2 for the full name and ≤ 1 otherwise. The bias B↑ of −1 in that component then makes the value positive if and only if the vector encodes Michael Jordan.
The width is a hardware convenience — GPT-3’s up-projection has just under 50,000 rows, “exactly four times the number of dimensions in this embedding space. There’s no specific reason why… having a clean multiple tends to be friendly for hardware.”
ReLU is what makes it an AND gate — the linear operation alone would also be partly triggered by Michael Phelps or Alexis Jordan; clipping negatives to zero yields the clean yes/no. Models often use GELU, “the same basic shape but a bit smoother.” The values leaving this ReLU are what people mean by the “neurons” of a transformer — active when positive, inactive at zero — and this linear-step-plus-nonlinearity is exactly what the dots-and-lines diagram from chapter 1 depicts.
Step 3: columns of W↓ are edits — read this multiplication column-wise instead, because the columns live in the embedding space and so are directions. If the first column is the basketball direction, it gets added whenever that neuron is active and contributes nothing when it is zero. The same column could also carry the Chicago Bulls, or the number 23.
The parameter count closes out at exactly 175 billion — W↑ is ~50,000 × 12,288 = 604 million, W↓ the same transposed, so 1.2 billion per block; across GPT-3’s 96 MLP blocks that is about 116 billion, roughly two-thirds of the network. Added to attention, embedding and unembedding, that is the full 175 billion. The skipped normalisation steps contribute about 49,000 parameters — trivial.
Then Sanderson takes the example back — “evidence suggests that individual neurons very rarely represent a single clean feature like Michael Jordan.” What remains true is structural: rows are directions, columns are edits.
Superposition, via Johnson–Lindenstrauss — you can fit only n mutually perpendicular directions in n dimensions (that is the definition of dimension), but if you tolerate nearly perpendicular — say 85° to 95° — the number that fits grows exponentially with dimension. So a space with 10× the dimensions stores far more than 10× the independent ideas, which may explain why performance scales so well with size. It also means the ~50,000-neuron layer could be probing orders of magnitude more features than it has neurons — and a feature would then appear not as one neuron lighting up but as a combination of them.
The lesson publishes its own error, with corrected numbers — the video’s demo pushed 10,000 vectors in 100 dimensions to angles between 89° and 91°, but a bad cost function let a few pairs escape to dot products near ±1. Sanderson states that 100 dimensions is not enough for that tight a range. Viewer Nick Yoder’s corrections: the (89°, 91°) range “doesn’t get interesting until dimensions > 250,000”; 85° (dot product 0.087) scales very fast; at 85° GPT-3’s 12,288 dimensions hold well over 40 billion vectors, likely more than 10¹⁷; at 116,000 dimensions, over a googol and likely over 10¹⁶⁰.
Where the interpretability work goes — the search term is sparse autoencoder, a tool for extracting true features even when superimposed across neurons; Sanderson points to Anthropic’s Toy Models of Superposition and Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning.


“Individual features aren’t going to be visible as a single neuron lighting up. It would have to look like some specific combination of neurons instead, hence a superposition.”

sections/machine-learning/sources/rlhf-r.title: RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
sections/machine-learning/sources/rlhf-r.content:
RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

The popular explanations for ChatGPT — more scale, better UX — skip the actual mechanism: a three-phase pipeline in which pretraining supplies capability, supervised finetuning supplies format, and a reward model trained on comparisons supplies preference, with each phase solving a problem the previous one cannot.

Key Concepts

Three phases, wildly unequal in cost — pretraining consumes ~98% of InstructGPT’s total compute and data. SFT and RLHF are best understood as unlocking capability the pretrained model already has but which prompting alone cannot reach.
Why SFT is needed — a pretrained model optimises for completion. Given “How to make pizza,” continuing with more context or follow-up questions is as valid as answering. SFT (OpenAI calls it behavior cloning) demonstrates the response users actually want. InstructGPT used ~14,500 (prompt, response) pairs from 40 labelers, ~90% of whom held at least a college degree.
Why RLHF is needed on top — demonstration data tells the model which responses are plausible, never how good or bad one is. RLHF adds a scoring function and optimises against it.
The reward model’s data trick — asking labelers for absolute scores produces inconsistency; asking which of two responses is better does not. Training data is therefore (prompt, winning_response, losing_response), and the loss −log σ(s_w − s_l) simply pushes the winner’s score above the loser’s. InstructGPT: 50,000 prompts, 4–9 responses each, 300K–1.8M comparison pairs. Inter-labeler agreement is about 73%.
The KL constraint is not a detail — PPO optimises the SFT model against the reward model, but a KL-divergence term keeps it from straying far from the SFT policy. Without it, the model drifts toward responses the reward model has never seen and mis-scores wildly. This is the concrete statement of “the reward model is the weak link.”
Human preference is not one function — Huyen prefers the losing response in an example from Anthropic’s HH-RLHF dataset and says so. Preferences are diverse and cannot be captured in a single mathematical formulation.
RLHF made hallucination worse — the honest finding. Schulman’s hypothesis is that behavior cloning causes hallucination: SFT teaches the model to mimic responses written using knowledge the labeler has and the model does not. Yet the InstructGPT paper shows RLHF increased hallucination relative to SFT alone — and labelers still preferred the RLHF model overall.
Three hypotheses for why RLHF works at all (via Yoav Goldberg) — diversity (SFT penalises valid-but-different answers), negative feedback (demonstrations only ever show good responses), and hallucination reduction. Huyen states plainly that she has not seen a foolproof argument.

sections/machine-learning/sources/super-.title: Super VIP Cheatsheet: Machine Learning
sections/machine-learning/sources/super-.content:
Super VIP Cheatsheet: Machine Learning

Binding four CS229 sheets to a probability, statistics, linear-algebra, and calculus refresher exposes a common mathematical substrate beneath supervised, unsupervised, deep, and evaluated learning systems.

What this is
The document, co-authored by Afshine Amidi and Shervine Amidi, is mostly a compilation. Sections 1–4 reproduce the four topic sheets in compressed form:



































§ContentPublished separately as1Supervised Learningvip-cheatsheet-supervised-learning2Unsupervised Learningvip-cheatsheet-unsupervised-learning3Deep Learningvip-cheatsheet-deep-learning4Machine Learning Tips and Tricksvip-cheatsheet-machine-learning-tips-tricks5Refreshersonly here
Dated 6 October 2018, roughly a month after the individual sheets, the compilation adds §5. For the details of §§1–4, the individual source pages remain the better hubs; the distinctive contribution here is how the refresher makes their shared dependencies visible.
The shared substrate
Probability begins with sample spaces, events, counting, and conditional probability. Bayes’ rule converts a prior and likelihood into a posterior, while independence specifies when a joint distribution factors. Random variables add mass or density functions, expectation, variance, covariance, and correlation; jointly distributed variables support the multivariate models used elsewhere in the sheets.
estimation-uncertainty extracts the parameter-estimation layer: sample mean and variance estimate population quantities, bias measures systematic estimator error, the central limit theorem motivates approximate sampling distributions, and confidence intervals express uncertainty. This vocabulary is what lets maximum likelihood, diagnostics, and reported performance be read as estimates rather than fixed truths.
Linear algebra supplies vector and matrix operations, rank, positive semidefiniteness, eigendecomposition, and singular-value decomposition. Norms connect geometry to regularization: the sheet associates L1 with LASSO and L2 with ridge penalties. Eigenvectors support PCA’s variance directions; SVD supplies a general factorization for rectangular matrices.
matrix-calculus-for-learning collects gradients, Hessians, trace identities, and matrix derivatives. These operations connect the normal equations, Newton-style updates, PCA, and backpropagation. A gradient specifies local first-order change; a Hessian describes local curvature for scalar-valued functions. The sheet is a reference of identities, not a derivation of their validity conditions.
Why the compilation is not merely convenient
Read in sequence, §5 acts as a dependency map. gradient-descent appears in linear models and neural networks; conditional probability supports Naive Bayes and expectation-maximization; eigendecomposition joins covariance to PCA; estimator uncertainty underlies the bias-variance-tradeoff and model diagnostics. The four application families are not mathematically isolated subjects.
The compilation remains a high-density refresher. It supplies definitions and formulas but little derivation, empirical qualification, or guidance on violated assumptions. Its value is navigation: it tells a reader which mathematical object to revisit when an algorithmic formula stops being transparent.
