sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: The Art of Non-Attachment (in Philosophy)
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Art of Non-Attachment (in Philosophy)

Detachment and non-attachment are not synonyms: trying to push a thought away rehearses it, while releasing the outcome dissolves the tension the attachment was generating.

Key Concepts

Attachment is normal, its excess is the problem. Attaching to things, people and worldly desire is treated as a basic feature of human nature and biology; the failure mode is when the external object begins consuming the person physically, emotionally or mentally.
The piece routes this through Eastern philosophy — Buddhism, Hinduism, Taoism tying desire to suffering — and quotes Naval Ravikant’s formulation: “desire is a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want.”
The distinction that carries the piece: detachment is pulling away, turning the cold shoulder; non-attachment is releasing the emotional claim on an outcome. They sound identical and behave oppositely.
The pink elephant demonstration — visualise a pink elephant in detail, then try to stop. Forced suppression makes the thought more available, not less, and in extreme cases triggers an emotional spiral. This is why detachment fails as a technique.
The cat analogy for the same dynamic in pursuit: run at it and it retreats; stop chasing, sit still, stop being reactive, and it approaches. Reported from personal experience — the harder the chase, the further the object receded.
The Stoics are placed in the same practice — Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius named as practitioners of releasing what is outside one’s control.
The protocol is order-dependent: feel the emotion first, recognise it as temporary, then practise acceptance. Suppression is precisely what is being ruled out; the release comes after the feeling is allowed.
Worked cases: someone wronged you and you want revenge (let it go, it isn’t worth it); compulsive comparison to others’ achievements (their lane differs from yours); fear of starting a project because of anticipated judgement (you have not attempted it yet).
“You shouldn’t fear an outcome that hasn’t played out yet.” Expectation is framed as the cage; what remains controllable is the reaction, never the circumstance.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: The Art Of Conversation: How To Have Conversations That People Never Forget
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Art Of Conversation: How To Have Conversations That People Never Forget

Memorable conversation is not produced by performing profundity. Ixcarus’s
framework creates trust, presence, calibrated lightness, and enough silence for
the live thread to deepen on its own.

Depth is a condition, not a question
A profound prompt offered before trust can feel like an attempt to accelerate
intimacy that has not been earned. The work instead recommends small honest
observations: one person departs slightly from the social script, the other meets
them there, and the exchange deepens incrementally. It describes this reflective
state as simultaneous engagement of the Default-Mode-Network and social-cognition
network, integrating memory, personal meaning, and understanding of another person.
The neurochemical account contrasts reward with effort. Intellectual and social
stimulation is associated with dopamine; moments of eye contact, being understood,
or having an unnamed feeling articulated are associated with Oxytocin and
attachment. A performative exchange costs monitoring effort without the same reward
and is described as mildly cortisol-producing. The practical summary is to create
more felt reward than social labor.
Follow what is alive
The “second question” is the central listening technique. After an answer, ask about
the detail actually given rather than moving to the next biographical category.
“What made you choose it?” or “What is making you consider leaving now?” keeps the
conversation inside the speaker’s sentence. The orientation changes from impressing
to understanding, and visible curiosity makes the listener memorable.
Silence serves the same tracking function. A pause after vulnerability shows that
the disclosure landed; a pause before ordinary speech makes the next words feel
considered. Compulsive filling lowers the informational value of every utterance and
signals discomfort with possible rejection.
Calibrate lightness and disclosure
Banter supplies relief from sustained depth. It requires fast listening, lateral
response, and enough security to tolerate an edge—but warmth must precede the edge.
Accurate, specific observations create humor more reliably than trying to perform a
joke. The same calibration determines whether a moment wants levity or seriousness;
overriding the room with either destroys the connection.
When sharing personal material, relevance and specificity create the bridge. A
concrete scene communicates lived similarity more effectively than the generic claim
that the listener has experienced something comparable. Then end near the natural
peak rather than dragging the exchange until its energy disappears; the peak and
close disproportionately shape the remembered whole.
Together these mechanisms form conversation-dynamics: be present, go honest
rather than prematurely deep, follow the live detail, tolerate silence, earn banter
through warmth, match the moment, disclose specifically, and leave while connection
is still the dominant memory.
Connects to: energy-and-presence (undivided attention and calibration),
Charisma (conversation as its applied form), and Reading-People (tracking
subtext without abandoning the speaker’s actual words).

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: art-of-silence
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Art of Silence: The Smartest Person In The Room Is Usually The Quietest

Quiet people are often the most capable — and the science explains why. Loudness is confused with competence through cognitive bias, but genuine expertise produces silence.

Core Argument
Three converging mechanisms explain the silence-intelligence correlation:

Loudness-Bias — the psychological tendency to equate dominant, assertive behavior with intelligence and competence. The brain reads certainty as knowledge because evolutionary history wired it that way — but certainty and correctness are not the same thing.
Dunning-Kruger-Effect — people with limited knowledge overestimate competence (loud); people with genuine expertise systematically underestimate it (quiet). Surviving the valley of despair produces intellectual humility, which produces silence.
Default-Mode-Network — silence activates the DMN, enabling creative synthesis and associative thinking. The quiet person in a meeting is often doing more cognitive work than the people filling the air.

Key Concepts

Loudness-Bias: confidence activates the social brain’s heuristic that equates assertiveness with authority; the loudest is most convinced, not most correct
Dunning-Kruger-Effect: the expertise curve; valley of despair; why masters are quiet and beginners are loud
Halo-Effect: confidence projects the same positive-trait assumptions as attractiveness — brain automatically assigns intelligence, authority, trustworthiness
Default-Mode-Network: silence activates DMN → creative connection and associative synthesis; the person sitting quietly is running it at full capacity
Introversion neurology: higher baseline cortical arousal → less need for external stimulation → more internal processing before output; PFC more active in deliberate, reflective thinkers
Prefrontal cortex: the quieter person runs more PFC processing before speaking — output is more considered and more accurate

Notable Passages

“The loud ones are usually still on the peak of the curve. The initial confidence spike before the reality check. The silent ones have usually been through it.”


“The person who interrupts constantly isn’t doing that work. They’re too busy producing output to deeply process input. And the quality of your output is directly constrained by the quality of your input.”


“Wise people speak because they have something to say. Fools speak because they have to say something.” — Plato

Connections

Creates Dunning-Kruger-Effect and Loudness-Bias (new entities)
Adds the silence → DMN activation angle to Default-Mode-Network
The gym anecdote illustrates loudness bias causing physical harm through misplaced confidence
Connects to Halo-Effect: confidence triggers the same automatic positive-attribute projection as attractiveness

Related Pages

Loudness-Bias — the social bias that rewards confident noise over accurate quiet

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: The Art of Perseverance
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Art of Perseverance

Perseverance is not willpower held longer but a purpose strong enough to make difficulty affordable — and resistance, read correctly, is confirmation of direction rather than a signal to stop.

Key Concepts

The “why” is the load-bearing element, via Nietzsche: “he who has a why to live for can bear almost any how.” A purpose one actually embodies is claimed to transcend the difficulty in front of it, where discipline alone does not.
Long-term framing as an antidote to tunnel vision — thinking past the present moment shrinks the apparent size of the current obstacle, and a defined purpose is said to flip the interpretive lens from cup-half-empty to cup-half-full.
The author’s own stated purpose, offered as a worked example rather than an abstraction: to inspire others, and to leave frameworks his future children can read. Written openly while describing his own growth as stagnating — the essay is itself an instance of the thing it argues for.
999 as an inversion device — taken from Juice WRLD, who died on the author’s birthday. Against 666 as the biblical mark of the beast, 999 flips a negative situation into something positive: turn pain into power, into progress.
Michael Jordan as the case study — cut from his high school team; his father James Jordan’s lesson was “turn something negative into something positive.” Three championships 1991–1993, and after his father’s death, three more 1996–1998. The second run is the point: grief did not stop the work.
Two reframes stated as rules — resistance is a sign you are on the right path, and pressure is a sign that what you want is getting closer. Both convert an aversive signal into a progress indicator.
Sisyphus is invoked in passing (“one must imagine sisyphus happy”), placing the piece in the tradition that locates meaning inside the struggle rather than after it.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: The Attention Economy: You Are The Product
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Attention Economy: You Are The Product
From information scarcity to attention scarcity
The work begins with Herbert Simon’s 1971 observation that abundant information consumes something finite: the human capacity to attend. Information that once required travel and effort is now effectively unlimited, but a person still has only so many waking hours and can direct sustained attention to one object at a time. Attention therefore becomes the scarce input around which an industry can form.
The commercial model predates the internet. In 1833 Benjamin Day sold the New York Sun for less than its production cost, accumulated readers with sensational stories, then sold advertisers access to those readers. Commercial television inherited the same structure: programming holds the audience so advertisements can reach it. Free digital platforms scale the arrangement. The reader or user is inventory; advertisers are the paying customers.
The capture-and-profile loop
Platform revenue rises with time spent, advertisements seen and behavioral data produced. That incentive explains design features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, notification badges, likes and unpredictable feed rewards: each removes a stopping decision or creates a cue to return. Variable rewards make checking persist even when most checks yield nothing.
Attention capture also produces a profile. Searches, location, purchases, pauses, activity times and demographic signals can be combined to infer private conditions and vulnerabilities. The work uses Target’s pregnancy-prediction model, predatory advertising aimed at financially distressed people, and Cambridge Analytica’s political targeting as examples. The data does not merely select a relevant product; it can identify a pain point and time pressure against it. This makes the Attention-Economy a psychology and surveillance business as much as a media business.
What the system spends
Attention is selective: attending to one thing requires withdrawing from others. It also cannot be stored or recovered after the fact. A platform session therefore spends time that could have formed a thought, relationship, skill or project, while repeated reactive checking trains the next allocation. The central conflict is not simply screen time versus abstinence, but algorithmic selection versus deliberate selection.
That conflict connects the business model to Dopamine-Hijacking and deep-work. Engagement systems use cues and uncertain rewards to initiate short reactive loops; focused work needs an uninterrupted container in which the person, not the feed, chooses what receives attention.
Moving from reactive to deliberate attention
The proposed response is environmental and procedural rather than total withdrawal:

Charge the phone outside the bedroom and keep the first 30–60 minutes phone-free, removing the morning cue.
Audit weekly screen time so the real allocation becomes visible.
Batch email, notifications and social media into designated windows, breaking continuous variable-reward checking.
Protect the first two or three high-signal hours for personally chosen deep-work before other people’s priorities arrive.
State a concrete intention before opening a device or platform, creating an exit condition before the algorithm supplies one.

The aim is to shift the ratio from reactive attention to deliberate attention. Awareness names the contest; changing cues, windows and entry intentions changes who allocates the resource.
Derived pages

Attention-Economy — scarcity, the advertiser-reader model, behavioral profiling and deliberate countermeasures
Dopamine-Hijacking — unpredictable rewards and notification cues as the capture mechanism
deep-work — the sustained, self-directed use competing for the same finite resource
Technology-and-Modern-Life — the wider domain in which the commercial and cognitive effects interact

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: attraction-health-signaling
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Why Attraction Is Health Signaling (And How to Optimize It)

ixcarus presents attraction as a holistic inference from visible cues associated
with health and reproductive fitness. The practical argument is to improve the
underlying system—sleep, nutrition, training, stress, skin, posture, and
movement—rather than optimize isolated cosmetic proxies.

A bundle of cues, not one perfect feature
The work points to facial symmetry, skin condition, body composition, secondary
sex characteristics, posture, and movement as cues an observer integrates. In its
evolutionary account, these features historically correlated with developmental
stability, metabolic and immune condition, physical capability, and fertility.
Attraction is experienced consciously as preference while the proposed assessment
operates without an explicit checklist.
The source often states these evolutionary claims with more certainty than the
essay itself can establish. Culture, personal history, orientation, disability,
fashion, and individual preference also shape attraction. The reusable model in
Attraction-as-Health-Signaling is therefore a source-attributed lens, not a
complete or universal law of beauty.
The proxy-versus-system critique
The looksmaxxing-community and blackpill are criticized for treating fixed
or purchasable morphology—jaw angle, eye area, height, isolated ratios—as the
entire assessment. ixcarus argues that this mistakes a proxy for what it may signal.
An observer sees the combined output of many systems, so one altered feature cannot
necessarily override poor sleep, movement, skin, or body composition.
The inverse is the practical claim: a systemic change can move several outputs at
once. Training affects body composition and movement; adequate sleep and nutrition
can affect energy and skin; strength and mobility can affect posture-and-movement.
The compound bundle matters more in this framework than perfection on one dimension.
Four changeable domains
The source groups its recommendations around body-composition,
hormone-optimization, skin-health, and posture or movement. It recommends
selecting one domain for a sustained period rather than trying to alter every
signal at once. Health is the target and attractiveness is framed as a possible
side effect.
Some physiological statements in the work—especially broad claims about sex
hormones, endocrine disruption, sunlight, and what clear skin proves—should not be
treated as individualized medical guidance. The safer graph boundary is that
sleep, stress, diet, activity, and medical conditions can affect appearance; causal
diagnosis or hormone treatment requires evidence beyond appearance alone.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: The Beauty of Latin Phrases: Five Powerful Sayings from Conquerors
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Beauty of Latin Phrases: Five Powerful Sayings from Conquerors

Five Latin sayings survive because they compress a whole disposition into a phrase you can carry, and the argument here is that they still function that way — four of them install ambition and resolve, and the fifth exists specifically to cap the other four before they turn into hubris.

The opening move is that veni, vidi, vici is famous enough to be a tattoo and a TikTok caption, and that four less-worn phrases do the same job. Latin is granted as technically dead and still spoken in academia and the Catholic Church; the interest is in the English translations and their modern application.
Key Concepts

Quo non ascendam? — to what heights can I not rise? From Nicolas Fouquet, superintendent of finances under Louis XIV in the 17th century. Read as: there is no limit to what you can achieve, and the question you ask yourself should be what you can achieve rather than what you can’t. Potential is “not bound to anything, other than limits that are self-imposed.” Modern application: carry delusional self-belief into a new endeavour even without the physical evidence beforehand, and treat challenges as exciting rather than intimidating because they compound — the combat-sports example is showing up daily 1% sharper in striking, grappling, fight IQ, wrestling, and jiu jitsu until “you won’t even notice how far you’ve come.”
Aut viam inveniam aut faciam — I shall either find a way or make one. Attributed to Hannibal during the Second Punic War, who marched war elephants across the Alps into Italy as Rome’s greatest enemy. The reading is that his resolve was unshaken against unfavourable odds and that he engineered his own outcomes where no path existed. The interpretation offered is a survivorship argument: “if you can survive 100% of all your bad days, you will always find a way” — and that reading this at all is evidence of the battles already survived. The worked case is refusing a conventional path against a limiting environment or a family imposing its own vision. “If someone else has done it, I can do it too. If no one else has done it, I can be the first.”
Vincere aut mori — either to conquer or to die. Unattributed but widespread among military leaders. The metaphorical reading is the whole point: death here means stagnation — letting yourself go, or giving up — which the piece ties to Einstein’s once you stop learning, you start dying. The function is to remove the middle: seeing outcomes as binary means complacency has no place to hide, because you are either moving toward your goals or away from them. Modern translation: not invaders but competition, not an empire but projects and skills that compound, not decisions over millions of lives but choices that shape your own and those around you.
Vincit qui se vincit — he conquers who conquers himself. From the Roman writer Publilius Syrus, and the phrase the author says he resonates with most. The claim: self-mastery precedes everything else, because “your external reality is a reflection of your internal state” — as within, so without. “How do you expect to conquer if you can’t even conquer yourself?” Extended to other virtues on the same logic: hard to love others without self-love, to be patient with others without patience for yourself, to be honest without integrity. Modern application: acknowledging emotions and sitting with them knowing they are fleeting rather than engaging each one impulsively, staying rational about what is outside your control, and reading other people through emotional intelligence rather than reacting to them.
Memento mori — remember that you will die. Attributed here to the Stoic lineage (Socrates, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius). Its function in this piece is corrective rather than motivational: glory, power, and money are fleeting, and the phrase exists to be recalled in the moment of victory, when pride and vanity are most likely to consume you. The historical cautions are Napoleon invading Russia and Rome spreading its territory too thin through continuous conquest — “winning can take you so far, but not at the cost of your own progress where it all can collapse in an instant.” Modern application: a viral post, a financial win, an award. Vanity is fleeting; your growth isn’t. Better to be mentally prepared for adversity in foresight than in hindsight.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: The Blueprint For Greatness: Lessons From Conquerors
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Blueprint For Greatness: Lessons From Conquerors

ixcarus reads Genghis Khan, Alexander, Napoleon, and Caesar as case studies in
adaptation: promote capability over inheritance, learn from opponents, move before
slower institutions, lead visibly, take bounded risks, and manage the story around
action. Their conquest and brutality are historical costs, not leadership virtues.

Genghis Khan: systems can outrank lineage
The source emphasizes promotion by demonstrated ability rather than bloodline and
the adoption of siege warfare, administration, and other useful systems from
conquered peoples. The proposed strategic trait is low attachment to inherited
procedure: if another group has a better tool, identity should not block learning.
That lesson cannot be separated entirely from coercive empire. A modern organization
can evaluate capability and import better methods without treating people as
disposable instruments or conquest as evidence of greatness.
Alexander: visible participation and cross-domain learning
Alexander is presented as leading from the front, sharing hardship, and studying
philosophy, science, literature, and local cultures. The source interprets visible
risk-sharing as credibility: a leader asking for difficult work has performed it
and bears part of its cost. Cross-domain learning expands the available models
beyond military technique alone.
The transfer is bounded. “Lead from the front” should not mean occupying every role,
normalizing danger, or refusing expert delegation. Its useful form is enough direct
contact with the work to understand its demands and consequences.
Napoleon: speed needs a stopping rule
The work treats mobility and rapid decision as Napoleon’s advantage over larger,
slower forces. Speed changes the situation before a competitor’s strength can be
deployed. Merit-based promotion appears again as a way to place capability near the
decision.
Napoleon also supplies the failure case: expansion continued after consolidation
would have been strategically superior. Action bias without a stopping condition
turns an advantage into escalation. strategic-adaptation therefore includes
both fast execution and explicit criteria for pause, defense, or exit.
Caesar: risk, learning, and narrative
Crossing the Rubicon represents a risk whose consequences were understood rather
than a random gamble. Caesar is also presented as controlling the record around his
campaigns and converting setbacks into demonstrations of resolve. The source’s
formula “reality plus perception” recognizes that coordinated action depends on
what others believe happened.
Narrative management is not a licence to falsify evidence. A reputation can reduce
friction or attract support, but propaganda also hides costs and silences subjects.
The ethical modern version is legible work: explain decisions, document results,
and make competence visible without replacing reality with image.
The shared pattern
Across the four portraits, the recurring sequence is observe without lineage or
ego, import the better method, decide under uncertainty, execute quickly, and update
from outcome. High discomfort tolerance supports that sequence but does not make
sleep deprivation, cruelty, or permanent expansion admirable.
Graph connections

Ego — identity must not block adoption of a better system

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Your Are Bound for Success

The bamboo growth metaphor applied to human achievement — most real growth happens invisibly before it becomes apparent; quitting right before the breakthrough is the most common failure pattern.

Key Concepts

Bamboo growth: 7 years underground (invisible), then 90 feet in 6 weeks — was it growing for 6 weeks or 8 years? Both
Most people quit in the invisible phase — they interpret no visible output as no growth, when in fact the foundation is being laid
“Quitting 5 minutes before the miracle” — breakthrough timing is unpredictable; the people who arrive at the same destination later did so because they kept going
Compounding: consistent effort compounds invisibly over time; the results look sudden when they become visible but represent years of accumulated work
Connects to Compound-Effect (Don’t Skip This): exponential growth curve starts below zero before crossing threshold

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: brain-deletes-99-reality
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Your Brain Deletes 99% of Reality Before You Ever See It

ixcarus argues that conscious experience is a selective, predicted model rather
than an unedited copy of the environment. The practical conclusion is
epistemic humility: attention changes which available evidence becomes salient,
but it does not manufacture objective reality.

Selection before awareness
The essay opens with the large mismatch between sensory input and conscious
capacity. It reports estimates of roughly eleven million sensory bits per second
and roughly forty consciously processed bits per second. Those figures are
estimates rather than a literal measurement of a single channel, but the contrast
anchors the essay’s central point: awareness cannot carry every signal at once.
The source places the Thalamus at the centre of sensory gating for most senses.
Current goals raise the priority of task-relevant patterns; repeated or unchanging
inputs such as clothing pressure, background hum, or the nose in the visual field
can recede from notice. The Reticular-Activating-System is related to arousal
and attention, but the essay does not establish it as one master switch that
personally decides every percept. perceptual-gating is therefore the broader
concept page for this work.
Filtering and prediction work together
Selection is only half of the account. The brain also predicts likely input from
context and prior experience. Familiar furniture can guide movement in the dark;
expected words make a writer miss a typo; a magician can direct an observer toward
one expected event while another occurs. On this model, conscious experience is a
simplified interpretation assembled from selected evidence and prior predictions.
The filters are not identical across people. Past experience, current goals,
emotion, and belief can make different aspects of the same room salient. A person
anticipating social threat may notice possible rejection while another notices
open invitations. That difference can produce conflicting interpretations without
implying that every interpretation is equally accurate.
Consciousness questions
The essay uses split-brain research to question how unified consciousness depends
on communication between hemispheres, then turns to simulation thought
experiments. These passages raise philosophical questions; they do not prove that
consciousness is two people, that reality is simulated, or that truth is merely
subjective.
Practical boundary
The author explicitly preserves the distinction between mediated access and truth:
truth may exist even though perception reaches it through systems shaped more by
survival and action than perfect accuracy. Attention can reveal opportunities or
threats that were previously unattended, and deliberate counter-search can test a
confident interpretation. It cannot make a false external claim true.
The useful move is therefore not “believe hard enough and reality changes.” It is:
ask what the current filter highlighted, what it suppressed, what prediction filled
the gap, and what disconfirming observation would revise the model. That connects
the essay to Identity-Setpoint, Subconscious-Mind, and
Consciousness-and-Identity without treating any of them as reality-creation
machinery.
Related Pages

Reticular-Activating-System — arousal and attentional relevance, not a sole reality editor
Subconscious-Mind — processing outside the narrow field of awareness

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: broken-foundation-unlearn
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
You Can’t Build A Better Life On A Broken Foundation: 5 Things You Need To Unlearn

Most self-improvement fails because it adds floors to a broken building. Real growth requires going underneath — identifying and dismantling the foundational beliefs quietly running your life.

Core Argument
Self-improvement culture is additive: read more, earn more, build more habits. Almost nobody examines the foundational beliefs beneath their behavior. You can build the physique, the income, the appearance of having it together — and still be derailed by what you never examined. The post identifies five beliefs most likely to be operating below conscious awareness.
The 5 Beliefs to Unlearn
1. “I Don’t Owe Anyone Anything”
Originally a self-protection framework for recovering people-pleasers — distorted into justification for treating people poorly while calling it independence or confidence. Unlearn: you owe basic human decency. Associative conditioning means people remember how you made them feel. Reputation = aggregate of a thousand ordinary moments. Trust, opportunities, and goodwill compound through genuine reciprocity.
2. “Comfort Is Fine / Safe”
Every day presents a choice between comfort and growth. Neuroplasticity (Neuroplasticity) is triggered by challenge — not by easy, familiar tasks. Easy tasks run existing pathways; challenge builds new ones. Unlearn: discomfort is not the price of growth — it is the process of it. The discomfort is the signal that rewiring is happening.
3. “Everyone Is Rooting For Me”
When someone in your social circle advances, it disrupts the implicit status hierarchy. The brain registers this as a mild threat — producing subtle sabotage, dismissal, or diminishment below the level of conscious intention. People operate from insecurity they probably haven’t examined. Unlearn: pay attention to whose face actually lights up at your good news. Invest there.
4. “More Work = More Value / Virtue”
Busyness as identity. The Pareto Principle (Pareto-Principle): 80% of outcomes from 20% of inputs. Cognitive resources deplete across a work session — quality in hour eight is categorically different from hour two. Unlearn: four focused deliberate hours beats twelve fragmented exhausting ones. Busyness is often a dissociation strategy — moving fast enough to avoid uncomfortable stillness. Measure by impact.
5. “I Must Manage Everyone’s Feelings”
The need for approval is installed early — children learn certain behaviors produce love, others produce withdrawal. Carried into adulthood it becomes People-Pleasing. Chronic suppression of own needs activates the same stress pathways as external threat. Unlearn: you are not responsible for managing everyone else’s happiness. Say yes when you mean yes. Say no when you mean no.
Key Concepts

People-Pleasing: approval-seeking installed in childhood nervous system; chronic self-suppression activates stress pathways identical to external threat; self-betrayal leading to identity erosion and resentment
Pareto-Principle: 80/20 rule — find the 20% of inputs generating 80% of outcomes; four focused hours > twelve fragmented ones; measure by impact not volume
Comfort-Zone: comfort is not safety — it is stagnation; every choice defaults to comfort or growth; the boat was built to sail
Neuroplasticity: challenge triggers new pathways; easy familiar tasks only run existing ones; discomfort is the biological signal that rewiring is occurring
Willpower-Depletion: cognitive resources are finite and deplete across a day; decision quality in hour 8 is categorically lower than hour 2; the Pareto 20% requires your peak cognitive state

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How To Build Wealth Psychology From Scratch
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How To Build Wealth Psychology From Scratch

Income is capped not by opportunity but by a subconscious ceiling installed before age ten, which the amygdala enforces as a physical threat — and the ceiling can be located, traced to its origin, and dissolved through accumulated behavioural evidence.

Core Argument
Wealth is defined as freedom — “the ability to do what i want, when i want, with whoever i want, for as long as i want” — with money as the tool that buys it in the society we built. The will to autonomy is placed as a primal drive alongside hunger, thirst and social connection, because independent decision-making was historically a survival mechanism.
The piece marks a threshold explicitly: crossing into single-digit millions makes quality-of-life differences against someone with a hundred times more “almost entirely insignificant.” Past that point, accumulation stops being about freedom and starts being about Ego — attaching identity to the bigger house, the newer car — at which point “you’ve become a slave to the money” and are working backward from the original goal.
The obstacle is not the market. It is that most people live at roughly 20% of their earning capacity because of a number their subconscious has fixed.
Key Concepts

The financial thermostat — the diagnostic is a single question asked quietly with no distractions: what is the maximum amount of money I could realistically earn in one year? The first reflexive number, before rationalising or aspirational inflation, is the ceiling. It was almost certainly set before age ten, usually around a money-related moment that left a mark — a parent getting fired, watching stress about bills, a stretch of not having enough, the house feeling unstable. “That moment froze. And it became the invisible upper limit you’ve been bouncing up against ever since.”
Money is processed by the amygdala, not the prefrontal cortex — the mechanism the piece rests on. Genuinely considering income beyond the internal ceiling fires the threat-detection centre with the same signal as physical danger, so the body interprets earning more as a threat. This is offered as the explanation for self-sabotage at specific income levels: undercharging, missing obvious opportunities, unconsciously staying inside the familiar range. The brain is protecting you using information it received decades ago — the childhood moment was real and the emotional response valid, but “money above this level means danger” is a category error.
Two ideological expressions of the same ceiling — both framed as rationalisations rather than positions. (1) Work hard, save carefully, it’ll add up — which had substance when labour markets rewarded loyalty and companies invested in employees, a world the piece says is mostly gone now that firms optimise shareholder value and treat labour as a cost to reduce. (2) The whole thing is rigged, trying is complicity — a worldview that “conveniently also makes inaction feel like a political stance rather than a fear response.”
The spending-identity audit — pull three months of transactions and ask of each category whether it reflects someone building toward freedom or someone reinforcing a story about why they can’t. Three patterns: spending to signal status not yet held (common where the money belief is rooted in shame — performing a self that feels safer than the real one); spending that numbs rather than nourishes (emotional eating, shopping as mood regulation, tied to unresolved scarcity anxiety); and spending that avoids investment — unconscious spending down to the comfort zone before money can be deployed.
Generational money beliefs — transmitted not by explicit teaching but by emotional tone: what happened in the room when money was discussed, what went unsaid, what was modelled. Four named beliefs and their function — “money is the root of all evil” (keeps you from wealth to preserve a self-image as a good person), “we’re not the kind of people who…” (scarcity as family identity, so earning above the ceiling feels like betrayal of tribal loyalty), “you have to work hard for money” (makes leverage and passive income feel undeserved), “save everything, spend nothing” (scarcity anxiety deep enough to prevent investment).
The 90-day protocol — month one makes the invisible visible: run the audit, name the ceiling number, trace its origin, log every instance of the ceiling enforcing itself, and begin deliberate exposure to income levels above it by researching how people at 2× the ceiling actually earn. The stated rationale is familiarity: “your amygdala tags things as dangerous partly because they’re unfamiliar.” Month two is identity votes — charge more, have the avoided conversation, pitch the thing — where “the specific action matters less than the vote it represents,” each one telling the nervous system I survived it. Month three consolidates by pointing at the accumulated evidence when the ceiling reasserts, because “evidence is the only thing the amygdala updates on.”
Honest scoping of the timeline — the author flags that 90 days is a starting point rather than a fix: “the ceiling was built over decades and it takes more than three months to fully dissolve.”

Notable Passages

“Wealth is the ability to fully experience life.” — Henry David Thoreau


“Money is only a tool. It will take you wherever you wish, but it will not replace you as the driver.” — Ayn Rand


“Honouring your parents doesn’t require carrying their limitations forward. You can love someone and update their operating system.”

Connections

The financial thermostat is Identity-Setpoint applied to income — the same homeostatic snap-back mechanism, with money as the variable.
Amygdala-enforced threat response ties directly to Amygdala and HPA-Axis-and-Cortisol; the dissolution protocol is subconscious-reprogramming-methods and Subconscious-Programming applied to money.
Identity votes in month two are identity-as-behavioral-architecture and Identity-Shift — behavioural evidence updating the self-concept.
The childhood installation of the ceiling is a case of childhood-wounds-and-adult-patterns and limiting-beliefs.
Wealth-as-freedom and the ego threshold connect to wealth-systems, Asset-vs-Labor-Income and Golden-Handcuffs; “you’ve become a slave to the money” past the threshold is Hedonic-Treadmill in financial form.
Deliberate exposure reducing threat response is the same familiarity mechanism described in Comfort-Zone.
The audit’s status-signalling category connects to social-signaling and status-and-dominance-signals.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Would You Rather Live in a Cage or Die Free

Reframes the Icarus myth — they tell it as a warning about ambition, but Icarus was a prisoner. Flying too high and falling was the free choice; staying in the labyrinth was the cage. Reframes risk-taking from recklessness to necessary freedom.

Key Concepts

Icarus reframe: the conventional reading (“don’t be too ambitious”) serves the interests of those who benefit from people staying in their assigned place
Icarus and his father were prisoners — the flight was the escape, not the mistake; falling free > living caged
The choice is not “be safe or take risks” — it is “live under someone else’s control or take full responsibility for your own life including its risks”
Fear as the cage: most people’s “safe” choices are choices made from fear, not from what they actually want — the cage is made of anxiety
The author’s pen name (ixcarus) is intentional — he identifies with the version of Icarus who chose to fly anyway
Connects to existentialist philosophy: authentic choice in the face of risk is the only real freedom

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: What You Can Learn from Icarus on Ambition
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
What You Can Learn from Icarus on Ambition

Icarus is usually read as a warning against ambition; read properly it is two lessons at once — find something worth flying for, and let pride not spend the altitude you gained.

Key Concepts

The myth, restated precisely — Icarus and his father Daedalus are imprisoned in the Labyrinth on Crete by King Minos. Daedalus, a master craftsman, builds wings of feathers and wax with a two-sided warning: fly too low and sea moisture weighs the wings down; fly too high and the sun’s heat melts the wax. Icarus complies at first, becomes exhilarated by flight, climbs, and falls into the Aegean.
The corridor is the point. The warning is not “don’t fly” but that both extremes are fatal — a constraint people remember only in its upward half.
Reading one — flight as freedom. For a prisoner, wings meant release from a life governed by another’s decisions. Icarus pursued what he wanted rather than what he was told, and is described as satisfied, almost euphoric, in his demise. Modern application: find something worth dedicating a life to and live for it daily — an aim no one can confiscate, described as “intellectual property that has no price tag”, which makes societal expectation non-binding.
Reading two — the fall as a warning against romanticising self-destruction. The fall was optional and entirely avoidable; pride cost him the very freedom he was enjoying, and left Daedalus flying on alone with the guilt. Modern application: when things start working — a business, education, a side project, a competition — control pride. “When it starts to work, shut your mouth.” Do not convert early success into a demand for validation, and do not overextend, with Napoleon’s invasion of Russia after conquering most of Europe given as the strategic analogue.
The two readings are explicitly held together as one double lesson: chase something for the vitality it supplies, and humble yourself against going too far.
Framed throughout as subjective philosophical interpretation offered “with a grain of salt”, not as the myth’s settled meaning.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How You Can Reach Excellence in a World that Demands Lesser
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How You Can Reach Excellence in a World that Demands Lesser

The gap between exceptional and average is not talent but a set of learnable behaviours — and regression to the mean is not a metaphor here, it is the literal statistical shape of how most people quit.

Key Concepts

Regression to the mean, used precisely. An unusually high or low measurement tends to be followed by one closer to the average, because extreme outcomes combine true ability and luck — the rookie’s exceptional first season followed by a worse second. Applied to self-improvement: beginner’s luck supplies initial momentum, the first real obstacle arrives, and most quit. The cycle stated flatly: try something new → initial success → first obstacle → give up and rationalise.
Why quitting is the default, mechanistically: the brain favours the path of least resistance to conserve energy, so difficulty triggers “divert, go to an easier route” — and each repetition myelinates the giving-up pathway until it becomes the coping response and then the self-identity.
Delayed gratification as the trainable separator, via the 1970s Stanford Marshmallow Test — one marshmallow now or two if you wait — which associated waiting with better later outcomes in academics, health and social skills. The author reports personally undergoing a sixth-grade version with homework passes as the reward. Explicitly not innate: “it’s something that can be trained by literally anyone.” The baseline it produces: long-term decision > short-term decision, which also eliminates bad options up front.
Internal over external validation — greatness requires not needing permission, and “selfish is the price to pay to greatness when it means giving up people-pleasing.” Engagement and fame are finite; potential is not.
Environment as a controllable input, through the brain’s association of behaviours with environmental stimuli — bedrooms mean sleep, so studying there creates cognitive dissonance. The optimal environment is stated as subjective: a clean office may suit one person less than a messy room. The rule is to find yours and stay in it.
Social circle, opened with Proverbs 13:20. The specific refinement beyond “you are the average of the five people around you” is the rejection of yes-men — an inner circle that tells uncomfortable truths rather than comforting lies, and that intervenes when a friend self-sabotages instead of enabling.
Solitude versus isolation — a deliberate distinction, isolation carrying a negative connotation while solitude is the voluntary choice to be alone. The claim is that the 99% are over-socialised, following the herd and neglecting inner work, and that only time alone permits genuinely independent thought. Opened with Pascal on humanity’s problems stemming from the inability to sit quietly in a room alone.
Relentless action, via Naval’s “impatience with actions, patience with results.” Napoleon’s independent corps system and high-speed manoeuvring are the case — hitting enemies before they consolidated — with his own line that he preferred a lucky general to a good one, read as preferring generals who created opportunities over ones who waited for perfect conditions. The hubris of the Russian invasion is noted as the counterweight.
Antifragility, credited to Nassim Taleb: systems that grow stronger under stress, disorder and uncertainty. The muscle analogy — micro-tears under load producing strength after recovery — extended to obstacles in business, sport and social life.
Closing reframe: success is not the achievement, the fame or the money, but “the person you are becoming.”

Unfortunately, The Clock is Ticking

A mortality audit using precise time accounting — 700,000 lifetime hours reduced to ~250,000 usable hours after sleep, childhood, and old age — triggers the urgency that the brain normally suppresses through comfortable deferral.

Key Concepts

700,000 hours lifetime breakdown: -230k (sleep) = 470k → -120k (childhood) = 350k → -100k (old age/incapacity) = ~250,000 usable hours left
The grandfather deathbed moment: “I wasted so much time, kid” — even a man who built businesses and traveled the world felt profound regret; the feeling of wasted time is universal
Terror Management Theory application: the brain suppresses mortality awareness because it’s too terrifying — this is adaptive but produces the “I’ll start tomorrow” loop
Making the calculation real and specific breaks the comfortable abstraction of “I have my whole life ahead of me”
Connects to parkinsons-law-starting: the absence of a deadline (felt mortality) allows the brain to defer indefinitely

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How To Combat The State Of Laziness
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How To Combat The State Of Laziness

Laziness is not a character flaw but a mechanical failure of task initiation — the anticipatory dopamine wave never fires — and it dissolves once five specific sources of fog are sharpened.

Core Argument
The piece opens by refusing the identity claim. “I’m just a lazy person” and “laziness is who I am” attach a temporary state to the self, and once attached, “your brain tries to protect it, because identity is something it defends with all its might.” The escape from being a type of person is far harder than ending a state, so the first instruction is to stop using the word about yourself.
Laziness is then distinguished from two things it gets confused with. Procrastination is postponing a task in favour of easier or more pleasant ones that are usually less important; to qualify it must represent ineffective planning and produce a higher overall cost in time, stress, guilt or lost productivity. Delaying a tax return until the figures are in is strategic; delaying it into a fine is procrastination. The decisive difference: the procrastinator keeps the intention and completes the task, at a cost — with laziness the intention does not stay. Idleness is simply not doing anything, which may be laziness but may equally be having nothing to do, being temporarily unable, or resting after finishing.
The piece notes idleness is romanticised (the Italian dolce far niente) and that many people work hard from a desire to be idle rather than valuing the work. But the natural inclination toward idleness reverses under duration: prolonged idleness becomes unbearable, which is why drivers take longer routes to avoid sitting in traffic — “moving in the wrong direction feels better than not moving at all.”
A definitional pass follows: willingness is being prepared to do the work voluntarily, disposing is arranging things in proper order, volition is using the power of choice. So being lazy means no conscious choice was made, therefore nothing was arranged to satisfy the need — “you blame your character for the result of a process you have never started.”
Key Concepts

The two dopamine waves — the mechanism the piece rests on, opening with the correction that dopamine is not the pleasure chemical but the one that rises during pursuit and anticipation, not attainment. The pursuit wave fires on the smell of coffee or a pizza advertisement and supplies the craving and the energy to get up and act. The consumption wave fires when the food hits, marking it as survival-valuable so the behaviour repeats — and it runs higher for calorie-, fat- and sugar-dense food, “that is why it is difficult to stop eating those foods but not broccoli.”
Laziness is the absence of the first wave — without it there is no craving and no adrenaline rush, so you feel heavy, sleepy and tired even after eight hours of sleep. “You are chemically unmotivated and your body understands that as fatigue.” The consequence drawn: forced discipline sustained too long will fail, because you are using conscious willpower against a system supplying no fuel, “and your brain does not tire in the way you do.” Once the wave fires, the task stops feeling like pushing a car uphill and starts feeling like steering one already rolling.
The effort-cost calculation — the brain runs expected reward minus expected cost on every task, and if cost outweighs reward the motivation is gone completely, not reduced. Cost includes uncertainty, fear of failure, social judgment, ambiguity, cognitive effort and emotional discomfort — not just physical effort. Hence the piece’s sharpest illustration: writing one email can be impossible while scrolling for forty-five minutes is easy, despite near-identical finger movement. One is priced at nothing; the other carries uncertainty and judgment “you do not consciously see but your brain sees and it prices accordingly.”
Manufacturing the first wave with delayed gratification — pair a genuinely desired reward with the dreaded task (the author’s own: the Italian corner shop sandwich, earned only after five consecutive days of running). The rule is that it must be something actually wanted, “not something that sounds healthy or virtuous.” Because the brain is a prediction machine, repetition makes it predict that the task reliably precedes the reward and spike dopamine before you start. Cited: the 1970s Stanford marshmallow experiment, and the prefrontal cortex as the seat of reasoning, planning and self-control that loses to emotional centres under constant instant reward. Crucially flagged as scaffolding — “it is the jump start, not the engine” — to be removed once the behaviour is automatic.
Friction and decision count — the diagnostic question is how many decisions are required before you can start? You think “put shoes on, go”; the brain sees find clothes, charge headphones, choose a playlist, find a water bottle, decide the workout, check the weather. Each decision burns glucose in the prefrontal cortex and is a real cost, and if motivation is already low the brain will seize any of them as an exit. The piece times a collapse at eleven seconds — a slow internet connection, a file loading — enough to trigger “I’ll do it later.” This is offered as the actual reason high performers strip decisions out: Steve Jobs’ identical clothes, writers at the same desk, athletes’ fixed pre-session routines. “None of it is about the discipline. It is about reducing the cognitive friction to such an extent that the decision never has to be made.”
The Zeigarnik effect as the cheapest lever — Bluma Zeigarnik observed in a 1920s Vienna restaurant that waiters held complex unpaid orders in detail and forgot them the moment the bill was paid. Unfinished tasks stay open loops that pull attention, which is why starting generates genuine desire to continue. The instruction is to commit to five minutes with permission to stop, because even if you stop the loop stays open and taps you on the shoulder all day. “The start is the expensive part. The continue is easier.”
The five levels of clarity — the closing framework, on the premise that an unclear goal reads to the brain as an overwhelming threat. (1) Destination — written in one sentence precise enough that a stranger could tell when you reached it, since “foggy goals produce foggy efforts, and foggy efforts feel like laziness” (Seneca’s port and wind). (2) Reason — Ikigai; a weak reason needs constant maintenance from motivation videos, mood, weather and sleep, a strong one needs none, and “if you are lazy, your ikigai is missing.” (3) Cost — Bezos’ regret minimisation, pulled close by vividly imagining yourself at forty with the same job, body, money and excuses, only older and more tired. (4) Next action — shrink it to the smallest five-minute move, because “your brain freezes on big tasks and runs on small ones.” (5) Environment — phone in another room rather than on the desk, junk food never bought rather than resisted; “stop fighting yourself with willpower you do not have.”

Notable Passages

“Being lazy means to be fully awake inside of a body that does not want to act. Your engine is running but you’re not stepping on the gas.”


“Nothing is so fatiguing as the eternal hanging on of an uncompleted task.” — William James


“While we are postponing, life speeds by.” — Seneca

Connections

Directly extends Procrastination by separating it from laziness on the intention criterion — a distinction that page should carry.
The two-wave model is the core of Dopaminergic-System and Neuroscience-of-Desire (wanting versus having), and the comfort critique — “nearly all the primal desires are satisfied almost instantly… so the system of pursuit quietens down” — is dopamine-baseline and Artificial-vs-Natural-Reward.
The “I am lazy” identity trap is identity-as-behavioral-architecture and Identity-Setpoint; the refusal to let a state become a self connects to limiting-beliefs.
Friction reduction and decision elimination connect to Willpower-Depletion and Energy-Management; the environment level restates environment-shapes-identity.
Reward pairing and its planned removal is Delayed-Gratification plus Habit-Formation — scaffolding removed once automaticity is reached.
Behavioural inertia and the five-minute start connect to Momentum-vs-Motivation and Compound-Effect.
Ikigai is invoked by name as the “reason” level.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: Comfort Is Killing You (And You Know It)
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Comfort Is Killing You (And You Know It)
Core Argument
Comfort — not failure, rejection, or laziness — is the true killer of human potential. Through “Mike’s” story (oil fields, dead dreams, golden handcuffs), ixcarus demonstrates how comfort compounds over time, making escape progressively harder until the wings forget how to fly.
Key Ideas
The Real Enemy: Comfort

“comfort is the biggest fucking killer of dreams. not failure, not rejection, not even laziness.”

That slow death where nothing scares you anymore. The routine that felt like stability but became a prison.
Golden Handcuffs
Making just enough to pay bills, not enough to escape. Comfortable enough to not starve; miserable enough to hate every day. The “stability” that has you working to death for scraps.
Mike’s story: smart, had business dreams, ended up in oil fields at 26 — body breaking down, wife who won’t cook, beer + phone until passing out, repeat. “Risk what? The soul-crushing routine that’s slowly killing you?”
Comfort Compounding (The Interest Analogy)

“comfort compounds just like interest. the longer you stay comfortable, the more you have to lose by leaving.”

At 20: one excuse (rent). At 25: more excuses (relationship, car). At 35: wife, kids, mortgage — wings have forgotten how to fly. The window doesn’t stay open.
Atrophy from Disuse
“The longer you stay in a nest, the less your wings remember how to fly.” Physical, psychological, and motivational atrophy from non-use. Once wings forget, desire alone isn’t enough to remember.
The Honest Trade-Off
Security in a prison is still a prison. “I’d rather fail trying to build something real than succeed at living a life that slowly kills me.” The trade: comfort now vs. a life worth remembering.
Key Concepts

Comfort-Zone — not just a motivational concept; a physical and psychological trap
Golden-Handcuffs — the economic mechanism of comfortable entrapment
Comfort-Compounding — why escape gets exponentially harder over time
Atrophy from Disuse — wings that forget how to fly

Connections to Other Sources

different-take-self-improvement — both essays warn against different failure modes: this one warns against too little challenge; the other warns against too much optimization

Standout Passages

“comfort whispers ‘just one more year, save a bit more, then you’ll take the risk.’ except that year turns into five, then ten”


“when you’re more afraid of change than you are excited about your future, you’re already dead. just waiting for your body to catch up.”

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: The Complete Testosterone And Estrogen Optimization Guide
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Complete Testosterone And Estrogen Optimization Guide

Hormonal decline is environmental rather than personal — the modern chemical and light environment systematically undermines endocrine function — so the protocol is not biohacking but deliberate compensation for conditions ancestors never had to engineer.

Core Argument
The numbers open the piece. Mean total testosterone in men fell from 605 ng/dL in 1999–2000 to 451 ng/dL by 2015–2016 — inside a single generation. Since the late 1980s levels have declined roughly 1% per year, and testosterone deficiency now has a prevalence of 20% among adolescent and young adult males. The rhetorical comparison: if average human height or lung capacity dropped a quarter in twenty years, “people would be losing their fucking minds.”
The causes are placed in the environment: synthetic estrogens in unfiltered tap water from pharmaceutical runoff, phthalates in shampoos and personal care products, microplastics shed by polyester clothing now found in human blood, organs and reproductive tissue, xenoestrogens leaching from plastic food packaging, and BPA absorbed through the skin from receipts. “You are living in a chemical environment that your endocrine system was never designed to handle.”
The piece is careful about the female picture rather than overstating it: there is no strong evidence women’s estrogen has seen the same steep generational decline. But endocrine-disrupting chemicals are linked to menstrual disruption, reduced fertility, miscarriage risk, PCOS, endometriosis, altered puberty timing and hormone-sensitive cancers. PCOS now affects roughly 10–15% of women of reproductive age and endometriosis approximately 10%.
The author also explicitly declines to speculate on intent: “I’m not going to get into theories about whether this is deliberate. I don’t know and neither does anyone who says they do with certainty.”
Key Concepts

The lock-and-key model of endocrine disruption — natural testosterone or estrogen is the correctly cut key that fits the lock and produces the right signal. Xenoestrogens are “duplicate keys cut to almost the right shape” that jam the lock, sometimes turning it partially, sometimes blocking the real key entirely. The system then runs on corrupted signals. In men, excess estrogen signal suppresses testosterone through negative feedback: the body reads estrogen levels as information about how much testosterone to make, so flooding it with mimics drops production.
Estrogen dominance — for women, the receptor sites are finite, and xenoestrogens compete for them. The result is not necessarily elevated real estrogen but a body flooded with estrogen-like signalling producing the same downstream effects: heavier and more painful periods, worse PMS, breast tenderness, difficulty losing weight around hips and thighs, mood instability, elevated hormone-sensitive cancer risk.
The cortisol axis compounding it — chronic cortisol directly suppresses progesterone, the hormone balancing estrogen in the luteal phase, so sustained stress load worsens estrogen dominance from a second direction. For men, chronic cortisol elevation is named “one of the most direct suppressors of testosterone production,” with the flat statement that “there’s no supplement protocol that overcomes a lifestyle producing sustained psychological stress.”
Load reduction as the foundation — stated as prerequisite to anything additive: “you cannot out-run or even out-supplement a body that’s being chemically undermined from every direction.” Reverse-osmosis water filtration (with actual price tiers — countertop 150–400, under-sink 200–600), glass instead of plastic storage since leaching accelerates with heat, avoiding synthetic fragrance where phthalates hide under the label “fragrance,” and organic produce prioritised for thin-skinned fruits and vegetables.
The female protocol — cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cauliflower, brussels sprouts, cabbage) for indole-3-carbinol supporting hepatic estrogen clearance, 2–3 servings daily, since the liver is the primary organ for estrogen metabolism. Strength training 3–4× weekly with moderate cardio rather than excessive high-intensity cardio, which spikes cortisol enough to suppress reproductive hormones — the reason competitive female athletes often experience cycle disruption. Daily walking as “one of the most underrated interventions.” Adequate dietary fat at 25–30% of calories, because estrogen and progesterone are built from cholesterol and decades of low-fat advice actively undermined production. Omega-3 (2–3 servings fatty fish weekly or 2g EPA+DHA). Magnesium glycinate 300–400mg before bed, required for progesterone production and cortisol regulation. Protein at 0.7–0.9g per pound — “your body literally cannot produce hormones without amino acid building blocks. It’s like trying to build a house with no bricks.” Strict circadian consistency, since the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis depends on consistent light-dark signalling. Reduced alcohol specifically in the luteal phase.
The male protocol — heavy compound movements (squat, deadlift, bench, overhead press) produce the strongest acute testosterone response, with 2–3 minute rest periods because 30-second rests keep cortisol elevated and blunt the response. Sleep in full darkness at 65–68°F, since testosterone production peaks in deep sleep between 10pm and 2am and any light in that window suppresses the cascade. Zinc as a direct precursor (oysters highest by a significant margin; 25–30mg daily if not eating red meat 2–3× weekly). Vitamin D as a hormone precursor — 10–30 minutes direct sunlight on significant skin area, or D3 at 3000–5000 IU with K2. Caffeine cut off by noon, since acute morning cortisol supports production while chronic elevation suppresses it. Alcohol reduced to 1–2 drinks weekly, as it suppresses production and accelerates aromatisation of testosterone to estrogen. Phone out of the pocket on precautionary EMF grounds. Pornography addressed as dopamine dysregulation that blunts hormonal response to real stimulation.
Evidence honesty — notable throughout, and worth recording as a feature of the piece. Seed cycling is presented with its limits: “the research is limited… the evidence isn’t strong enough to call this proven,” recommended only because downside risk is essentially zero and the fibre, magnesium and fatty acids help regardless. Red light therapy, EMF and the onion/luteinizing-hormone claim are each flagged as limited or animal-model evidence. The author also discloses a practice he does not personally follow while still reporting the research.
Balance rather than maximisation — “men need some estrogen. Just not excess. Women need some testosterone. Just not excess.” The closing frame is compensatory: ancestors got sunlight, real food, constant movement and darkness at night automatically, so “you have to engineer all of it deliberately because modern life stripped it away.”

Notable Passages

“Your body doesn’t know the difference between real hormones and synthetic mimics. It responds to the signal regardless of where the signal came from.”


“They’re selling you the solution to a problem the modern world created.”


“Comfortable modern life is what got you here. And deliberate, slightly inconvenient choices are what get you out.”

Connections

The author reports his own testosterone moving from ~550 ng/dL to ~700 ng/dL after applying the protocol — a personal-measurement data point rather than a claim of typical results.
Extends hormone-optimization and maximize-testosterone-estrogen with the environmental-disruptor mechanism rather than only the lifestyle levers.
Cortisol as the shared suppressor connects to cortisol and HPA-Axis-and-Cortisol; the sleep window connects to sleep-architecture, circadian-rhythm and melatonin.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: The Conscious And Subconscious Mind: Everything You Need To Know
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Conscious And Subconscious Mind: Everything You Need To Know

The part of you that feels like you processes roughly four ten-thousandths of a
percent of what reaches your senses — so emotions, judgements and most decisions
arrive from a system you never consented to program, and the leverage is not
thinking harder but changing what that system runs.

The argument
Assembled from a named reading list — Joseph Murphy’s The Power of Your Subconscious
Mind, Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow, Tor Nørretranders’ The User Illusion,
Jung’s collected works on the unconscious, and Freud. The essay’s structure is to
establish the size asymmetry first, then work outward to what follows from it.
Key Concepts


The asymmetry, in numbers. The conscious mind holds about seven items
(plus or minus two) and processes 40–50 bits per second, against a total
sensory input of about 11 million — leaving conscious awareness with roughly
0.0004% of what arrives. It is also slow, effortful, single-focus and
metabolically expensive, burning glucose, which is offered as why hard thinking is
physically tiring.


What the subconscious actually runs: heartbeat, breathing, digestion, immune
function; every memory including the unrecallable ones; learned motor programs like
walking, driving, typing and speaking; snap judgements from micro-expressions never
consciously registered; and the filtering that decides what the conscious mind gets
shown at all. Freud’s unconscious, Jung’s collective unconscious and modern
implicit processing are treated as three descriptions of the same substrate.


The CEO analogy. Conscious mind as chief executive — big decisions, direction,
novel problems, but only a few things at once; subconscious as the thousands of
employees running operations. The loop: input arrives, the subconscious filters it
against stored patterns and generates an emotional response, routine matches are
handled automatically, and only novel or complex cases are escalated. Whatever the
conscious mind then decides becomes a new pattern stored for automatic handling
next time. That is learning — conscious struggle converting into subconscious
automation, which is why driving starts exhausting and ends invisible. The
conclusion drawn is that the goal is not to use the conscious mind more but to
train the subconscious to run better programs.


Programs installed without permission. Emotional reactions are subconscious
output rather than choice — the immediate anger at an insult, the fear at a spider,
nostalgia at a smell. Their origin is childhood conditioning: parental relationship
patterns absorbed and later replayed with partners; being shouted at for mistakes
installing mistakes = danger and anxiety around imperfection; being praised for
quietness installing expression = risk. The developmental window given is the
third trimester to about age seven, when the brain sits in a theta state and
absorbs indiscriminately — offered as why political views so often track whoever
raised you. This is also why conscious knowledge does not dislodge them: the
subconscious is older, faster and more myelinated, so the emotion has already
flooded the system by the time the conscious mind objects. Knowing something
intellectually while feeling otherwise is two systems running on different
information.


The Reticular Activating System as the bridge, and the piece’s most practical
claim. A bundle of neurons at the brainstem decides what gets through the filter,
and you program it with conscious focus: buy a car and suddenly see that model
everywhere, because it was always there and previously discarded as irrelevant.
Focus on problems and it surfaces problems; focus on solutions and it surfaces
those. The author is careful to separate this from manifestation — the mechanism is
filtering rather than causation, same reality, different filter.


Cognitive biases as subconscious heuristics — speed-and-pattern shortcuts that
once aided survival and now produce systematic error. Five are worked:
confirmation bias, why opposed partisans watch one event and see two; the
availability heuristic, where ease of recall stands in for likelihood, so recent
news about crashes makes flying feel riskier; anchoring, which is why the
struck-through original price makes an overpriced sale price feel like a deal;
sunk cost, keeping people in failing situations to avoid conceding a past
decision; and fundamental attribution error, blaming others’ character and one’s
own circumstances. Named as features rather than flaws, correctable only by
effortful conscious attention — which is why they persist.


Reprogramming needs repetition and emotion, not understanding. A hundred books
on confidence leave insecurity intact, because knowing is not rewriting. The
channels given: repetition in the thousands rather than tens (the mechanism behind
affirmations working when they do); strong emotion, which is why trauma encodes so
deeply and why peak experiences can shift programming faster than years of talk;
hypnosis, as direct access past the conscious filter; visualisation with sensory
and emotional detail, since the subconscious does not sharply distinguish vivid
imagination from experience, which is the basis of athletic mental rehearsal; and
meditation, which creates observation space between stimulus and response.


Dreams as offline processing. The conscious mind shuts down while the
subconscious sorts the day, consolidates memory and works through emotional
content — offered as why unprocessed trauma recurs as nightmares, and why sleeping
on it works. Three interpretations are laid side by side without adjudication:
Freud’s wish fulfilment, Jung’s symbolic messages, and the neuroscientific reading
of largely random firing retrospectively narrativised. The problem-solving cases
cited are Mendeleev on the periodic table, Kekulé on benzene, and Howe on the
sewing machine.


The superconscious, explicitly flagged as theory rather than science — Jung’s
collective unconscious as the account of why separated cultures generate similar
myths and archetypes. The author declines to adjudicate, noting the experience is
real even where the explanation is contested, and lists deep meditation, flow,
psychedelics and crisis as the reported routes.



“your conscious focus programs your subconscious perception… same reality, different filter.”

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: The Consumption Dilemma
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Consumption Dilemma

Humans are built to create and are being farmed as consumers — and the exit is not moderation but replacing consumption with production.

Key Concepts

Short-form video as the specific mechanism. 5–15 second clips exploit a brain that is a prediction machine craving certainty; the algorithm runs a variable-ratio reward schedule explicitly compared to a slot machine, so the uncertainty of the next scroll is what hooks, not the content.
Emotional cycling — one video makes you happy, the next outraged, the next empowered, the next depressed. The claim is that users scroll through emotional states without registering that they are doing so.
The physiological chain: repeated dopamine spikes → sympathetic nervous system activation → norepinephrine and cortisol secretion → anxiety and stress. Downstream effects named as a weakened attention span, lowered dopamine baseline, and increased mental fatigue.
Akrasia — Aristotle’s term for acting against one’s own better judgement — is used for the resulting state of lost self-control.
The attention economy stated as arithmetic: each view = engagement, engagement = ad revenue, ad revenue = corporate profit. The user is the statistic being monetised.
Authenticity traded for approval — internal validation swapped for external. Rented supercars, performed relationships, the staged matcha thrown out five seconds after the photo. Identity fuses with the brands sold to it, and “without these products or sold lifestyles, they are nothing.”
The bandwagon effect — adopting behaviour because others have — illustrated with the 2018 Tide Pod challenge: real health risk accepted for engagement, “minimal upside for massive downside.”
Evolutionary mismatch. Humans evolved for scarcity, movement and communal entertainment — hunting, gathering, folklore, dancing, presence. The modern substitutes (DoorDash, Netflix, Uber, short-form feeds) supply abundance, sedentism and isolation to hardware calibrated for their opposites.
The vocabulary argument — supporting someone is “glazing”, making something is “corny”, privacy is “nonchalant”. Read as evidence that mediocrity has been normalised to the point where trying is punished.
Three prescriptions, in order: cut the source (delete the apps, add blockers); read 20 minutes a day, genre irrelevant, because long-form reading encodes into long-term memory where short-form does not; and walk daily — listed benefits include mental clarity from increased blood flow, enhanced creativity, reduced cortisol, dopamine-sensitivity reset, nervous-system regulation, cardiovascular health.
Creation is the terminal prescription — writing, painting, coding, building — because it produces “real dopamine”, trains delayed gratification, and validates internally rather than by permission.
Notable for being the author’s stated first piece of writing ever, which places it at the start of this corpus.
