sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: covid-neuropsychological-effects
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Lasting Neuropsychological Effects Of COVID-19

The essay concerns the psychological conditions of the pandemic—unresolved
threat, isolation, masks, remote interaction, and collapsed environments—while
separately acknowledging bereavement, infection, and long COVID. Its population-
level neurological claims should be read as the author’s synthesis, not as a
diagnosis of every person who lived through 2020–2022.

Threat without a clean ending
ixcarus contrasts an ordinary alarm cycle—danger appears, action occurs, resolution
arrives—with a threat that remained uncertain for months. Changing guidance,
infection risk, news, and other people’s fear supplied recurring cues with no
single completion signal. The source describes this as chronic activation involving
the Amygdala, cortisol, and norepinephrine.
It connects sustained stress literature to hippocampal and prefrontal effects, then
generalizes those mechanisms to pandemic experience. The bounded claim is that
prolonged stress can affect memory, regulation, and threat sensitivity. The essay
does not establish that every exposed brain physically shrank, nor can behavioral
changes be separated here from infection, grief, economic conditions, prior mental
health, or other causes.
Social routines lost automaticity
Isolation removed repeated practice in reading rooms, navigating conflict,
calibrating distance, and building intimacy. The work uses a “use it or lose it”
model: formerly automatic social behavior can become effortful after long disuse,
especially for young people whose formative practice was interrupted. Its literal
claim that myelin on social circuits thinned is not demonstrated within the essay;
the safer graph link is to experience-dependent Neuroplasticity and skill
deconditioning.
Masks reduced facial information and video calls changed gaze, timing, and spatial
cues. The source argues that consciously compensating for missing cues contributes
to fatigue. This does not imply that masks alone caused a uniform social deficit;
it identifies one altered input among isolation, stress, remote interaction, and
developmental timing.
One room acquired incompatible predictions
Work, school, exercise, entertainment, and rest were compressed into the home.
Because environments become associated with states, the same room could cue
concentration, sleep, vigilance, and leisure at once. environmental-context-collapse
names this collision. Difficulty focusing or relaxing can then reflect ambiguous
context rather than a lack of effort.
The source’s most useful recovery implication is reversibility: if repeated
conditions helped train vigilance, avoidance, or social effort, repeated safe
practice and clearer contexts can supply new learning. That is a direction for
reconditioning, not a promise of uniform recovery or a substitute for care.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How To Create Your Own Reality: The Reticular Activating System
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How To Create Your Own Reality: The Reticular Activating System

The reality you experience is not objective — it is what a brainstem filter let
through, and that filter is programmed by what you have repeatedly signalled is
important, which makes it trainable rather than given.

The argument
The framing case is two people walking into the same room. One sees the
opportunities, the connections, the doors cracked open, and leaves with a contact and
something that moves their life forward. The other sees the awkwardness, the people
who did not acknowledge them, the reasons nothing here is for them. Same room, same
people — and the piece refuses the usual explanation that one of them got lucky.
The mechanism
The brain receives approximately eleven million bits per second from the senses;
the conscious mind processes around forty to fifty. Everything else is filtered,
and the filter is the reticular activating system, a bundle of neurons in the
brainstem gatekeeping between the world and conscious experience of it. It decides
what you notice, what registers as important, which opportunities appear and which
threats feel real.
The load-bearing claim is what programs it: beliefs, repeated thoughts, dominant
emotional states, goals and fears. So what you experience is not objective reality
but a curated projection of what your nervous system has been trained to treat as
relevant — you are experiencing your filter of life, which is why two people with
different filters in one room are living in different worlds.
The demonstration is the car. Decide you want a particular one and you see it
everywhere; the cars were always there and the brain was always receiving that
information, but the RAS had no reason to flag it until you marked it important.
The generalisation is the point: fixate on rejection and you find disrespect in tones
of voice and slow replies; fixate on opportunity and doors appear with timing that
seems almost suspicious. Wake up convinced the day will be bad and the filter
collects the evidence effortlessly. Hence the diagnosis — people think they need a
new life when most of the time they need a new filter; the circumstances are often
fine and what is broken is the lens.
Attention as emotional fertilizer
Dopamine is restated as a pursuit chemical rather than a pleasure one, with the
consequence that whatever you repeatedly attend to becomes emotionally charged.
That is offered as why anxiety becomes addictive, why heartbreak becomes obsessive,
and why revenge can feel like purpose — it produces the same neurological drive as
motivation. Years focused on lack build a brain exquisitely sensitive to evidence of
lack; the same environment yields evidence of progress to someone focused on what
they are building.

“most people are building prisons with their focus and calling the prison their circumstances.”

Identity as memorized focus
A significant part of what is experienced as identity is a pattern of repeated
attention. Running a thought like I’m always the one who gets left myelinates a
neural pathway and trains the RAS to seek confirmation, which the brain — an
efficient confirmation machine — supplies every time. So the person you believe
yourself to be is the person you have been rehearsing, and someone different can be
rehearsed: not through hollow affirmations but by directing attention toward evidence
contradicting the old story. This is given as the shared mechanism behind therapy and
journaling when they work.
The same logic covers belief generally: believe people are selfish and ambiguous
behaviour reads as self-interest, believe they are generous and the identical
behaviour reads the other way. The extended example is two people from the same
neighbourhood and school — one treating it as a launching pad with hardship as fuel,
the other as a ceiling with hardship as identity — in completely different places
twenty years later. Circumstances are held to be less predictive of a future than
the filter is.
Retraining it
Understanding the RAS intellectually does nothing if the filter does not change, and
change comes through deliberate repeated signal — offered as a guideline requiring
continuous effort, not a quick sequence. Audit what your mind returns to when
nothing demands it (the shower, driving, lying in bed): that is the current filter.
Name the new signal specifically, since I want to be successful is too vague for
the RAS to work with where opportunity in your industry or evidence of your own
capability is not. Saturate the inputs, because the RAS responds to frequency and
intensity — read about it, be around people who embody it, journal daily looking for
evidence it already exists. For identity, one entry a day answering what happened
today that supports who I’m becoming.
Audit the inputs you did not choose, named as the step people skip: two hours of
doom-scrolling through catastrophe, comparison and conflict is two hours training the
filter to find those things in your life. And expect the lag — years built the
current filter, the old interpretations keep running for weeks, and what matters is
feeding the new signal without flinching, because the RAS always updates toward the
strongest, most repeated signal.
The close returns to the room: one person built a world that let the opportunity in
and the other built a world that filtered it out. Both were constructing reality the
entire time — one of them knew it.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How To Curate An Internal World So Unshakeable that Nothing Can Stop You
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How To Curate An Internal World So Unshakeable that Nothing Can Stop You

Genius Series Part V. Marcus Aurelius ran an empire through plague, invasion, rebellion and economic collapse without folding — six lessons from Meditations on why the internal world is the only one that was ever controllable.

Key Concepts

The historical setup, given properly. Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, last of the Five Good Emperors, defender of the Pax Romana, and the first philosopher-emperor — someone who ruled by Stoic principle rather than merely professing it. The calamities are enumerated: the Antonine Plague in the East killing millions, Germanic tribes pressing the northern borders, the rebellion of Avidius Cassius, and an economic crisis from warfare and plague relief. Meditations is noted as private journal entries never meant for publication — “he would honestly have a heart attack if he knew this was all leaked.”
Lesson one — the dichotomy of control, stated as a binary: release what is external and outside your control by non-attachment; concentrate on the internal — thoughts, judgement, reaction. Mapped to the psychological internal locus of control, and spending energy on the uncontrollable is called a sunk cost fallacy. Worked cases: traffic (you cannot control the cars, you can control impatience), interpersonal drama (you cannot control behaviour, you can create distance), news (you cannot control the world stage, you can stop being drained by it).
Lesson two — your thoughts determine the quality of your life. Routed through neuroplasticity: the narratives you feed the mind are formative. “Life doesn’t happen to you, it’s a reflection OF you.” The chain given: thoughts shape habits, habits shape actions, actions dictate your future.
Lesson three — the best revenge is not to be like your enemy. Retaliation prolongs the cycle of hurt; the alternative is releasing the grudge, because the tension itself consumes your energy, and letting success do the answering — someone who wronged you feels guilt at your rising, not satisfaction. Illustrated at length with Jesus of Nazareth declining the twelve legions of angels at his crucifixion, choosing forgiveness of Judas, Pilate and the crowd over retaliation under maximum pressure.
Lesson four — be a good man rather than debate what one is, with the Epictetus resonance noted (“don’t explain your philosophy, embody it”). The target is performed morality: scripture in a bio contradicted by behaviour, charity done for the posting. “You don’t have to tell anyone you’re going to improve, just improve.”
Lesson five — do not waste your remaining life. Framed as acceptance rather than nihilism: existence is finite and fragile, so the choice is to intellectually justify inaction or to make the most of it. The reframe is sharp — “maybe death wasn’t the enemy after all… it might just be complacency and stagnation.”
Lesson six — gratitude on waking, with a mechanism attached: reduced limbic and amygdala activity, dopamine and serotonin release, and repetition myelinating the pathway until morning contentment becomes automatic and other morning states are pruned. Grounded in the text itself — the opening chapter of Meditations is Marcus thanking specific people by name: his grandfather Verus, his parents and sister, Diognetus and Rusticus, his adoptive father Antoninus Pius, and the gods. The prescription: find three things each morning.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: The Curated Life That's Making You Miserable
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Curated Life That’s Making You Miserable
Social media turned everyone into cultural narcissists — people whose self-worth depends on external validation, whose mood is ruined by low engagement, who manufacture fake moments for strangers. Existence has become performance. The core trap: everyone knows the highlight reel is fake, and everyone compares their real life to everyone else’s fake one — creating universal inadequacy from a universal lie. The underlying mechanism: when you’re performing your life instead of living it, you’re optimizing for how things look rather than how things feel, which means you never actually experience the things you’re documenting. Consequence: strip away the performance and there’s nothing left — the identity IS the brand. The solution: stop curating, stop performing, find freedom in being average and real. Real moments (lazy Sundays, conversations that go nowhere, failures) are where life actually lives.
Key concepts: Cultural Narcissism (external validation dependency), Highlight Reel Comparison (fake vs. real), Performance vs. Experience, Identity as Brand, Curated Existence

“real life is better than the curated version. the moments that don’t make good content are usually the ones that actually matter.”

Connects to: Performativity (curated existence = performativity at civilizational scale; identity IS the brand), Social-Comparison (highlight reel comparison — everyone comparing real life to everyone else’s fake one, creating universal inadequacy from a universal lie), Attention-Economy (platform optimization drives performance behavior; curation rewarded by algorithm), different-take-self-improvement (performative productivity = same curated performance, different domain), has-the-world-lost-its-color (dopamine hijacking prevents authentic presence)

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How To Design Your Day For Maximum Cognitive Output
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How To Design Your Day For Maximum Cognitive Output

The brain is not a machine you can run at maximum for sixteen hours. It moves
through predictable performance phases, each with its own chemistry and its own
best work — so the productivity problem is a scheduling problem, and the fix is
matching the task to the state rather than trying harder.

The stake
The opening is a study in the New England Journal of Medicine — nearly 500
people over five years — finding that those who regularly did cognitively
demanding things, reading, problem solving, learning difficult material, carried a
significantly reduced risk of dementia; among those who coasted, decline came
faster and earlier than expected. Set against that is how a day actually goes:
phone in hand before sitting up in bed, hours of consumption requiring zero
cognitive effort.
The principle drawn from this is use-it-or-lose-it, stated without exceptions.
Coast through a day with no deep thinking, no creation and no hard problem to sit
with, and the pathways for high-level cognition weaken — the myelin thins, the
pathways go quiet — and the loss goes unnoticed. The people running that loop are
described not as stupid but as asleep. The proposed repair is explicitly not
motivation, an app, or a copied morning routine: the brain runs on states, and
once you know them you stop fighting your own biology.
High signal
In the hours after waking the brain runs at peak dopaminergic activity. Dopamine
is treated here not as the feel-good chemical but as the primary signal molecule
for focus, motivation, working memory and executive function. The prefrontal
cortex — where complex reasoning, creative synthesis and novel problem solving
live — is at its most active, working memory is sharpest, and the brain is most
capable of building new connections. Most people spend this on their phone.
The supporting evidence is Anders Ericsson, who studied elite performers —
musicians, athletes, chess grandmasters, surgeons — for decades: one of the most
consistent findings was that the best protected their morning hours for their
hardest cognitive work. Not meetings, not email, not admin.
What belongs here is creating and writing, learning genuinely new and difficult
material, and hard problem solving with real stakes. And the highest-signal task
goes first, not after warming up: spending the opening of the window on something
easy is likened to showing up to the most important meeting of the year and
spending the first hour organising your desk. The author’s own test case is
writing, and mornings burned on notifications produce visibly worse writing every
time.
Stable output
A few hours in the peak dopamine window closes, novelty-seeking drops and the
prefrontal cortex keeps working in a different register. This is framed as a
transition rather than a crash: focus narrows from expansive and creative to
reliable, and the shift is described as moving from dopamine-driven exploration
toward more stable serotonergic activity — the system associated with patience,
consistency and methodical execution. The brain is now less built for generating
ideas and more for executing known ones.
The distinction that carries the section: the tasks belonging here are not easy,
they are just not novel. Reviewing material already encountered, drilling a skill,
editing and refining what the morning produced, structured problem solving inside
frameworks you already understand.
Underneath it sits a claim about routine. The brain loves predictability — when
it knows what is coming it stops spending energy on novelty processing and routes
resources into the task, which is offered as the reason consistent people outperform
spontaneous ones. Routine placed correctly lowers cognitive resistance, so the brain
stops deliberating about whether to do the thing.
Low signal
Late afternoon into evening, dopamine is lower, mental noise rises, and the
prefrontal cortex hands the wheel back to more automatic, lower-effort systems.
Forcing creative work through this is named as a cause of the quiet kind of
burnout — undramatic, a slow erosion of output quality that gets blamed on lack of
discipline when the real fault is timing.
The phase is not wasted, only differently useful: planning tomorrow, so the next
high-signal window is protected before it starts; reflection and journaling;
admin and low-stakes communication; and light consumption that demands no original
output. The author names this as the phase he respected least, forcing night
writing on caffeine and stubbornness — “the writing was shit every time” — not
from incapacity but from running an engine that had already downshifted. Stopping
the fight is what makes the next morning land harder.
Scheduled autopilot
The closing move ties the phases to habit. Motivation is a feeling that fades in
about three days and cannot be built on; structure runs whether you feel like it
or not. Align it with the performance phases and the brain begins to predict what
is coming — the same myelinated pathways built by repetition, working in your
favour. Do deep work at the same time each morning without exception and the brain
pre-loads the neurochemical state before you sit down, the prefrontal cortex
warming up before the document is open. Consistently productive writers and
researchers are not more motivated, on this account, but have trained the system to
expect the demand at a fixed time — which is why the unmotivated Monday stops
mattering.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How to Destroy Your Potential in 90 Days
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How to Destroy Your Potential in 90 Days

Written as an instruction manual for failure: because self-improvement advice is saturated with what to add, the more useful exercise is inversion — specify precisely how potential is destroyed, and the anti-vision does the work that another optimisation tip cannot.

Key Concepts

Inversion as the method. Rather than asking how to make life better, ask how to make it worse — explicitly framed as exploiting loss aversion, since an anti-vision motivates where a vision does not. The reader is told outright not to follow the instructions.
Destroyer one — overstimulate the central nervous system. The CNS (brain and spinal cord) is the command centre handling cognitive load, attention regulation and stress. To exceed its capacity: loud music frequently, habitual doomscrolling, maximal information intake, and above all pick up your phone first thing in the morning. Yield: brain fog, a fragmented attention span, and emotional dysregulation from dopamine pumps and crashes.
Destroyer two — stay in the comfort zone, with the neuroscience made explicit. Comfortable, familiar pathways keep getting myelinated while no new ones are built; the brain is fed evidence that a behaviour is safe, and thereafter treats growth-directed discomfort as dangerous. The result is a nervous system rewired to crave the short term — “a subconscious ceiling to what you can achieve.”
“If you are not consciously growing, then you unconsciously decay. There is no in-between.”
Destroyer three — optimise for distraction via pleasure, i.e. impulsive egoistic hedonism, opened with Viktor Frankl: “when a person can’t find a deep sense of meaning, they distract themselves with pleasure.” Vices named specifically — smoking, drinking, drugs — with dependency reshaping personality and producing behaviour a rational version of the person would not choose.
Destroyer four — think in instant gratification. Days and weeks rather than years and decades produces shiny object syndrome: constant path-switching in expectation of immediate reward, and each switch resets the progress baseline to zero. Short-term thinking also installs scarcity — counting limited opportunities rather than future ones — which locks the nervous system into playing safe.
Destroyer five — please everyone. Never learning to say no is presented as the single most destructive habit: unnecessary hangouts, draining parties, low-value obligations, for people you neither like nor align with. Boundaries crumble, self-respect goes, and time owed to your own purpose is spent on approval from people whose appetite for it does not end.
The 90-day frame: research is cited for a habit becoming a permanent lifestyle change after ninety days — the reason the anti-vision has a deadline attached.
The closing move is rhetorical rather than instructional: having read this far is offered as evidence the reader is not the intended student.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How to Develop an Iron Mindset to Dominate
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How to Develop an Iron Mindset to Dominate

Genius Series Part IV. Michael Jordan’s accolades are the least interesting thing about him — the transferable part is a mentality that converted rejection into fuel and set a work-rate standard that dragged an entire team upward.

Key Concepts

Playing for the game rather than for what it pays. Jordan is noted becoming emotional simply describing his style, because it was his identity. Money, fame and status are conceded as valid motives; the argument is that intrinsic love of the work is what survives the cost.
The costs are itemised rather than glossed: bearing media pressure to maintain an image, ridiculing teammates who slacked (and receiving it back), and absorbing the physical damage of an aggressive style. “The average people would fall out of this path, intimidated by the cost.”
Failure as fuel — the founding instance. Cut from his high school varsity team for being too short, Jordan cried and it mattered to him; what separated him was converting the resentment into obsessive practice with the JV team, where he dropped multiple 40-point games. His own verdict is quoted: “the best thing that could happen to me was to get cut.”
The work-rate standard, stated as a ratio: if you ran two miles he ran four; if you did twelve reps he did twenty-four; if you shot 500 free throws he shot 1,000. The point is not the arithmetic but that this became the team’s baseline, on and off the court.
“I’ll see you tomorrow.” After the Bulls’ 1995 Eastern Conference semifinal elimination, Jordan went back to training rather than recovering — with the piece explicitly refusing to condemn the ordinary alternative (“we can’t judge people that would go these routes”).
Obligation to the audience as a driver of standard: if people spend their money and three hours to watch, they get spectacle. Explicitly linked to Topuria’s “I want to dominate, I want to maul people” from Part III, with the shared trait named as an insatiable drive for total domination.
Manufactured fuel. Jordan is described converting trivial slights — an opponent declining to greet him — into targeted motivation, remembering it and answering on the court. “That’s all I needed.” The greatness is framed as dominating the mental game as much as the physical one.
Recommends The Last Dance (Netflix, 10 episodes) as the primary source on the dynasty, and closes with the “Maybe It’s My Fault” commercial quoted in full — “failure gave me strength… my pain was my motivation” — which is the piece’s thesis in Jordan’s own words.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How to Develop Unwavering Confidence and Self-Belief
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How to Develop Unwavering Confidence and Self-Belief

Genius Series Part III. Ilia Topuria’s confidence is not bluster but a system — faith that outsources the outcome, first-principles mastery of each discipline separately, and self-belief acted on before the evidence exists.

Key Concepts

Faith as the load-bearing source. Topuria, a devout Orthodox Christian, is quoted: “I’m a God believer, and my mindset is, if he destroys my plans, it’s because maybe my plans could destroy me.” The generalisation offered is denomination-neutral — atheist, agnostic, Muslim, Buddhist, Taoist, or simply the universe — the mechanism being that placing the outcome outside yourself releases inner tension. The consequence: either you win or you learn, so failure is only a delay.
Humility as the asymmetry — Topuria credits victories to God and takes defeats as his own. Named as a separator of the 1% from the 99%.
Stated intention preceding the result. Before the Volkanovski title fight he told himself “God is with me… I will win in spectacular fashion”, then knocked Volkanovski out in the second round. His JRE formulation is quoted at length: two kinds of champion, those who prepare to win and those who prepare to dominate — “I prepare myself not to win because I already know that I’m gonna win.”
Conviction backed by follow-through. The piece is careful that this is not affirmation alone: “intentions don’t matter, actions do.” What makes Topuria the case study is that the promises get cashed.
First-principles training — he masters boxing, wrestling and jiu-jitsu as separate disciplines rather than training generic MMA, decomposing the problem into fundamentals before recombining them in camp. His line: “belts are earned in training” — the octagon is only where they are collected. Paired with meticulous opponent study: patterns, weaknesses, positioning, footwork.
Acting as though the result is already secured, with three documented instances: a *pre-*fight celebratory dinner with family and team the night before UFC 317 against Charles Oliveira, followed by the first-round finish he had explicitly predicted; and updating his Instagram bio to his future record before each fight — 15-0 for Volkanovski, 16-0 for Holloway, 17-0 for Oliveira, 18-0 pending against Gaethje.
“El Matador” — the bullfighter — and the rose left in the octagon after each dominant win, a Spanish bullfighting tradition, offered as evidence that the confidence coexists with class.
The author’s own application, stated with numbers: writing as someone who “already operates at a 10,000 subscriber caliber… it’s just that the statistics and metrics haven’t caught up yet” — at 78 subscribers at time of writing. An unusually falsifiable use of the principle being argued.
A contradiction worth recording. This piece predicts Topuria beats Gaethje; the same author’s rid-yourself-these-cognitive-biases-so later uses that exact fight — Topuria losing by TKO in round four — as the worked example of overconfidence bias. The corpus therefore contains its own correction, and the tension between “delusional optimism” and “stay close to objective reality” is one the author names but never fully resolves.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: A Different Take On Self Improvement
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
A Different Take On Self Improvement
Core Argument
The obsession with self-improvement has become its own kind of cage. Grind culture creates psychological damage, is neurologically misguided (brains need rest to consolidate), and produces people who are optimized for looking productive rather than being effective. Balance is a neurological requirement, not a soft concept.
Key Ideas
The Social Comparison Trap
For most of human history: 150-person comparison pool (tribe/village). Now: millions simultaneously. Your amygdala cannot distinguish between curated highlight reels and reality — it registers “everyone is ahead of me” as a real threat. This triggers the self-improvement addiction: you’re trying to resolve a threat your brain thinks is real, but isn’t.
The Grind Culture Problem

18-year-olds posting 4am alarm screenshots as status signals
Performative suffering: competing over who sleeps less, sacrifices more
Suffering ≠ progress. Many successful people work less than expected — they work smarter and delegate
If you’re optimizing for the appearance of productivity, you’ve already lost

Prefrontal Cortex Development
The brain isn’t fully developed until 25 — specifically the prefrontal cortex (decision-making). You’re not supposed to have your entire life planned at 20. Being lost is developmental, not failure.
The Hedonic Treadmill
Hit your goal → feel good for a week → set a new goal → repeat. Satisfaction never lasts because the brain adapts to new baselines. Successful people are often miserable precisely because they optimized for achievement without building satisfaction into the process.
Delayed Gratification Has a Limit
Self-control predicts success (marshmallow test, etc.) — but pathological deferral is the failure mode. If happiness is always conditional on future achievement, you’re building a prison. The brain adapts; the future reward never feels like enough.
The Neurological Case for Rest
Creativity and insight happen during downtime — the default mode network consolidates learning during rest states. Constant work mode prevents integration. Rest is not laziness; it’s required for the brain to perform.
Key Concepts

Hedonic-Treadmill — why achievement never satisfies
Social-Comparison — amygdala can’t distinguish curated highlights from reality
Grind-Culture — performative suffering as status signal
Prefrontal Cortex — not fully formed until 25
Delayed-Gratification — useful up to a point; pathological beyond it
Default-Mode-Network — rest state needed for consolidation and creativity
Amygdala — threat detection that misreads social comparison as danger

Connections to Other Sources

Standout Passages

“your brain wasn’t designed for infinite comparison. for most of human history, you compared yourself to maybe 150 people max.”


“neurologically, your brain needs downtime to consolidate learning. creativity happens in rest.”


“if you optimize humanity out of your life in pursuit of success, what the fuck was the point?”

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: Discard These Excuses Immediately Before You Severely Cap Your Potential
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Discard These Excuses Immediately Before You Severely Cap Your Potential

An excuse is not a one-off decision but a neural pathway being reinforced — repeat it enough and avoidance becomes as automatic as brushing your teeth, at which point the excuse manufactures the reality it claimed to describe.

Key Concepts

The mechanism, stated in neuroscience. Each excuse myelinates the connections that produced it, making them more automatic, more efficient and faster to fire. The endpoint is reflexive: discomfort appears, the excuse deploys before conscious thought. Crucially, excuses become self-fulfilling — false expectations generate the behaviour that makes them true.
Exceptions are conceded up front — sometimes you genuinely are tired, sometimes a system genuinely is unfair. The target is the excuse as default unconscious coping mechanism, not the excuse as occasional fact.
“I’m not ready yet” → ready isn’t a feeling, it’s a decision. The perfect moment is an illusion masking discomfort with uncertainty.
“It’s too risky” → uncertainty always contains opportunity in both directions. Losing money is data not to repeat; winning is a strategy to double down on.
“I’ll do it later”, against Naval: “if there’s something you want to do later, do it now. there is no ‘later.’” The excuse simply says: I will sacrifice the long term for the short term.
“I’m too tired” → the danger is being robbed of skin in the game, the experience needed for the next level. Counter by confrontation, not avoidance.
“It’s too late” → the bus-stop analogy: buses come all day, missing some is permissible, there is always a next one, and you only need one to change everything.
“What if it goes wrong?” → the piece is careful here, granting that Stoic negative visualisation and Munger’s inversion are legitimate versions of this thinking. The pathology is the constant version that produces anxious paralysis. The switch: ask “what if I succeed?”
“What if people judge me?” → judgement is opening holes in your own ship. “People judging you haven’t done what you’ve done, so why listen?”
“It’s not my fault” → victimhood robs you of accountability; mistakes get overlooked, and mistakes are the growth mechanism.
“Everyone’s ahead of me” → comparing level 1 to someone’s level 50 while their sleepless nights, self-doubt and ego deaths remain invisible. “Success always looks like nothing before it looks like everything.” The Substack instance: writers tying self-worth to engagement, crashing, and stopping.
“That’s just how things go for me” → the most structurally dangerous, because it is identity-based coping. Identity builds actions, not the other way around — internalise an identity of failure and behaviour follows it. Named as learned helplessness; the antidote is an internal locus of control.
“I’ll start when everything falls into place” → perfectionism, and a category error: you figure things out after you start, not before.
The three roots underneath all of them: an easy way out of discomfort, protection of the ego and the old identity, and the forfeit of accountability.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: Do You Actually Have Free Will?
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Do You Actually Have Free Will?

If the brain initiates a decision seconds before you are aware of making it, and
the subconscious outprocesses the conscious mind by five orders of magnitude, then
the self that experiences choosing may be explaining decisions rather than making
them.

Key Concepts


The Libet experiment. Participants on brain scanners were asked to move a hand
whenever they felt like it. The piece reports brain activity showing the decision
seven seconds before conscious awareness of wanting to move — the subconscious
deciding, the conscious mind taking credit.


The processing gap: roughly 40 bits per second conscious against 11
million subconscious. The subconscious runs breathing, heartbeat and digestion,
filters sensory input down to what awareness can carry, and selects emotional
reactions before you notice having them.


Programming laid down early. The subconscious is described as a recording
device running since birth — personality largely patterned before age seven,
political belief substantially inherited, career choice shaped by childhood
association. Attraction is the sharpest case: symmetry, pheromones, attachment
patterns and genetic markers cross-referenced in milliseconds, so by the time you
decide you like someone the background check has already returned, and the
conscious mind supplies a story for the feeling.


The conclusion, stated as a lean rather than a proof. With 97–98% of mental
activity subconscious and most of its programming installed before age seven, what
is experienced as free will may be post-hoc rationalisation.



“your conscious mind is basically the PR department for decisions already made.”

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: Don't Skip This (It'll Change How You See Success)
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Don’t Skip This (It’ll Change How You See Success)

Growth is exponential while expectation is linear, so the phase where real
accumulation happens produces no visible result — and that mismatch, not talent
or luck, is what makes people quit immediately before critical mass.

Key Concepts


The invisible growth phase. Every action stacks below the surface — posts,
emails, calls, reps — until accumulation crosses a threshold and becomes visible
at once. The bucket metaphor carries it: water drains as fast as you pour, then
you outpace the leak, then it fills, then it overflows. What outsiders read as a
lucky break is the overflow.


The expectation mismatch, given as arithmetic: hours 1–100 return nothing,
101–200 return a thousand, 201–300 return ten thousand. Identical effort,
exponentially different result, because skills, networks and reputation compound
rather than accrue.


Compounding is bidirectional. The same mechanism runs in reverse — small
negative actions accumulate the same way. Missing one workout or one post is
genuinely irrelevant; missing a hundred is not.


Nothing is random, is the conclusion drawn: overnight successes had years of
compounding nobody watched, and lucky breaks came from positioning nobody saw.



“your problem isn’t that you’re not talented enough or lucky enough. your problem is you’re not patient enough to let compounding work.”

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: dopamine-detox-failing
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Why Your Dopamine Detox Is Failing

Dopamine doesn’t disappear when you remove sources — it panics, then finds new pathways. “Detox” is the wrong framework; “redirect” is correct. Replace low-value dopamine sources with high-value ones; don’t create a void.

Key Concepts

Dopamine is an evolutionary survival mechanism — 10,000+ years of wiring to seek it; you can’t “detox” a system that kept your ancestors alive
Removing all sources causes withdrawal-like panic → the brain finds replacement sources (often worse) → “detox” fails
The correct framework is redirection: identify what needs the low-value source is filling (boredom, anxiety, social validation) and substitute a high-value source that fills the same need
Dopamine hierarchy: exercise, cold exposure, achievement, real social connection (high-value, build baseline) vs social media, porn, junk food (low-value, deplete baseline)
The void problem: people who try to quit cold turkey without replacing create an intolerable emptiness — the nervous system will fill it with whatever is most accessible
Permanent change requires building the high-value habits strong enough that low-value sources are no longer needed, not simply removing them

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: dopamine-superpower
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Your ‘Dopamine Problem’ Is Actually a Superpower

Dopamine is the hunt, not the reward — once you understand this, you stop trying to eliminate the wanting and start engineering pursuit into your work so the very process of doing generates the motivation to continue.

Key Concepts

Dopamine = pursuit, not reward: spike happens during the chase, crashes on arrival — “dopamine problem” is actually the engine of ambition misdirected
Rich people aren’t happier despite achieving more — because achievement delivers no dopamine; the pursuit did
Reframe: if dopamine is the hunt, structure your work as a series of hunts — never arrive completely; always have the next challenge visible
This is the superpower: a person who can engineer continuous pursuit into their work has an intrinsic motivation engine that never runs dry
Applied: gamification of goals (milestones, leveling up, challenges just above current ability), “process over outcome” reframe, avoiding the post-achievement crash by immediately pivoting to the next hunt
Connects to the Dopaminergic-System deep dive and the one-ability-delayed-gratification piece

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: dopaminergic-system-breakdown
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Dopaminergic System: The Complete Neuroscience Breakdown

Dopamine is not the pleasure chemical but the wanting chemical — it encodes
the gap between what was expected and what arrived, fires during pursuit rather
than consumption, and runs an economy in which every artificial peak is borrowed
from the baseline that makes ordinary life feel worth doing.

The argument
The piece is positioned against the “dopamine detox” genre, which it treats as
confidently wrong rather than merely simplified: you cannot reset dopamine in
twenty-four hours, because that is not how the neurobiology works. Its own stated
reading list is unusually specific for this corpus — Sapolsky’s Behave twice for
the reward chapters, Anna Lembke’s Dopamine Nation, David Burns’s Feeling Good
for the clinical angle, and a paid neuroscience course for the pathway mechanisms.
Key Concepts


Four pathways, not one substance. Most talk about “dopamine” means the
mesolimbic pathway (ventral tegmental area → nucleus accumbens) without
knowing it: reward prediction, craving, pursuit, and the system that drugs,
feeds and pornography hijack. The mesocortical (VTA → prefrontal cortex)
governs motivation, planning, focus and delayed gratification — impaired
signalling here is offered as the basis of ADHD. The nigrostriatal
(substantia nigra → striatum) encodes habit and movement, and is the pathway
that degenerates in Parkinson’s. The tuberoinfundibular (hypothalamus →
pituitary) regulates prolactin and impulse control.


Wanting, not liking. Pleasure is attributed to serotonin and opioids;
dopamine fires during pursuit and drops on consumption. Three worked cases:
the notification seen (spike) then opened (drop); food smelled then eaten
(dopamine falls, opioids and serotonin rise); the goal chased then achieved.
The gambler’s peak is while the reels spin, not at the result — which is why
gambling addicts whether it pays out or not, and why achievement so often
registers as empty.


Reward prediction error. Dopamine encodes the difference between expected
and actual. Expected nothing and got something good → large spike, tagged
valuable. Expected good and got nothing → crash, tagged avoid. Expected good and
got good → small spike. This is the brain continuously updating a model of which
actions produce which outcomes, and it runs below awareness: “you don’t decide
to want something. your dopaminergic system decides for you based on past
prediction errors, then makes you feel like you want it.”


The baseline/peak economy. Baseline is default motivation and drive; peaks
sit above it. The claim that does the work: peaks are borrowed from baseline,
because the brain holds the average stable. Chronic spiking depletes baseline
until nothing feels worth doing — anhedonia, low motivation, effortfulness. This
is why an addict escalates: not chasing the high, but trying to reach baseline.
The piece insists the mechanism is identical for the non-addict scrolling for
hours, differing only in increment size. It names chronic depletion as the
neuroscience underneath burnout, and the post-peak dip as dopamine debt.


Your goals are not chosen freely. A goal only feels worth pursuing if the
system predicts a positive prediction error from it. Where it predicts effort
exceeding reward, the goal feels pointless and cannot be forced. The system can
also be trained on bad data: if scrolling has supplied more prediction errors
than building, the brain concludes that is where value lives — building is slow
with delayed reward and a weak signal, scrolling is immediate with constant
novelty. The resulting preference is not laziness but programming. Identity is
described as accreting the same way: rewarded behaviours are encoded as who you
are, public failure as avoid this.


Attention is downstream of dopamine. Prefrontal executive function runs on
mesocortical dopamine. Too low and focus collapses, distractions win, thoughts
scatter, immediate gratification dominates — a state anyone can reach by
depletion without having ADHD. Flow is presented as a dopaminergic phenomenon
specifically: dopamine and norepinephrine optimally elevated in the prefrontal
cortex, too low being unfocused and too high being anxious and scattered. It
cannot be willed — only the conditions can be arranged, which means protecting
baseline.


Why willpower loses to habit. Habits encode through the nigrostriatal
pathway into the basal ganglia on a cue → craving → response → reward loop. In
learning, dopamine spikes on the reward; once established, it shifts to the
cue and fires before the behaviour happens. So resisting a habit means
resisting an automatic neurochemical event, not a decision — which is why
willpower fails. Only two exits are offered: remove the cue, or expose yourself
to it repeatedly without the reward until the prediction is revised, which takes
dozens to hundreds of repetitions.


Environment design over discipline. Every reward-associated cue in a room is
firing this loop — the phone on the desk, the open laptop, visible snacks — so
willpower is being asked to resist dozens of signals at once while the work
itself supplies a weaker one. The prescription is symmetrical: strip cues for
what you don’t want, make cues for what you do want visible.


What it prescribes
Restoration, explicitly not detox, and on a scale of weeks rather than days:
reduce artificial spikes, regular movement (which raises baseline rather than
producing peaks), cold exposure, adequate sleep, morning sunlight, and real
non-digital social connection. The behavioural half is to protect baseline above
everything, build habits through consistent small wins rather than large ones
because the brain learns by repetition rather than intensity, keep goals oriented
to process so dopamine stays elevated instead of crashing on completion, pursue
voluntary discomfort so the brain learns that difficulty pays, and track which
inputs spike and which deplete.

“Once you control your dopamine, you control your behavior. once you control your behavior, you control your life.”

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: emotional-control-vs-intelligence
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Why Emotional Control Is More Valuable Than Intelligence

Intelligence only becomes strategically useful when executive control can place a pause between feeling and action—and can choose how much knowledge to display in a social setting.

Key Concepts
Control is not absence of emotion. The essay contrasts an immediate “I feel, therefore I do” path with the ability to feel an impulse and choose a response. It assigns planning, working memory, inhibition, and social calibration to the Prefrontal-Cortex, with the Amygdala standing in for fast emotional signalling. That simple two-part picture is useful as a metaphor, but real regulation is distributed across interacting systems; the prefrontal cortex does not single-handedly suppress every emotion.
Intelligence needs a deployment policy. Knowing an answer and showing that one knows it are separate decisions. The essay’s “play the fool” maxim becomes strategic-understatement: withholding a correction or asking another person to explain can reduce perceived threat, preserve information asymmetry, and reveal how they reason. The useful mechanism is control over disclosure, not pretending to lack capacity in every setting.
Delayed response creates options. The marshmallow study, the case of Phineas Gage, and a stimulus-response quotation are used to argue that inhibition protects long-term goals from immediate impulses. These examples do not prove the essay’s stronger hierarchy in which emotional control is universally more valuable than intelligence. Later reassessments complicate the marshmallow study’s causal interpretation, and Gage’s outcome cannot be compressed to “intelligence intact, regulation destroyed.”
Practice is framed as training. Meditation, long-form reading, silence, exercise, fasting, cold exposure, and deliberate withholding are presented as exercises in tolerating an impulse without obeying it. The shared principle is rehearsal of the pause, not a demonstrated equivalence among the practices. The essay’s claim that social media is “destroying” prefrontal function also exceeds what it cites; notification-driven reactivity is not the same as acquired brain injury.
Boundaries
Emotional control can become suppression, strategic understatement can become deception, and silence can protect bad information when correction matters. The source does not establish that high intelligence reliably threatens others or that people who disclose emotion have weak executive function. Its defensible insight is narrower: Emotional-Intelligence includes deciding when and how to express a reaction, and this decision can matter as much as the reaction’s content.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How To Enhance Your Immune System To Another Level
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How To Enhance Your Immune System To Another Level

Two people breathing the same air get different outcomes, and the difference is
not luck but what was done to the immune system in the preceding weeks — so the
model is not a single magic intervention but stacked layers, none of which is
sufficient alone.

The argument
The framing observation is three colleagues falling ill in one week in the same
office, same air, same virus, while the author did not. The claim drawn is that
getting sick only feels random.
The structural statistic is that 93% of time is spent indoors — 86% inside
buildings, 6–7% inside vehicles — against an immune system that evolved in
sunlight, fresh air, movement and a real day/night rhythm. The essay is pointed
about the incentives: nobody profits from telling you that fifteen minutes of
sunlight might outperform half the pharmacy shelf.
Two organising models are given. NEWSTART — nutrition, exercise, water,
sunlight, temperance, air, rest, trust — as the frame physicians use, with the
observation that every intervention shown to move immune performance maps onto one
of those pillars. And the swiss cheese model: every layer has holes, but stack
enough and nothing gets a clear path through.
Key Concepts


Sunlight, beyond vitamin D. The part the essay rates most interesting is
infrared: 52% of solar energy sits in that spectrum, long-wavelength photons
that pass through clothing and skin and scatter up to 8cm into tissue.
Mitochondria absorb it and produce intracellular melatonin — distinct from
pineal melatonin, made and used on site, never entering the bloodstream, and
reportedly at concentrations up to 20× higher than the pineal gland releases.
Since melatonin is a powerful antioxidant, this mops up the free radicals and
reactive oxygen species that energy production generates, on site. The link to
immunity is via mitochondrial dysfunction, named as sitting at the root of the
major chronic diseases and of compromised immune function alike.


The epidemiology cited. A Swedish cohort of roughly 30,000 women followed for
20 years found the highest sun exposure associated with lower all-cause,
cardiovascular and cancer mortality, in a dose-response curve — and the effect
large enough that high-sun smokers carried roughly the mortality risk of non-smokers
who avoided sun. A Harvard study is cited for sunlight protecting against
influenza, and a European analysis of the autumn COVID surge for the finding that
temperature and humidity showed no correlation while latitude correlated
perfectly, the surge dates tracking the sun’s descent from Finland to Greece.


Fever as a mechanism, not a symptom. Interferon is described as the immune
system’s broadest antiviral weapon, effective across strains and acting before
adaptive immunity engages — important enough that viruses evolve dedicated
countermeasures, with SARS-CoV-2’s MAC1 gene named as one. Heating lymphocytes to
38°C, one degree above normal, sharply increases interferon secretion across
multiple pathways. Hence the caution against reflexively suppressing every fever.
The historical comparison offered: 1918 sanitariums using hydrotherapy, sunlight
and fresh air reported one sixth the rate of progression to pneumonia against
army hospitals on conventional treatment.


Heat then cold. Around 20 minutes of sauna, hot bath or hot shower to raise
core temperature and trigger interferon, followed where possible by cold — which
produces demargination, white blood cells attached to vessel walls being knocked
into circulation by cold-induced vasoconstriction. Heat to trigger the response,
cold to mobilise.


NAC, distinguished from supplements the essay dismisses as marketed placebo.
A multi-centre double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 600mg twice daily across a
flu season did not reduce infection count but substantially reduced symptom
severity, most notably runny nose and sore throat. Two mechanisms: mucus is
thickened by disulfide bonds, which NAC breaks, clearing airways; and NAC
replenishes glutathione against the oxidative stress infection amplifies. Protocol
given as seasonal rather than continuous — no more than three months at a stretch —
with the practical warning that taking it at night produces a running nose as it
works.


Zinc, at 40mg elemental — the essay flags that labels show compound weight
rather than elemental content, and that long-term use warrants monitoring copper,
which higher doses deplete.


Forest air. Japanese research walked Tokyo executives through hinoki cypress
forests for three days and measured significant gains in innate immune markers,
specifically chromogranin A, persisting seven days afterwards. The follow-up
infused a Tokyo hotel room with phytoncides — the compounds trees emit — and
produced similar results, isolating something airborne as the active agent. The one
difference was cortisol, lower when actually walking outside, adding a second
pathway since chronic cortisol suppresses immunity. The essay’s conclusion resists
reductionism: sometimes the environment is the medicine.


Sleep, described as causal rather than nuanced. Participants exposed to
rhinovirus after monitored sleep were 4.2× more likely to catch it on under six
hours than on seven or more; antibody response to vaccination is markedly better
with adequate sleep; and poor sleep raises cortisol, which suppresses immunity,
compounding the cycle. Stated flatly: no supplement stack compensates for chronic
sleep deprivation.



“you’re not trying to be invincible. you’re trying to make sure that when the virus… tries to set up camp in your body, it finds conditions that make survival very difficult.”

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How Your Environment Psychologically Shapes Your Identity
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How Your Environment Psychologically Shapes Your Identity

Ixcarus argues that identity is partly context-dependent: rooms, objects, sensory
cues, routes, and social groups repeatedly call up different behavioral defaults.
The practical move is to reverse the direction—choose a desired identity, then
construct conditions that make its behavior easier and its competitors harder.

Context selects the available self
People commonly act differently at work, at a parent’s home, at the gym, or with
different friends. The essay treats this not as fakery but as context-dependent
behavior. To save the cost of conscious choice, the brain associates each setting
with a default pattern. Light, color, temperature, smell, sound, furniture, and
ceiling height are presented as inputs that can shift focus, creativity, abstraction,
or detail orientation without becoming the object of attention.
Repeated cues stabilize these modes. A desk can become an entry signal for work;
a bedroom repeatedly paired with a phone can become an entry signal for distraction.
Changing cities is the extreme version: many physical cues, social norms, routes,
and reference points disappear at once, forcing broad recalibration.
Other people set the baseline
The social environment shapes more than mood. Ixcarus invokes mirror neurons to
describe behavioral simulation—speech, posture, energy, habits, and values are
rehearsed while they are observed. Social proof supplies a second mechanism: the
group’s repeated behavior becomes the reference point for what counts as normal,
after which the brain stops treating it as a question.
This connects environment to Identity-Setpoint. A sixty-hour workweek, chronic
complaint, physical neglect, or ambitious building can each become ordinary when it
is the surrounding group’s ordinary. The source leaves open how much stable “core
self” remains apart from these context-selected versions, but treats their
malleability as leverage for change.
Design backward from identity
The environmental-design rule is to start with the person and behavior wanted,
then alter friction and cues. Put the book closer than the screen, remove food that
should require effort to obtain, choose a gym on the route home, keep equipment
ready, remove the phone from the work room, or work near people whose behavior
should become normal. The proposed high-leverage trio is where one sleeps, where
one works, and whom one spends time with.
Optimization has a limit. When a setting is saturated with cues and people pulling
toward the old pattern, leaving may be more realistic than asking finite willpower
to oppose continuous conditioning. Either way, the environment already exerts an
influence; design means choosing more of that influence deliberately.
Connects to: Subconscious-Programming (automatic cue-response patterns),
Neuroplasticity (repetition strengthens what the setting keeps activating), and
deep-work (a protected context for one cognitive mode).

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: Everyone is Selfish (Including You)
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Everyone is Selfish (Including You)
Core Argument
Universal selfishness is not a character flaw — it’s human nature. Every action, including ostensibly altruistic ones, serves the ego. Recognizing this lets you use it strategically: motivate others through self-interest, protect yourself from manipulation, and channel your own ego productively.
The Uncomfortable Truth
Every seemingly selfless act has an ego component:

Volunteering → wanting to feel like a good person
Donating to charity → social credit and tax deduction
Helping a friend move → building a favour balance
Sharing a restaurant recommendation → feeling smart and expert

Even being humble is ego — you’ve made being humble your identity. It’s ego all the way down.
Ego in Social Situations

At parties: Everyone’s waiting for their turn to speak. Even the quiet ones are performing — their performance is “I’m above shallow conversation.” Still ego.
At work: The always-helpful coworker wants to be seen as indispensable. The generous friend who picks up the check wants control and to display wealth.
On social media: “Hoping this helps someone” = wanting likes, comments, validation.

The Strategic Implications
How to Use This Knowledge

Motivate people through self-interest — “this will make you look good” beats “it’s the right thing to do”
Make people feel important — ask for their advice, compliment expertise, let them teach you; their ego gets fed, you get what you want
Protect yourself from manipulation — when someone makes you feel special/chosen, ask: what do they want from me?
Channel your own ego productively — want to feel superior? become actually superior at something valuable

The Warning
The people who pretend they don’t have egos are the most dangerous. They’re playing the ego game on expert mode while convincing you they’re not playing at all.

“the moment you think you’re above ego — that’s when it has complete control over you.”

Key Concepts

Universal-Selfishness — every action serves the ego in some way
Ego — human nature, not character flaw; driver of all social behaviour
Ego-Games — the social dynamics of ego-serving behaviour; use strategically
Fake Altruism — selfless-looking acts with ego motivations underneath

Connections to Other Sources

Standout Passages

“everyone has this voice. everyone. that friend telling you about their promotion? they’re not sharing because they’re excited. they’re sharing because they want to feel superior.”


“use your ego as fuel, not as a weapon.”

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: Everywhere at the End of Time: The Scariest Album Ever Created
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Everywhere at the End of Time: The Scariest Album Ever Created

Leyland Kirby’s six-and-a-half-hour album works as a functional model of Alzheimer’s rather than a piece about it — the audio degrades on the same schedule the disease does — and the piece reads the album’s structure against the actual neuropathology to argue that experiencing the decline from inside is what makes the case for protecting the brain land at all.

Carries the author’s own listening warning: do not attempt the whole album in one sitting if you are not in a stable headspace. He reports being unable to sleep after his first listen in 2021 and stopping at stage four.
Key Concepts

What the disease does structurally. Alzheimer’s is named as the seventh leading cause of death worldwide and the most common form of dementia, with age the highest risk factor and onset primarily above 65. On MRI it shows atrophy of the cerebral cortex (frontal, parietal, occipital, temporal), hippocampal atrophy — the region for forming new memories, learning, and spatial awareness — and ventricular expansion, the dilation of cerebrospinal-fluid spaces that is a passive consequence of tissue loss and serves as a clinical progression marker. Compared to CTE brains, which atrophy similarly from repeated blunt-force trauma. There is no cure.
What it does microscopically. Two mechanisms. Amyloid-beta plaques: Aβ42 overproduces, clumps into oligomers, and those clump into plaques that cannot be dissolved, sitting between neurons, disrupting communication and causing inflammation and cell damage. Tau tangles: tau normally transports nutrients inside the neuron and requires a specific structure to do so; misfolding collapses that function and accumulates into neurofibrillary tangles that damage the neuron’s inner skeleton. Both together severely impair neurogenesis and neuroplasticity.
The unrecognisable-image demonstration. The reader is shown a photograph in which nothing is coherent enough to name — the mind fills blanks because “our minds are expectation machines” — as a direct analogue for how late-stage patients experience the world: confusion without any recoverable referent.
The Caretaker. Leyland James Kirby, who works with memory and its deterioration by sampling and manipulating pre-WWII ballroom pop, and was influenced by the haunted ballroom of The Shining. The persona’s purpose was “killing the caretaker” — walking a character through six stages of dementia so listeners feel the decline. Motivated partly by a grandfather who suffered dementia following strokes, and aimed at building empathy for patients and their families.
The six stages as structure. The album runs alphanumerically (A–B, C–D, E–F, then G/H/I/J, K–N, O–R), each stage carrying Kirby’s own official description. Stage 1 is “most like a beautiful daydream” — lucid ballroom music with minor static. Stage 2 is self-realisation and denial, with a lower mood and titles like a losing battle is raging and surrendering to despair. Stage 3 holds the last coherent memories before the post-awareness stages; E3 – Hidden Sea Buried Deep loops the easiest piano phrase roughly nine times because the rest of the song is gone. Stage 4 is where serenity gives way to confusion, entanglement, and rupture. Stage 5 is the most aggressive — M1 – Synapse Retrogenesis names retrogenesis, degeneration that reverses the order of normal developmental acquisition, a return to childhood. Stage 6 is “without description.”
The recurring track as the disease’s signature. A1 – It’s just a burning memory returns throughout the album, degrading each time — slower and more somber at C3, more distant and static-laden at E2. The piece reads the accumulating static as neurons undergoing apoptosis.
The “hell sirens.” In H1 – post awareness confusions, warped horn samples break through the static: low, melancholic, dark, and recurring in later stages. Read as war sirens, as a panic attack, or as sundowning — the increased confusion, agitation, and anxiety that peaks in late afternoon or early evening in dementia patients, triggered by a disrupted internal clock and low lighting.
Terminal lucidity. The rare phenomenon in which severely impaired individuals regain clear thinking, memory, and communication shortly before death — humming a favourite song, holding a full conversation and remembering names, walking around energetically. Neuroscience has not explained it. The hypotheses given: that dementia inhibits rather than permanently destroys neural structures; that a massive end-of-life neurotransmitter release or a drop in inhibitory activity reconnects dormant circuits; that the blood-brain barrier breaks down and releases blocked chemical reserves. The album’s last five minutes, in R1, are a phantom choir with no static, no distortion, no drone — terminal lucidity rendered — cutting to silence for the Caretaker’s death.
Aphasia in the artwork. Ivan Seal’s covers grow more abstract by stage, and the cover titles decay into invented words like giltsholder — deliberate, representing aphasia, the “word salad” stage where patients know what they want to say and cannot find it. The final cover’s name carries the prefix necro-; the image is a blank canvas whose reverse you can never see, read as the complete absence of memory.
William Utermohlen as the same decline in paint. Diagnosed in 1995 at 62 after memory loss from 1991, he continued painting self-portraits at a nurse’s suggestion as a record of the disease. He lost the ability to paint in 2000, made his final drawings in 2002, and died in 2007. The 2001 self-portrait Erased Head I has no colour and barely a facial feature — the loss of self made visible.
The countermeasures, stated as the article’s point. Sleep — 6–8 hours; deprivation accelerates brain ageing and promotes accumulation of the same beta-amyloid and tau proteins, and the glymphatic system clears metabolic waste during sleep. Movement — walking, running, or lifting promotes cerebral blood flow, lowers cortisol and inflammation, and secretes BDNF, which supports neuron survival and growth and underwrites neuroplasticity and myelination. Diet — whole foods, omega-3s, antioxidants, magnesium and B-vitamins; avoid processed sugar, seed oils, and inflammatory foods. Cognitive load — read voraciously and play games that demand pattern recognition, strategy, and prediction (chess, sudoku, mahjong), since the path of least resistance costs unused synapses and compounds negatively. And time with people: “understand that time is finite, but unconditional love and memories are not.”

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: The Execution Dilemma
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
The Execution Dilemma

Confidence and clarity are outputs of action rather than prerequisites for it, so waiting to feel ready is not preparation — it is the mechanism of stagnation.

Key Concepts

Analysis paralysis — the brain, overwhelmed by decision load, simulates outcomes instead of choosing between them. The cost is not only the forgone move: prolonged indecision converts into anxiety, which raises the bar for acting later.
The fears underneath it are ordinary and named — making the wrong choice, being judged, rejection, consequences “if it doesn’t go your way” — and bite hardest exactly where stakes are personal: a high-stakes project, a creative idea that matters, the next phase of a life.
“The cold water won’t get any warmer if you jump late.” Hesitation compounds rather than decays; delay makes the jump harder, not easier.
The opportunity cost of hesitation is specific — the confidence, progress and clarity the attempt itself would have produced — compounded by the chance that the opportunity does not recur.
Clarity and confidence succeed choice, never precede it. Bold decisions are the input; the felt readiness people wait for is the output.
Perfect conditions are an illusion that keeps you stagnant. The test is executing in the rain, on under six hours of sleep, with the morning routine already broken — presented as the separator between mediocre and exceptional.
The gap between current and desired reality is only a set of actions — one decision, one opportunity, one conversation — which makes consistency, not intensity, the operative variable.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: existential-crisis-consciousness
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Warning: This Post Will Give You an Existential Crisis

The hard problem of consciousness — science can map every neuron but cannot explain where subjective experience comes from. “You” cannot be found in the brain. This is either the most terrifying or most liberating realization available to a human being.

Key Concepts

Hard problem of consciousness (David Chalmers): science can explain neural correlates of experience but cannot explain why there is a subjective “what it’s like” at all
No single brain region contains consciousness — it seems to emerge from the whole system, but the mechanism is unknown
The question: how do unconscious neurons become conscious? At what point does a collection of cells become “you”?
The self as illusion: the “you” experiencing this moment cannot be located — it emerges from the system but is not any particular part of it
This is either existentially destabilizing OR liberating: if “you” are not a fixed thing, you are not stuck as the current version

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How To Fall In Love With The Grind
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How To Fall In Love With The Grind

Ritual, visible progress, and identity framing can change what beginning work predicts, but making rest feel wrong is a warning sign—not proof that effort has become a healthy reward.

From avoidance to approach
The author describes an earlier association in which opening a laptop predicted distance from the desired outcome, discomfort, and several hours of avoidance. He then deliberately changed the setting and interpretation: the same coffee, music, workspace, and early schedule became cues for “building”; tracked tasks made movement visible; repetitive work was linked to a future identity rather than only an external payoff.
process-reward-association captures the reusable mechanism. A cue acquires motivational meaning through repeated pairing with an activity and its consequences. Ritual reduces the number of decisions required to begin, progress records make delayed gains perceptible, and identity language supplies a reason for otherwise boring repetitions. The article’s “romanticization” is an attentional and narrative layer around those behaviours.
What the dopamine story cannot establish
The source describes the brain as learning to release dopamine when work begins and says the association becomes addictive. It offers personal experience, not measurements. Dopamine participates in learning and motivation, but a craving for laptop light cannot be attributed to a measured dopaminergic change here; nor is the relation shown to be Myelination. RAS language about repeatedly signalling importance is likewise a metaphorical extension, not a demonstrated causal pathway in the essay.
The useful behavioural contrast is work predicting progress rather than only pain, while avoidance stops being the only immediate relief. That shift can occur without claiming that the brain “cannot tell the difference” between mythology and reality.
Boundary: process attachment versus compulsion
The essay treats 2 a.m. work, 5 a.m. blue light, restless weekends, and days off feeling wrong as status or evidence of commitment. Those can also describe sleep loss, anxiety, or compulsive productivity. Grind-Culture becomes hazardous when suffering itself is the metric and recovery is interpreted as failure.
A bounded practice keeps the useful elements—consistent cue, pleasant workspace, visible progress, and process identity—while measuring results, protecting sleep and rest, and permitting the ritual to stop. Loving a process should expand sustainable action, not make non-work intolerable.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: How To Find Peace In Struggle
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
How To Find Peace In Struggle

Through Camus’s reading of Sisyphus-Myth, ixcarus locates a remaining freedom
inside an unchosen constraint: the boulder may return, but the stance and next push
are not fully specified by it. This becomes response-within-constraint.

The myth supplies maximal repetition without final completion. Waiting for the
boulder to remain at the summit makes peace depend on an outcome the punishment
forbids. The essay instead places meaning in engagement
with the climb. The gods control the task; Sisyphus’s conscious relation to it is
his rebellion.
Applied outside the myth, a “boulder” is a recurring demand, limitation, or problem.
Naming a response within it can preserve agency when eliminating the condition is
not immediately possible. That is different from claiming every struggle is good,
chosen, or educational.
The essay sometimes treats struggle as strength training and says the boulder is
not a curse. A bounded reading distinguishes unavoidable difficulty from avoidable
harm. Acceptance of the present constraint does not require staying in abuse,
refusing help, romanticising deprivation, or abandoning attempts to change the
environment. One can work on removal and still choose the next response while the
condition remains.
The source’s “peace” is therefore not pleasure in suffering. It is the end of making
all present action conditional on final resolution. Meaning can occur during the
push even when completion remains desirable.

sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.title: Five Belief Systems You Need to Remove to Become Greater
sections/psychology-neuroscience-self-ma.content:
Five Belief Systems You Need to Remove to Become Greater

Complacency is installed, not chosen — five inherited beliefs run as subconscious programs from childhood, and removing them is subtraction work that awareness starts but only repeated evidence completes.

Key Concepts

The timescale is stated honestly: recognising a belief takes a day; genuinely switching it takes weeks, months or a year, because new thought patterns have to be myelinated and old ones pruned. Awareness is the necessary first step and explicitly not the sufficient one — “it requires evidence to fully rewire your subconscious mind, not just knowledge.”
Learned helplessness is named as the state that makes the whole project look impossible: believing life is fixed and outcomes are outside one’s control.
Belief one — “I have time.” Reframed with a countable unit: roughly 75 winters, 75 summers, 75 springs, 75 falls. “I’ll do it tomorrow” is legitimate for recovery and corrosive as a response to resistance, because each deferral trades long-term position for short-term comfort.
Belief two — discomfort means change course. Doing so produces shiny object syndrome: constant strategy-switching that resets progress to zero. The correction is to sit with discomfort rather than act on it, since growth is located on its far side and the comfort zone contains none.
Belief three — victim mentality, opened with Tom Bilyeu: “victimhood is an excuse to not try. and if you don’t try, you can’t win.” Described as self-fulfilling and as a theft of accountability, with the ego stepping in to defend the identity doing the holding back. “Life happens from you, not to you.” Explicitly identified as the Stoic dichotomy of control.
Belief four — more is better. Traced to industrial-revolution factory measurement, where more hours meant more production meant more profit, and argued obsolete now that inputs and outputs are non-linear. The law of diminishing returns applies to life: four hours of focused, recovered deep work outperforms twelve fragmented burnt-out ones. Twelve-plus-hour days are called performance and bragging rights past the point of optimal function. “Simplification always scales; anything further is just diminishing returns.”
Belief five — never disappoint anyone, via Aesop: “if you try to please all, you please none.” Others’ perceptions are outside your control, so letting them steer costs agency; the ship analogy — a ship does not open holes to let water in. Approval-seeking is framed as keeping the nervous system in survival mode. “Disappoint people if it means improving. The ones aligned with you will respect you for it.”
